title: Mirendil raises $1B in funding to speed up AI model development
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 16:22 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026

Mirendil raises $1B in funding to speed up AI model development

Mirendil Inc., a provider of software that speeds up artificial intelligence development, has raised $1 billion in early-stage funding.

The startup stated on Thursday that Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital jointly led the Series A investment. They were joined by more than a half-dozen others including Google LLC.

Mirendil was launched last year by two former Google DeepMind and Anthropic PBC researchers. Chief Executive Officer Behnam Neyshabur is a co-inventor of SAM , a popular algorithm that makes AI models better at tasks they were not specifically trained to perform. Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pretraining projects. Pretraining is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow.

Mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company says that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents.

Large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically.

Earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil says that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete.

The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality.

The LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the company unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10

summary.tldr:
Mirendil Inc., a startup focused on accelerating AI model development, has secured $1 billion in Series A funding led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital, with participation from Google and others. Founded last year by former Google DeepMind and Anthropic researchers Behnam Neyshabur (CEO) and Harsh Mehta (CTO), the company aims to automate the AI training lifecycle. Neyshabur is known for co-inventing the SAM algorithm, while Mehta brings expertise in pretraining workflows.

The company’s core platform, Lor, utilizes fleets of hundreds of AI agents to automate model training, infrastructure setup, data collection, and error correction. Mirendil demonstrated the platform's efficacy by having a single researcher build 'Mirendil-Base,' a coding-focused LLM, in 3.5 months for $10 million. The company claims agents wrote over 99% of the code for this model. Mirendil-Base serves as the foundation for 'Fern,' a specialized coding model capable of processing 10 million input tokens per prompt—reportedly 10 times the capacity of Claude Opus 5.5—equivalent to 500,000 lines of code.

Fern is built on a version of Mirendil-Base containing 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Mirendil has also previewed larger iterations of the base model, ranging from 500 billion to 10 trillion parameters, which the company intends to leverage for future, more capable LLM development.
takeaways: **Funding:** Mirendil raised $1 billion in Series A funding led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital.

**Agentic Workflow:** The Lor platform uses hundreds of AI agents to automate infrastructure, training algorithms, and data refinement, reportedly writing >99% of the code for the Mirendil-Base model.
**Model Performance:** The Fern coding model supports a 10 million token context window, claimed to be 10x the capacity of Claude Opus 5.5.
**Model Scaling:** Mirendil-Base currently exists in 100B–500B parameter versions, with larger variants up to 10 trillion parameters in development.
**Efficiency Benchmark:** A single researcher used Mirendil's automation to build a competitive coding LLM in 3.5 months for $10 million.

title: Advancing science & engineering with Antigravity’s /teamwork
author: Google AI Research Blog
contentSnippet:
November 13, 2026 Vahab Mirrokni, Google Fellow and VP, Google Research

We share recent results from Antigravity’s /teamwork multiagent systems, which enhance human-AI collaborations to solve open problems across mathematics, chemistry, systems software, and ML engineering. All of this work is done in collaboration with human experts, and we are making these tools available externally.

Over the past several weeks, teams across Google and academic partner institutions have tackled open problems in math, science, and complex systems engineering that had remained open for years. Using Gemini 4 Argon , Gemini 4 Carbon , Gemini 4 Hydrogen and multi-agent workflows such as Antigravity’s /teamwork (building on various Gemini models), these collaborations have produced new innovations across information theory, formal verifications, molecular structure discoveries, and kernel optimization, along with several production infrastructure gains at Google. We are making these agentic tools available in Antigravity’s /teamwork (alongside /boost and other agents) so that researchers and developers can apply them to their own work.

Frontier research and systems engineering require navigating vast literature, building custom computational pipelines, testing against physical measurements, and verifying every step. Progress comes from an interactive discovery loop where researchers frame questions and define the theoretical or physical constraints, while long-horizon agents write custom solvers, explore large search spaces, test candidate designs, and check long chains of logic.

Scaling long-horizon reasoning

Two limits of current language models motivate /teamwork's design . First, model generation can be unpredictable, leaving a gap between a single attempt and finding the correct answer. The system bridges this gap by pairing parallel exploration with dedicated falsifiers (e.g., the Lean 4 proof checker, unmodified software test suites, execution simulators, web search, or hardware counters) to automatically verify which candidate solutions work.

Second, AI models often lose track of details over multi-day tasks because attention disperses across growing context windows. To prevent this, /teamwork partitions context by construction: each specialized agent receives only the exact files and tools it needs for a specific step. summary.tldr:
Google Research has unveiled /teamwork, a multi-agent system designed to facilitate human-AI collaboration on complex open problems in mathematics, science, and systems engineering. The platform leverages the Gemini 4 model family—specifically Argon, Carbon, and Hydrogen—to execute long-horizon reasoning tasks. By utilizing specialized agentic harnesses like 'Stellar Colosseum' and '/boost,' the system automates the discovery loop by pairing parallel model exploration with external falsifiers, such as the Lean 4 proof checker, software test suites, and hardware counters. This architecture addresses model unpredictability and context degradation by partitioning tasks into specialized, isolated contexts where coordinators hand off work to fresh successor agents.

In recent applications, /teamwork has achieved significant breakthroughs, including the formal proof of the 2013 Courtade–Kumar conjecture in information theory, which involved generating 50 million lines of Lean 4 code. Other notable results include resolving a 2014 open question in quantum computing regarding n-bit Boolean functions, achieving near-optimal sample bounds for adaptive data analysis, and developing a deterministic algorithm for Boolean matrix multiplication that surpasses the cubic-time barrier. The system also produced a C implementation for n-bit integer multiplication that matches the GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library (GMP) bit-for-bit up to a billion bits. These tools are being integrated into the Antigravity platform for external researcher and developer access.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** Utilizes Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon, and Hydrogen models within a multi-agent framework that partitions context to prevent attention dispersion over long-horizon tasks.
**Verification Methodology:** Employs dedicated falsifiers including Lean 4 for formal proof verification, unmodified software test suites, and execution simulators to validate candidate solutions.
**Information Theory Milestone:** Proved the 2013 Courtade–Kumar conjecture by reducing it to a 14-variable optimization problem and formalizing the proof in 50 million lines of Lean 4 code.

**Algorithmic Breakthroughs:** Resolved a 2024 STOC open question in Boolean matrix multiplication, a 2022 FOCS open question in cut sparsification, and provided a new O(n log n) algorithm for n-bit integer multiplication.

**System Availability:** The /teamwork and /boost agentic harnesses are being deployed to the Antigravity platform for external use, allowing users to route prompts through declarative, self-improving natural-language patterns.

title: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
author: Julie Bort
contentSnippet: Posted: 11:37 AM PST · November 13, 2026 Image Credits: Getty Images Julie Bort AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday. That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP. LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence. With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use. True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce. Newsletters See More Subscribe for the industry’s biggest tech news Related AI Amazon’s new AI agent will shop third-party sites for you

summary.tldr:
LangChain, the AI agent management startup, has secured $300 million in a Series C funding round, bringing its total valuation to $3 billion. The round was led by CapitalG, with participation from GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures. This valuation represents a significant increase from the $1.25 billion valuation the company reached approximately one year ago following a $125 million funding round led by IVP.

Originally launched in 2022 as an open-source project designed to assist early-stage LLMs with tasks like web searching and API integration, LangChain has pivoted its primary focus toward the management of AI agents. Its core product, LangSmith, is positioned as a model-agnostic platform that allows businesses to build and manage agents without being locked into specific cloud providers or proprietary AI ecosystems. The company claims to have reached 7,000 customers for LangSmith, including major enterprises such as Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce, as well as startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay.
takeaways: **Funding Details:** Raised $300 million in Series C funding at a $3 billion valuation.
**Investor Syndicate:** Round led by CapitalG, with participation from GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures.
**Customer Base:** Reports 7,000 customers for its LangSmith platform, including Nvidia, Toyota, Salesforce, Harvey, Rippling, and Clay.
**Strategic Positioning:** Focuses on model-agnostic agent management to prevent vendor lock-in across cloud and AI model providers.

title: Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS with Amazon EC2 Spot
author: Belair Albahagwi
contentSnippet: Speech-to-text inference is computationally intensive. Each audio file triggers a pipeline of deep learning models (acoustic models, language models, and post-processing stages) running on NVIDIA GPUs to meet latency requirements. At scale, this means thousands of GPU instances running continuously. AssemblyAI needed a way to run GPU-intensive inference workloads cost-effectively at scale, without sacrificing the availability and latency guarantees their customers depend on. Running entirely on On-Demand Instances would be cost-prohibitive. Spot Instances offer significant savings, while Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning when capacity is needed elsewhere. AssemblyAI needed an architecture that absorbs Spot interruptions gracefully while maintaining service level agreement (SLA) commitments. Additionally, customers in regulated industries, including healthcare, finance, and legal, must keep audio data within specific geographic boundaries. They implement strict data residency configurations in European AWS Regions. Available on AWS Marketplace , AssemblyAI provides an API for transcription, speaker detection, sentiment analysis, chapter detection, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction. Their models transcribe and analyze speech for high-volume workloads across industries including technology, media, healthcare, and financial services. In this post, we show you how AssemblyAI runs cost-optimized AI inference at scale for their speech-to-text platform. The architecture uses Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Spot Instances, and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Together, these services combine a flexible fleet of NVIDIA GPUs, ECS capacity providers, and a queue-based retry mechanism. The result is significant cost savings while maintaining SLA commitments across European AWS Regions. Solution overview AssemblyAI’s inference platform runs on Amazon ECS with compute capacity managed through ECS capacity providers. The fleet mixes Amazon EC2 Spot Instances and On-Demand Instances across multiple NVIDIA GPU instance families, running a single inference model per GPU at a scale of thousands of instances. The architecture is built on four pillars that work together to deliver cost-optimized and resilient inference: Amazon ECS capacity provi

summary.tldr:
AssemblyAI has optimized its large-scale speech-to-text inference pipeline by migrating to a hybrid Amazon EC2 Spot and On-Demand instance architecture on Amazon ECS. The platform, which processes audio through acoustic models, language models, and post-processing stages, requires thousands of NVIDIA GPU instances to maintain latency SLAs for transcription, speaker detection, sentiment analysis, and PII redaction. By utilizing ECS capacity providers, the company balances cost-efficiency with the necessity of handling the 2-minute interruption warnings inherent to Spot Instances.

The architecture relies on a queue-based retry mechanism powered by Amazon SQS to manage workload resilience during instance reclamation. To meet strict data residency requirements for customers in regulated sectors like healthcare and finance, the infrastructure is deployed across specific European AWS Regions. The system utilizes a heterogeneous fleet of NVIDIA GPU instance families, ensuring that the inference pipeline remains performant while significantly reducing the financial overhead compared to a pure On-Demand deployment.
takeaways: **Infrastructure Stack:** Utilizes Amazon ECS with capacity providers, Amazon EC2 Spot and On-Demand instances, and Amazon SQS for queue-based retry logic.
**Compute Hardware:** Employs a flexible fleet of NVIDIA GPU instances to handle high-volume transcription and analysis tasks.
**Resilience Strategy:** Implements a retry mechanism to handle the 2-minute interruption warning window provided by EC2 Spot Instances.
**Compliance:** Maintains strict data residency by deploying inference workloads within specific European AWS Regions to serve regulated industries.

title: How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
author: Kaitlyn Ridel
contentSnippet: Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics , governance , and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges. “AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance. Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union , the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology , and the International Organization for Standardization . The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias , security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap. Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies. Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust. Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance. The benefits of microcredentials Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program. Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigo

summary.tldr:
Engineering teams are facing significant operational friction as they attempt to integrate AI ethics, governance, and auditing into standard development workflows. These requirements, often mandated by frameworks from the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), aim to address systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks. However, a persistent skills gap exists because traditional computer science and engineering curricula lack formal training in AI-specific safety protocols, data tracking, and regulatory auditing.

Microcredentials are being positioned as a solution to this gap, allowing mid-career engineers to acquire specialized competencies without the time commitment of traditional degree programs. These programs focus on mastery of specific skills—such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing—validated through assessment. By stacking these credentials, engineers can demonstrate a verifiable progression of expertise, helping organizations mitigate the risk of product delays, legal exposure, and loss of public trust associated with non-compliant AI deployments.
takeaways: **Regulatory Frameworks:** Compliance standards are primarily driven by the EU, NIST, and ISO, focusing on safety, fairness, and transparency.
**Skills Gap:** Traditional engineering education lacks training in AI auditing, data tracking, and human-AI interaction safety protocols.
**Microcredential Mechanics:** These programs require learners to demonstrate mastery through validation assessments, with the ability to stack credentials to show growing expertise.
**Core Competencies:** Targeted training areas include bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing.

title: Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock
author: Aamna Najmi
contentSnippet: Amazon Bedrock provides built-in, zero-instrumentation cost attribution that traces every inference call back to the IAM principal that made it. The identity flows along with organizational tags, into AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) and AWS Cost Explorer while keeping data inside the AWS security boundary. This post shows you how to use these capabilities to answer three questions that every FinOps and AI Platform leader asks as AI tool adoption scales: What is the real per-user cost? Which teams generate the most spend, and does that spend correlate with the value they deliver? How should next year’s budget scale with headcount and adoption? The approach works identically regardless of which AI coding or productivity tool makes the call. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT Work, and OpenCode all invoke Amazon Bedrock through one of two inference endpoints: bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle , and Bedrock’s attribution mechanism operates at the endpoint layer, beneath any tool-specific logic. You configure identity propagation once, and every tool that routes inference through Bedrock inherits per-user cost visibility automatically. By the end of this post, you will have AWS IAM Identity Center configured with your external identity provider for per-user attribution, session tags (team, cost center) flowing into CUR 2.0, Amazon Athena queries and dashboard options for ongoing cost visibility, and a clear understanding of Bedrock-native usage controls to enforce spending limits. How Amazon Bedrock attribution works Amazon Bedrock records the IAM identity of every inference caller with no changes required to your API calls. When a user invokes a model through either the bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle endpoint, Bedrock captures the caller’s full IAM ARN, including the session name for federated users and publishes it to CUR 2.0 in the line_item_iam_principal column. In billing data, usage is aggregated per principal and per usage type for each export interval: one hour in an hourly export, one day in a daily export. CUR does not contain per-request cost. For per-prompt detail, use model invocation logs or request metadata tagging. Optionally, you can attach tags to IAM principals or pass session tags during federation to add organizational dimensions. These tags appear in CUR 2.0 with the iamPrincipal/ prefix and in Cost Explorer as filter

summary.tldr:
Amazon Bedrock has implemented native, zero-instrumentation cost attribution that tracks inference calls to the specific IAM principal responsible for the request. By capturing the caller’s full IAM ARN—including session names for federated users—at the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoint layers, the system automatically propagates identity data into AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) and AWS Cost Explorer. This mechanism functions independently of the specific AI tool being used, supporting applications such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT Work, and OpenCode without requiring modifications to tool-specific logic.

To enable granular financial oversight, organizations can leverage AWS IAM Identity Center to integrate external identity providers, allowing session tags like 'team' or 'cost center' to flow directly into billing reports. While CUR 2.0 provides aggregated usage data per principal and usage type at hourly or daily intervals, users requiring per-prompt cost granularity must utilize model invocation logs or request metadata tagging. The platform also supports the enforcement of spending limits through Bedrock-native controls, enabling FinOps and AI platform leaders to correlate AI spend with headcount and organizational value.
takeaways: **Endpoint Attribution:** Bedrock captures IAM identity at the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, ensuring visibility regardless of the client application.
**Reporting Integration:** Identity data is published to the line_item_iam_principal column in CUR 2.0, with organizational tags appearing under the iamPrincipal/ prefix.
**Granularity Limits:** CUR 2.0 provides aggregated cost data per principal per hour or day; per-request cost analysis requires separate model invocation logs.
**Identity Propagation:** The system supports federated users by capturing session names, allowing for per-user cost attribution when integrated with AWS IAM Identity Center.

title: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh oh, Jensen!
author: Tim Fernholz
contentSnippet:
The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims.

The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service.

While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang.

U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff.

Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips.

White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination.

That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revol

summary.tldr:
Research conducted by Will DePue of the nonprofit Unemployment Labs suggests that leading Chinese AI models, specifically DeepSeek’s V4 and Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, exhibit technical 'fingerprints' consistent with training on Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. These chips are currently subject to U.S. export bans intended to restrict China's access to advanced AI compute. The findings imply that despite strict regulatory frameworks, Chinese frontier labs are successfully utilizing high-end hardware, potentially through offshore data centers or illicit smuggling networks.

Epoch AI estimates that approximately two million advanced Nvidia chips entered China during 2024 and 2025 via diversion schemes. A significant portion of this compute is reportedly accessed through offshore facilities, with Malaysia emerging as a major hub, having imported 275,000 Nvidia accelerators in the same period. The situation is further complicated by allegations involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his professional ties to Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed—a firm accused of facilitating the smuggling of banned chips into China. These developments have triggered scrutiny regarding Nvidia’s corporate liability and the efficacy of U.S. export controls, which currently lack stringent requirements for tracking the end-use of chips once they leave the manufacturer's direct control.
takeaways: **Model Fingerprinting:** Analysis of model weights by Unemployment Labs indicates that DeepSeek V4 and Moonshot Kimi K3 were likely trained on Blackwell-class hardware.
**Smuggling Volume:** Epoch AI estimates that 2 million advanced Nvidia chips were diverted into China throughout 2024 and 2025.
**Offshore Hubs:** Malaysia imported 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators in 2024-2025, serving as a primary conduit for Chinese firms to access compute outside mainland jurisdiction.

**Regulatory Loophole:** Current U.S. export controls do not mandate that companies track the downstream usage of chips once they are sold, allowing for the use of offshore data centers to bypass domestic restrictions.
**Stockpile Status:** Approximately 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly held in Hong Kong, awaiting clearance for import into mainland China.

title: Build a model improvement flywheel with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Data Capture
author: Shantanu Tripathi
contentSnippet: Foundation models deployed on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod meet inputs that no pre-curated dataset covers: domain-specific jargon, unexpected formats, new products, and changing user behavior. Without a record of production inference data, teams can’t detect drift, find failure patterns, or use real interactions to improve the model. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now provides Data Capture, a built-in capability that records live inference inputs and outputs to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at three independent tiers, with minimal latency impact and zero impact on model availability. In this post, we walk through one complete example on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster. A home-appliance support router captures its production traffic, Amazon Athena queries surface a new-product blind spot, a SQL policy labels the captured records, and a fine-tune on that data teaches the router the new product. We measure accuracy before and after, on data that could not have existed before the model was deployed. The inference operator serves the model on one node, and the training operator runs the fine-tuning on another. We use synthetic data for the walkthrough. The scripts, manifests, SQL, synthetic datasets, and expected outputs are available in the accompanying GitHub repository . Three-tier Data Capture architecture HyperPod Data Capture provides three independent tiers, each at a different point in the request path. You can turn on any combination in the same dataCapture block. Tier 1: SageMaker endpoint Tier 2: Load balancer Tier 3: Model pod What’s captured Full request/response payloads Application Load Balancer (ALB) access-log fields: request line, status codes, timings, client IP, user agent Full request/response payloads plus event metadata Managed by SageMaker native data capture ALB access logs HyperPod inference operator (NGINX + OTel collector + S3 uploader sidecars) Best for Compliance, Model Monitor, audit Traffic and error-rate monitoring at low cost Debugging, analytics, training-data collection Configuration sagemakerEndpoint: — sampling %, input/output, AWS KMS loadBalancer: { enabled: true } modelPod: — sampling %, input/output, buffer, max payload size, AWS KMS, content types Tiers 1 and 3 both store full payloads, so enabling both stores every record twice. Use Tier 1 for compliance and Model Monitor, Tier 2 when you only need traffic metad

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced a three-tier Data Capture capability for SageMaker HyperPod, designed to address the challenge of capturing production inference data for model improvement. The system records live inputs and outputs directly to Amazon S3, enabling teams to detect drift, identify failure patterns, and curate datasets for fine-tuning. By capturing domain-specific jargon and evolving user behaviors that were not present in original training sets, the tool facilitates a continuous improvement flywheel where production traffic is labeled and fed back into the training pipeline.

The architecture operates across three distinct tiers: Tier 1 (SageMaker endpoint) captures full request/response payloads for compliance and Model Monitor; Tier 2 (Load Balancer) logs ALB access fields like status codes and client IPs for traffic monitoring; and Tier 3 (Model pod) captures full payloads plus event metadata using NGINX, OpenTelemetry (OTel) collector, and S3 uploader sidecars. The system is designed for minimal latency and zero impact on model availability. AWS provides a reference implementation using a home-appliance support router scenario, demonstrating how to use Amazon Athena for querying captured data and SQL policies for automated labeling before triggering a fine-tuning job on a separate HyperPod node.
takeaways: **Capture Tiers:** The system offers three independent capture points: SageMaker endpoint (Tier 1), Load Balancer (Tier 2), and Model pod (Tier 3).
**Technical Stack:** Tier 3 implementation utilizes NGINX, an OpenTelemetry (OTel) collector, and S3 uploader sidecars to manage data flow.
**Operational Workflow:** The architecture supports a split-node approach where the inference operator runs on one node and the training operator executes fine-tuning on another.
**Configuration:** Users can enable tiers via the dataCapture block, specifying sampling percentages, AWS KMS encryption, and buffer settings.
**Resource Availability:** AWS has released a GitHub repository containing scripts, manifests, SQL queries, and synthetic datasets for a full end-to-end walkthrough.

title: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm , Robotiq 2F-140 gripper , and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central , an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog .

What makes a robot asset SimReady?

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

Profile: a group of features for a use case, such as a robot body.

Features: capabilities needed for the use case, such as joints that can be controlled.

Requirements: checks on the settings needed for each feature, such as a joint’s drive settings.

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

What comes with the asset, and what do you add?

The UR17G , Robotiq 2F-140 , and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

What should you check before running a pick-and-place task?

Joint settings: Review the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings.

Movement: Test a small arm movement and open and close the gripper.

This technical guide details the implementation of a pick-and-place robotics simulation within NVIDIA Isaac Sim 6.2, utilizing SimReady assets to ensure physics-ready OpenUSD models. The workflow centers on the UR17G robotic arm and the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, with assets sourced from SimReady Central, an open library hosted on Hugging Face. SimReady assets are pre-configured with essential simulation properties—including mass, collision meshes, and joint drive settings—validated against specific profiles like Robot-Body 4.0.0 and Robot-Gripper 3.0.0 to ensure consistent behavior across simulation environments.

The assembly process involves integrating these assets into an Isaac Sim scene and employing an AI agent to generate Python-based control scripts. The agent leverages bundled Isaac Sim skills, specifically 'isaac-sim-remote', 'usd-articulation', 'manipulation-ik', and 'physics-simulation', to manage the arm-gripper assembly and execute the pick-and-place sequence. The simulation tests the full grasp-to-release lifecycle, requiring manual or agent-led verification of joint limits, drive settings, and contact physics to ensure the beverage can remains stable during movement. The current implementation uses a fixed setup without vision-based sensing, and the grasp effort is capped at 2 N·m for the horizontal maneuver.
takeaways: **SimReady Architecture:** Assets are defined by a three-tier hierarchy consisting of Profiles (use-case groups), Features (e.g., controllable joints), and Requirements (validation checks for settings like drive parameters).

title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench , a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem : a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

Building XYBench

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated fr

summary.tldr:
XYBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate how AI assistants handle the 'XY problem,' where a user asks for help with a misguided approach (Y) rather than their actual underlying goal (X). Developed by researchers from Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, and awarded the Best Resource Paper at EMNLP 2026, the dataset comprises 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming, cooking, and home repair. It aims to measure whether models can identify implicit misconceptions, explain why a proposed approach is flawed, and redirect users toward effective solutions.

The benchmark evaluates models—including Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro—across three metrics: pragmatic solution (presence of answers for X and Y), pragmatic emphasis (focus on X vs. Y), and misconception identification. Automated evaluation is performed using Claude Sonnet 4.5 as a judge, with human validation showing 74.2–100% agreement across metrics. Results indicate that while models frequently provide solutions to the stated request (75–86% on Stack Overflow), they struggle to prioritize the underlying goal, focusing on it in only 35–41% of responses.

Experiments revealed a significant 'capability gap' between recognition and generation: while models correctly identified superior, goal-focused advice in 71–84% of multiple-choice scenarios, they failed to produce such advice in open-ended generation. Furthermore, providing models with the explicit underlying goal did not close the performance gap compared to human benchmarks, suggesting that current models struggle to act on inferred intent even when it is provided. The current dataset is limited to English-language procedural queries, with future work planned for multilingual and conversational contexts.
takeaways: **Benchmark Composition:** XYBench contains 8,115 questions sourced from Stack Overflow (1,557), Stack Exchange (184), manual curation (102), and WikiHow (6,272).
**Performance Gap:** On Stack Overflow, models focused on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of responses, compared to 47–57% focusing on the mistaken stated request.
**Evaluation Methodology:** The benchmark uses Claude Sonnet 4.5 as an automated judge, with human validation showing 84.6–93.3% agreement on misconception identification.
**Recognition vs. Generation:** Models correctly identified goal-focused advice in 71–84% of multiple-choice tests but failed to generate that same quality of advice in open-ended tasks.
**Oracle Experiment Findings:** Supplying models with the explicit intended goal (X) increased solution rates but actually decreased the rate of misconception identification.

title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet:
Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.

On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.

Turning a Windows defense against itself

The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.

By manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links, the attacker causes Defender to open the CLFS container in the security context of the antimalware engine. If an associated authentication file is missing, CLFS creates it using Defender’s System privileges. Because CLFS assigns the newly created file the Discretionary Access Control List of the original file, the attacker may gain access to a file created with System privileges, allowing the file-creation operation to be abused as part of a privilege-escalation attack.

Ironically, the vulnerability stems from a security measure Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to prevent attackers from exploiting other vulnerabilities in CLFS.

“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation [of] privileges,” Nightmare Eclipse wrote . “Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.”

What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR.

Nigh

summary.tldr:
An independent researcher operating under the pseudonym Nightmare Eclipse disclosed a Windows zero-day vulnerability named SignDrop, which grants local users full System privileges. The flaw resides within the Common Log File System (CLFS) and weaponizes a security mitigation introduced by Microsoft in October 2025. By manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links and invoking ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature—a legitimate Windows Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates—an attacker forces a privileged process to open a crafted CLFS container, enabling arbitrary file creation under System context.

The vulnerability allows local attackers to bypass self-defense and tamper-protection mechanisms of antivirus and Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions, as file creation requests originate from the legitimate antimalware process itself. According to the disclosure and analysis by researcher Will Dormann, the exploit affects Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental. However, Dormann noted specific prerequisites for successful exploitation, including that the target Windows 26H2 system must have existed for more than 90 days and the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode must be set to 0 or 1.

Microsoft stated it is currently investigating the disclosure, confirmed it has no evidence of active exploitation in the wild, and maintained that Windows Defender blocks potential exploitation attempts. Users can verify vulnerability status by checking the CLFS authentication mode, where learning or enforcement modes indicate vulnerability alongside the provided proof-of-concept script.
takeaways: **Vulnerability Name and Impact:** SignDrop is a local privilege escalation zero-day discovered by researcher Nightmare Eclipse that grants standard local users full System rights and allows the disabling of arbitrary antivirus and EDR solutions.
**Affected Operating Systems:** The exploit targets Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental.

**Exploit Mechanism:** The attack forces Windows Defender to open a crafted Common Log File System (CLFS) container by abusing ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature and manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links.

**Exploitation Requirements:** Researcher Will Dormann verified the exploit requires a Windows 26H2 system that has existed for more than 90 days, with the registry value HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode set to 0 or 1.

title: Perplexity Releases Decider v1.3: Open-Weight Decision Models Add Locate
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Perplexity has released pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3 , the latest versions of its open-weight decision models. Perplexity Decider v1.3 is a decision model that returns probabilities, not generated text. It answers yes/no, multiple-choice and score questions about a text or image input. The main addition is Locate, which extracts exact text spans by type or instruction. Weights ship under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face . Both models also run in the Perplexity Decisions API and on OpenRouter . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 27B on Qwen3.8-27B ; Flash is 4B on Qwen3.5-4B . Hugging Face lists 26B and 5B params. API input: under 256K tokens. Local default: 32,768. Runs on: a CUDA GPU fitting ~49 GiB of BF16 weights (v1.3) or ~8.5 GiB (Flash). No quantized variants. Performance: leads TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 on most of Perplexity’s self-reported evaluations. Best: 91.6% mean accuracy on 63 query-classification tasks. Worst: Locate averages 69.0, its lowest absolute score. Flash trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming and law. Bottom line: Best: a 0.27% answer-flip rate and $26.47 per 1M production requests. Worst: every figure is self-reported. What is Perplexity Decider v1.3? Decider is Perplexity’s family of decision models, inspired by TypeSafe’s Jev . Each request has a shared ‘state’ plus one or more questions with labeled options. The model returns a probability per option instead of writing an answer. v1.3 succeeds v1.2 and Flash v1.2 . Flash v1.3 is distilled from the large model. How does Decider v1.3 work? Perplexity adapts a generative LLM backbone into a classifier. The output layer starts from the base model’s LM head, pruned to option tokens (A, B, C). A linear decision head reads the hidden state at a <|marker|> token and outputs option probabilities. Full-attention layers are made bidirectional, which Perplexity’s ablations showed helps. v1.3 also changes attention between questions. In v1.2, every question saw every other question, so answers could shift. In v1.3, the state sees all questions, but each question sees only the state and itself. All questions about one input still run in a single forward pass. Training runs in 3 stages: a full fine-tune on hundreds of public datasets a LoRA specialization adapter a LoRA vision adapter Weights are averaged acro

title: ElevenLabs’ new app combines meeting note-taking and dictation for teams

Launched during its 11/11 Summit in New York, ElevenAI is still in preview, and you have to sign up for early access instead of just downloading an app. ElevenLabs, valued at $22 billion , is very much positioning this as a product that lives within a team as compared to a productivity tool for an individual.

ElevenLabs also allows companies to integrate ElevenAgent and take follow-up actions such as writing a draft email based on meeting notes.

Plus, there’s a dictation feature, which lets users convert speech to cleaned-up text in any app with support for over 90 languages. The company said that the app is capable of understanding industry-specific terms across dictation and meeting transcription.

ElevenAI allows the company to use its own model as a showcase and also utilize its agent platforms for better context funneling. The startup’s positioning might not be to directly compete in the productivity market, but rather to give enterprise teams an option to not buy licenses to a notetaker and use its solution instead. All meeting-related tools are rushing to become central knowledge hubs for companies while aiming to automate knowledge extraction and follow-up actions

In the last week, the company also launched its v3 series of Scribe speech-to-text models with live transcription capabilities and the ability for companies to fine-tune models using their own data, a tool to pick the right language model based on use case , and a routine creator that automates tasks based on the transcript.

title: Agents idling while they wait on humans push Kubernetes to hand back unused resources
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 09:22 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026

Agents idling while they wait on humans push Kubernetes to hand back unused resources

Agentic AI workloads are handing Kubernetes an unexpected second act . The orchestrator once dismissed as reliable but boring is now at the center of how enterprises plan to run autonomous software.

Past platform shifts, from physical servers to virtual machines and from virtual machines to containers, forced companies to wipe the slate clean and start over. This shift is different because Kubernetes was built as a platform for building platforms, according to Bobby Allen (pictured), cloud therapist at Google Cloud LLC.

“Kubernetes now, 11, 12+ years in, has this whole new life,” Allen said. “You don’t need a new platform this time. … This shift doesn’t mean that you’ve got to retool and rebuild and replatform everything, and I think that could be comforting for folks to realize that they don’t have to start from scratch.”

Allen spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Kubernetes is recovering resources spent on idle agentic AI workloads. (* Disclosure below.)

Running agentic AI workloads in the open

Google is putting that view into practice. The company has donated Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, while engineering teams are tuning Kubernetes for agents rather than building a new stack.

“Google is doubling down on our commitment to not just open source but community-driven, collaborative, multiple-partner-involvement open source,” Allen said. “These concepts are foundational, but they’re important enough that we need to all contribute and shape these together.”

Efficiency is a big part of the motivation. Agents spend long stretches idle while they wait for human input, and the projects aim to give those resources back during the downtime, Allen explained.

“These are kind of different efforts that contribute to an open, flexible, transparent, collaborative way to make agentic workloads run better so that we can have these amazing outcomes but also be efficient with our resources,” Allen said. “We don’t want to have this sci-fi Star Trek moment where we’re stepping into the future and kill the planet.”

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconA

summary.tldr:
Google Cloud is positioning Kubernetes as the primary orchestration layer for agentic AI workloads, aiming to avoid the need for new, specialized infrastructure platforms. Bobby Allen, a cloud therapist at Google Cloud, stated that Kubernetes' maturity allows it to adapt to agent-based architectures without requiring enterprises to rebuild their existing stacks. The core technical challenge addressed is the inefficiency of AI agents that remain idle while awaiting human input, which currently consumes significant compute resources.

To optimize these workloads, Google has donated three key projects to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF): Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL. These projects are designed to improve the efficiency, transparency, and flexibility of agentic AI execution. By integrating these tools, Google aims to enable Kubernetes to dynamically reclaim resources during agent downtime, ensuring that large-scale AI deployments remain resource-efficient rather than relying on static, over-provisioned infrastructure.
takeaways: **Project Donations:** Google has contributed Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation to support agentic AI on Kubernetes.
**Resource Optimization:** The initiative focuses on reclaiming compute resources from AI agents during idle periods while they wait for human interaction.
**Platform Strategy:** Google advocates for evolving Kubernetes rather than creating new platforms, citing the orchestrator's 11-12 year maturity as a stable foundation for autonomous software.
**Sustainability Goal:** The effort is framed as a move to prevent excessive resource consumption and environmental impact associated with scaling agentic AI workloads.

title: Claude’s Duet agent is a little neurotic and surprisingly helpful
author: Allison Johnson
contentSnippet: Normally, the products I test don’t offer to help me write up my experience with them. Duet is different. Claude Duet is Anthropic’s AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don’t write code. It’s been an interesting couple of months: Instinct gave us an impressive text-based assistant, Meta offered us its cute little guy, Muse, to help us buy things, and OpenAI gave us the more work-oriented Dots. Claude Duet is even more focused on work than those. It’s also more consumer-friendly than Claude Cowork, which was more consumer-friendly than Claude Code — the coding agent that kicked off a whole hype cycle earlier this year. I’ve been testing it over the past week as I navigate a busy travel and work schedule. At turns it has been truly useful, kind of a nag, and very eager to write about itself. Duet is still a “research preview” according to Anthropic, and access is limited to Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the US, with a waitlist to join. It’s not here to order you burritos, either; it’s for “professionals and small business owners” and is meant to use its judgment about what needs your attention most. Like Meta’s Muse, Duet has its own app. (If you’re keeping score at home, yes, it has been updated to fully support the iPhone Duo). Duet uses Claude’s characteristically cheery, minimalist design. The app is consumer-friendly and approachable. Once you’ve connected all the productivity and chat services you want, it’ll look for ways to help out with and suggest them as cards you can swipe left or right to hide or accept — kind of a to-do list Tinder. In the name of testing, I went all in on Duet and gave it everything: my work email, calendar, Google Docs, and Slack. This gave it plenty of grist for the mill in more ways than I’d even realized at first. Because our biweekly staff meeting is automatically summarized in an email from Gemini, and Duet had access to my email, it was able to connect the dots between something said in a meeting and a direct message in Slack. Duet also worked out who my boss is because we have a shared Google Doc for our weekly 1:1 meetings. AI is at its most useful when it can suck up lots of data, and Duet wasted no time doing so. summary.tldr: Anthropic has released Claude Duet, a consumer-focused AI agent designed for professionals and small business owners. Currently in a "research preview" phase, the tool is available to Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the US via a waitlist. Unlike previous Anthropic offerings like Claude Code or Claude Cowork, Duet is specifically engineered to integrate with productivity suites—including email, calendars, Google Docs, and Slack—to proactively manage workflows, summarize meeting action items, and identify discrepancies across communication channels.
takeaways: **Integration Capabilities:** Duet functions by ingesting data from connected services (email, calendar, Google Docs, Slack) to generate "cards" that users can swipe to accept or hide, functioning as an automated task manager.

**Proactive Workflow Management:** The agent provides daily morning briefings and identifies potential scheduling conflicts or missed deadlines by cross-referencing disparate data sources, such as linking meeting summaries in email to Slack messages.

**Platform Availability:** The service is delivered via a dedicated mobile app that supports the iPhone Duo and is restricted to Anthropic's higher-tier subscription plans (Pro, Max, and Ultra) in the US.

**Transparency Features:** AI-generated communications sent via the agent, such as Slack messages, are automatically tagged with a "sent with Claude" label to ensure transparency in professional correspondence.

**Current Limitations:** The agent is currently undergoing testing regarding its "judgment" on notification frequency and tone, as it has demonstrated difficulty in distinguishing between hard deadlines and flexible project timelines.

title: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
author: NVIDIA Writers
contentSnippet: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications. Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care. Friday, Nov. 13, 5:00 a.m. PT Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts . Dyania Health , a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would. The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision. Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall. The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital. Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on. Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers. Synapsis AI in the Real World Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021. Synapsis AI reasoned across each pati

summary.tldr:
Dyania Health, a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, has developed Synapsis AI, a clinical reasoning engine designed to parse decades of unstructured patient data, including physician notes, operative reports, and pathology results. The system functions by connecting disparate clinical findings across years of records to generate traceable clinical signals, effectively automating the manual chart review process to assist clinicians in identifying patients requiring immediate attention.

Technically, Synapsis AI is built using NVIDIA NeMo open libraries for model training and utilizes NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM for inference optimization. To address data privacy concerns, the platform is designed to run entirely on-premises within a health system’s firewall, ensuring patient data remains localized. The tool is strictly assistive, requiring clinician verification for all surfaced evidence and subsequent medical decisions.

In a practical application, the Cleveland Clinic utilized Synapsis AI to analyze a cohort of over 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients spanning data from 2005 to 2021. By automating the synthesis of longitudinal records, the tool aims to reduce the administrative burden on hospital staff, allowing for increased direct patient interaction.
takeaways: **Core Technology:** Synapsis AI uses NVIDIA NeMo for training and TensorRT/TensorRT-LLM for optimized, on-premises inference.
**Data Privacy:** The system operates entirely behind a hospital's firewall, ensuring patient records are processed locally without external data sharing.
**Clinical Application:** Cleveland Clinic deployed the tool to process longitudinal records for a study involving 7,800+ aortic valve replacement patients.
**Operational Scope:** The engine processes unstructured data including free-text physician notes, imaging reports, pathology reads, and discharge summaries.

title: Israel’s VCs see opportunity for challengers in Nvidia’s turmoil
author: Anna Heim
contentSnippet:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation has been received with worry in Israel, the company’s “second home,” as Huang described it in 2023. The company’s importance flows both ways, as the semiconductor giant has provided a major boost to Israel’s economic forecasts in recent years.

Intel, Microsoft and many homegrown startups also conduct a sizable share of their R&D in Israel. But owing to Nvidia’s stronghold on AI given the centrality of its GPUs for training LLMs and using them, many in the country are wondering how much of a reshuffle will result from its leadership crisis.

As with everything at Nvidia, Huang drove the company to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox for $6.9 billion in 2019 and use the company as the base for its largest R&D facility outside of the U.S. Nvidia also made plans to build a multibillion-dollar campus in northern Israel.

“Jensen brought Nvidia to Israel with the acquisition of Mellanox, so there is a strong positive sentiment towards Nvidia and Jensen in Israel’s tech community,” Israeli repeat cybersecurity entrepreneur Pavel Gurvich told TechCrunch.

Beyond the 6,000 locals Nvidia employs, the bigger question is whether the company will remain as committed to Israel with someone else at the helm. As a result, his line of succession is being observed just as closely by those who hope the company continues to do so as by those who don’t want it to happen.

The latter have already gathered that they may be in for disappointment. In a 2023 interview that is now doing the rounds on X, interim CEO Colette Kress had declared that as Nvidia’s CFO, she typically started her day “with Israel meetings, and only then continue[d] to California.”

Kress may not remain in charge in the long run, but the many names floated for the role include two Israelis , Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan — although they’re not at the top of the still quite tentative list .

Regardless of who gets chosen, Huang’s successor will likely have less of a grip on Nvidia and the tech industry as a whole. But investors don’t think that would cause demand for Nvidia’s product to fade away.

According to Yanai Oron, a general partner at Vertex Ventures Israel, “slower decisions at Nvidia could give competitors an opening, but if that uncertainty also slows AI spending, they could end up with a bigger share of a smaller opportunity.”

summary.tldr:
Nvidia is facing a leadership transition following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang, creating significant uncertainty within Israel’s technology sector, where the company maintains its largest R&D presence outside the U.S. Nvidia employs approximately 6,000 people in Israel, a footprint established largely through the $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox in 2019. The Israeli tech community, which views Nvidia as a critical economic pillar, is closely monitoring the succession process to determine if the company’s commitment to local R&D and planned multibillion-dollar campus infrastructure will persist under new leadership.

Industry analysts and venture capitalists suggest that while Nvidia’s core technology and ecosystem remain robust, the leadership vacuum may provide a strategic opening for competitors. Yanai Oron of Vertex Ventures Israel notes that while slower decision-making at Nvidia could benefit rivals, it risks cooling overall AI spending, potentially shrinking the total addressable market. Investors like Adi Levanon of Selah Ventures argue that while the company is unlikely to collapse, the transition may prevent Nvidia from achieving a total monopoly, allowing challengers in AI-specific chips and inference software to compete on economic efficiency and alternative architectural approaches.
takeaways: **Israel Footprint:** Nvidia employs 6,000 people in Israel and operates its largest R&D facility outside the U.S., a legacy of the 2019 Mellanox acquisition.
**Succession Candidates:** Potential candidates for the CEO role include Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan, though neither is currently considered a frontrunner.
**Interim Leadership:** Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is currently serving as interim CEO, having previously managed daily operations with a heavy focus on Israeli R&D coordination.
**Market Impact:** Analysts suggest that leadership uncertainty may allow competitors to gain market share in AI-specific hardware and inference software by offering better unit economics.

title: Jensen Huang didn’t show confidence in his successor, report says
author: Ivan Mehta
contentSnippet: Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang described Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who has now replaced him as interim CEO, as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation earlier in the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported , citing an anonymous source. Huang made the comment during a meeting with Nvidia’s finance team about the company’s plans to provide guarantees worth billions of dollars to data center operators that couldn’t afford to buy its chips upfront, according to the report. He reportedly also said Kress was a person who couldn’t help him steer strategy or decision-making. Kress has been with Nvidia for over 13 years now, after serving as SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance. The report said she has questioned Nvidia’s program-focused, credit-based deals involving Huang’s son-in-law Nico Caprez, and wanted to know how to decide which deals are beneficial, how to value guarantees, and determine returns. Earlier in the year, she had scaled back on Nvidia’s commitment for OpenAI’s ambitious Ohio data center project. The company was in talks to provide $250 billion in credit to OpenAI, but ended up committing $105 billion . Huang resigned Thursday after reports of two extramarital affairs , including one with the company’s VP for healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The company is also investigating a possible Chinese espionage plot . After his resignation, Reuters reported that he was having a third affair with another employee . Nvidia is currently searching for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, who had the top job for over 33 years. title: Google Releases TPU Sync: Open-Source KV Cache Transfer for TPUs
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Google Cloud has released TPU Sync , an open-source C++ library for moving KV caches and model weights on Cloud TPUs. The Google TPU Sync KV cache transfer library treats TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage and the data center network as one memory hierarchy. It targets a growing bottleneck: moving model state, not computing it. Google reports over 90% lower KV transfer latency on 235B to 480B parameter MoE models. TL;DR Library: Native C++ core with Python wheels for PyTorch and JAX. Tested on 235B to 480B MoE models. Runs on: Cloud TPU v7x (Ironwood) and v6e per the README . Benchmarks used TPU v7x (2x2x1), PCIe Gen5 and 200 Gbps NICs. Performance: Large cuts to KV transfer latency and time to first token (TTFT) in Google’s internal lab tests. Best: Up to 90% lower average TTFT (480B P/D serving at low concurrency, and 64K-context prefix caching). Worst: No RL numbers published. The README says it is not yet recommended for general use. Bottom line: Best: Qwen3 235B KV transfer drops from several seconds to ~230 ms. Worst: every number is self-reported and early-stage. What is TPU Sync? TPU Sync is an open-source C++ library from Google that moves TPU-tiled tensors across memory tiers with asynchronous DMA. It handles 2 jobs: KV cache state during inference, and trainer-to-sampler weight broadcast in reinforcement learning (RL). The repository is licensed Apache-2.0. How does TPU Sync work? The library spans TPU HBM, pinned host DRAM, shared storage and multi-host DCN. Storage uses experimental POSIX backends, including local SSDs and Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Google lists 4 design choices: Layout-preserving direct DMA: It reads JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place. Data keeps its native TPU tile layout, with no Python serialization or bounce buffers. Compute-overlapped transfers: Raw PJRT buffer aliases let transfers run during computation. Built-in DMA pacing stops large copies from delaying kernel launches. No XLA compilation in the data path: Transfers and resharding run in native C++ outside the XLA graph. High-bandwidth PCIe and DCN: It reaches up to 223 GB/s per Ironwood host, against a 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 ceiling. DCN streaming hits ~192 Gbps on 1 NIC, or ~350 Gbps across 2. Above this sit a global KV store for prefix lookups, a transfer controller and a KV cache manager. How does disaggregated prefill/decode serving use it? The prefill no

summary.tldr:
Google Cloud has open-sourced TPU Sync, a C++ library designed to optimize the movement of KV caches and model weights across Cloud TPU memory hierarchies. By treating TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and data center networks as a unified memory space, the library aims to mitigate bottlenecks in large-scale model inference. It supports PyTorch and JAX via Python wheels and is specifically engineered for massive Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, with testing conducted on 235B to 480B parameter architectures on TPU v7x (Ironwood) and v6e hardware.

Technically, TPU Sync utilizes asynchronous DMA to move TPU-tiled tensors without Python serialization or bounce buffers, preserving native layouts to avoid XLA compilation overhead. The library achieves up to 90% reduction in average Time to First Token (TTFT) for 480B parameter models at low concurrency with 64K-context prefix caching. In specific benchmarks, Qwen3 235B KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds to approximately 230 ms. The architecture leverages PCIe Gen5 and 200 Gbps NICs, reaching throughputs of 223 GB/s per host and up to 350 Gbps across dual-NIC DCN configurations.

While the library is available under an Apache-2.0 license, Google explicitly notes it is not yet recommended for general production use. The system integrates with experimental POSIX backends, including local SSDs and Google Cloud Managed Lustre, to manage state across multi-host environments. Despite the performance gains, the current documentation lacks reinforcement learning (RL) benchmarks, and all reported metrics are internal, early-stage results.
takeaways: **Performance Gains:** Achieves up to 90% lower average TTFT for 480B MoE models and reduces Qwen3 235B KV transfer latency to ~230 ms.
**Hardware Throughput:** Reaches 223 GB/s per Ironwood host (near the 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 ceiling) and up to 350 Gbps across two 200 Gbps NICs.
**Architectural Design:** Operates outside the XLA graph using native C++ to perform layout-preserving direct DMA, avoiding Python serialization and bounce buffers.
**Supported Environments:** Compatible with TPU v7x (Ironwood) and v6e, utilizing experimental POSIX backends like local SSDs and Google Cloud Managed Lustre.
**Integration:** Provides Python wheels for PyTorch and JAX, treating TPU HBM, host DRAM, and DCN as a unified memory hierarchy.
