title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
author: Gerhard Trippen (University of Toronto)
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets has been studied as a handwriting-recognition problem: read the move in each box and check that it is legal. This framing misses the errors that matter most. A misread that yields an illegal move is loud. One that yields a legal-but-wrong move is silent, because a legality-only pipeline accepts it and reads every later move against a wrong position. We therefore treat the task as game reconstruction and present Zugwise, which repurposes computer-chess machinery (quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, pin detection) to ask not "what should be played?" but "could a human plausibly have written this?" An absurdity detector makes silent errors loud at or near where they occur, and a backward search traces late symptoms to their cause. Candidate ranking excludes chess-quality signals. A Needleman-Wunsch merge adds the second player's sheet as evidence, and review stops send every disagreement between the sheets' legal readings to a human. In oracle replay of two tournament sections, a release adding them cuts silent errors from 16 to 1 and from 50 to 13. Two learned signals, CTC re-scoring against the recognizer's raw output and a Maia-style human-move prior, raise the correct fix's top-rank rate from 58.8% to 78.0% of the replacement decisions where it is a candidate, and hold without refitting on a later section. On the first section, the human-verified output matches an independent expert transcription move for move on 34 of 45 games, and adjudication against the sheets found errors in both records, on different plies. We do not establish that either workflow is faster or more accurate. The system runs entirely in the browser and is free, private, and offline-capable; alongside it we offer a three-way adjudication protocol for a domain where no single record is ground truth.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced Zugwise, a domain-aware system for digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets that shifts the paradigm from simple handwriting recognition to game reconstruction. Unlike traditional pipelines that rely solely on move legality, Zugwise utilizes computer-chess machinery—including quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, and pin detection—to evaluate the plausibility of human-written moves. By incorporating an 'absurdity detector' and backward search, the system identifies silent errors where a legal but incorrect move causes subsequent moves to be read against an invalid board state.

The system integrates a Needleman-Wunsch merge to reconcile discrepancies between two players' scoresheets, flagging disagreements for human review. Performance metrics from oracle replay on two tournament sections show a significant reduction in silent errors, dropping from 16 to 1 and 50 to 13, respectively. The inclusion of two learned signals—CTC re-scoring and a Maia-style human-move prior—improved the top-rank rate for correct move replacements from 58.8% to 78.0%. In expert verification, the system matched independent transcriptions move-for-move in 34 of 45 games, with adjudication revealing errors in both the system output and the expert records.

Zugwise is designed for privacy and accessibility, running entirely in the browser as a free, offline-capable tool. The authors propose a three-way adjudication protocol to address the lack of a single ground truth in handwritten chess records, though they note that they have not yet established whether this workflow is faster or more accurate than traditional manual transcription methods.
takeaways: **Error Reduction:** Oracle replay testing demonstrated a reduction in silent errors from 16 to 1 and 50 to 13 across two tournament datasets.
**Ranking Improvement:** Integrating CTC re-scoring and a Maia-style human-move prior increased the top-rank rate for correct move replacements from 58.8% to 78.0%.
**Technical Architecture:** The system leverages computer-chess primitives including quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, and pin detection to validate move plausibility.
**Reconciliation Protocol:** The tool uses a Needleman-Wunsch merge to compare dual scoresheets and mandates human review for any legal reading disagreements.
**Deployment:** The software is fully browser-based, offline-capable, and free to use, with a focus on privacy and multi-record adjudication.

title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
author: Egor Pakhomov, Anurag Koul, Hongjun Liu, Bo Pang, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
contentSnippet:
Authors: Egor Pakhomov , Anurag Koul , Hongjun Liu , Bo Pang , Shafiq Joty , Erik Nijkamp

Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

Notes: 23 pages, 6 figures; code and data in ancillary files

summary.tldr:
Researchers Egor Pakhomov, Anurag Koul, Hongjun Liu, Bo Pang, Shafiq Joty, and Erik Nijkamp investigate how editing the history of tool-using language model agents impacts performance when the underlying environment state remains inconsistent with the history. Using their custom AgentCE-Bench and the AppWorld environment, the authors demonstrate that simply providing the 'correct' information in an agent's history is insufficient if it contradicts the actual state of the world, potentially degrading performance below that of an unedited history.

In AgentCE-Bench, the team found that adding a truthful note beside a preserved error increased recovery rates from 51% to 66%, whereas replacing the error with a completed action—making the history look 'clean' while the world remained unchanged—dropped recovery from 50% to 44%. Similarly, in AppWorld, reporting a 'success' receipt for a database write when the effect was actually absent dropped task success from 45% to 28%. Conversely, when the effect was present, the same success receipt raised success rates from 38% to 49%. The study concludes that history editing must be synchronized with the world state, as 'cleaning' a history while an error persists in the environment can leave an agent worse off than if no intervention had occurred.
takeaways: **AgentCE-Bench Performance:** Truthful notes beside errors improved recovery to 66%, while 'clean' history edits (completed actions) dropped recovery to 44%.
**AppWorld Inconsistency:** Reporting success for a database write when the effect was absent reduced task success by 17 percentage points (45% to 28%).
**World-State Dependency:** The impact of a history edit is statistically significant, with success rate differences between present and absent effects reaching 27 points across two receiver models.
**Methodology:** The study utilized a 'freeze' technique, stopping agents mid-task to perform controlled edits to either the history or the world state before passing the state to a receiver model.

title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
author: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, Drew Wadsworth, Venkata Hasith Vattikuti, YuTong Julia Zhang, Jung Hwan Heo, Taeksang Kim, Kesavan Ramakrishnan, Evangelene Stanley, Xinyu Fang, Daniel Y. Fu, Simran Arora
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.

summary.tldr:
Together AI has introduced Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-based system designed for continual optimization of AI inference workloads. Unlike traditional systems that rely on offline benchmarks or slow end-to-end engine re-launches, TKCC utilizes a Tiered Persistent Engine architecture to decouple engine launch overheads from forward pass computation. This approach allows the system to adapt to shifting traffic distributions and diverse model architectures in real-time, addressing the inherent throughput-fidelity tradeoff found in existing inference optimization frameworks.

TKCC employs a cost model to seed its agent-based hill-climbing optimization process with optimal parallelism configurations. In performance testing on the InferenceX benchmark, TKCC demonstrated significant gains over hand-written Megakernels and leading open-source engines. Specifically, it achieved up to 1.7x higher performance on Llama 1B and up to 2.6x higher tokens-per-second (TPS) on frontier models including Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. At a batch size of 1, the compiler reached 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. The system is currently deployed in production at Together AI, where it serves trillions of tokens.
takeaways: **Performance Gains:** TKCC outperforms hand-written Megakernels by 1.7x on Llama 1B and improves TPS by up to 2.6x over existing open-source engines on frontier models.
**Batch Size 1 Benchmarks:** The system achieved 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash at batch size 1.
**Architectural Innovation:** TKCC utilizes a Tiered Persistent Engine to separate engine launch overheads from forward pass computation, enabling continual optimization.
**Optimization Methodology:** The system uses agent-based hill-climbing combined with a cost model to select parallelism configurations for seeding the optimization process.
**Production Scale:** TKCC is currently active in production environments, managing the inference of trillions of tokens.

title: When Should Semantic Priors Enter Partially-Identified Causal Discovery?
author: Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin, Saad Bin Ather, Valentin Six, Lancelot Da Costa, Tommaso Salvatori, Bernhard Scholkopf
contentSnippet:
Authors: Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin , Saad Bin Ather , Valentin Six , Lancelot Da Costa , Tommaso Salvatori , Bernhard Scholkopf

Abstract: Observational causal discovery often leaves causal di- rections unresolved or unstable. Large language mod- els (LLMs) can provide semantic information to resolve these directions, but incorrect proposals can exclude the true causal graph and invalidate downstream inference. We study three separate decisions: where to allocate semantic queries, which proposals to admit, and which causal graphs to retain. Our framework distinguishes population non-identifiability from finite-sample insta- bility, evaluates semantic orientation against statistical and random controls, and examines calibrated admis- sion and error-tolerant DAG retention. Experiments across benchmark networks show that semantic infor- mation improves recovery over coin-flip orientations, but targeting unstable edges has no established ad- vantage over matched-random allocation. The tested admission certificate cannot support nontrivial admis- sion with the available calibration tasks. Moreover, downstream retention depends on reference adequacy: learned references contain the true DAG in only three of 80 planned tasks. These findings separate the value of semantic information from the reliability of its alloca- tion, admission, and retention, and identify calibration size and reference adequacy as key limitations.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin, Saad Bin Ather, Valentin Six, Lancelot Da Costa, Tommaso Salvatori, and Bernhard Schölkopf investigate the integration of semantic priors from Large Language Models (LLMs) into causal discovery processes. The study addresses the challenge of unresolved causal directions in observational data by evaluating how LLM-derived semantic information can be used to orient edges in causal graphs. The authors propose a framework that manages three critical decision points: the allocation of semantic queries, the admission of LLM-generated proposals, and the retention of causal graphs, specifically distinguishing between population non-identifiability and finite-sample instability.

Experimental results across benchmark networks indicate that while semantic information generally outperforms random coin-flip orientations, targeting unstable edges provides no measurable advantage over matched-random allocation. The study reveals significant limitations in current methodologies: the proposed admission certificate failed to support nontrivial admission using available calibration tasks, and learned references contained the true Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) in only three out of 80 planned tasks. These findings highlight that while semantic priors hold potential, the current reliability of their allocation, admission, and retention remains insufficient for robust causal inference.
takeaways: **Research Scope:** The study evaluates the integration of LLM-based semantic priors into causal discovery across 80 distinct tasks.
**Performance Metric:** Semantic information consistently outperformed random coin-flip orientations in recovering causal directions.
**Allocation Findings:** Targeting unstable edges for semantic queries showed no performance advantage compared to matched-random allocation strategies.
**Reference Adequacy:** Learned references successfully contained the true DAG in only 3.75% (3 of 80) of the tested tasks.
**Primary Limitations:** The authors identify calibration task size and the adequacy of reference sets as the two primary bottlenecks preventing reliable causal graph retention.

title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents
author: Jiani Zhang, Manav Garg, Eugenie Lai, Cheng Zhen, Eva Sharma, Yang Pan, Yaming Lin, Alon Halevy
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current benchmarks for LLM-driven data agents saturate quickly and cannot target specific capabilities. We present SynthCorp, a platform that creates customizable data estates and benchmarks by simulating how business events produce and modify corporate data over time. Each data estate combines relational databases, a document store, and a data catalog, paired with evaluation tasks and executable gold programs. First, given a scenario and target complexity dimensions, SynthCorp synthesizes reusable event types and compiles each into a program over predefined simulation primitives. Second, SynthCorp schedules event instances on a virtual calendar, interleaving routine and disruption events so that tables, documents, and catalog entries remain consistent. Third, SynthCorp executes the calendar to materialize the data estate and records every operation in a simulation log. Fourth, SynthCorp generates analytical tasks and derives verified gold programs from the log. We use SynthCorp to generate initial evaluation benchmarks comprising seven data estates (up to 1K operational tables) and 256 tasks across five domains. The data estates pass deterministic pipeline checks (such as foreign-key violations, undeclared writes, recurrence violations, and database execution failures) with a near-zero error rate, introduce cross-asset complexities, and cover all requested dimensions. Evaluating three models across four data-context settings shows that the benchmarks separate data contexts and model tiers. Auditing candidate queries against causal provenance in the simulation log verifies gold programs without manual annotation, including on multi-event composite tasks that expose reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents. We hope the community uses SynthCorp to generate more challenging and useful data estates and benchmarks that foster the development of enterprise data agents.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced SynthCorp, a platform designed to generate customizable data estates and benchmarks for evaluating LLM-driven data agents. Addressing the issue of benchmark saturation, SynthCorp simulates business events to create complex, evolving data environments that include relational databases, document stores, and data catalogs. The platform operates through a four-stage pipeline: synthesizing event types based on target complexity, scheduling events on a virtual calendar to ensure consistency, materializing the data estate, and deriving verified gold programs from the simulation logs.

The initial SynthCorp benchmark suite consists of seven distinct data estates, scaling up to 1,000 operational tables, and 256 analytical tasks across five domains. The system ensures data integrity through deterministic pipeline checks, including foreign-key and recurrence validation, achieving a near-zero error rate. By auditing candidate queries against causal provenance recorded in simulation logs, the platform enables automated verification of gold programs without manual annotation. Testing across three models and four data-context settings demonstrated that the benchmarks effectively differentiate between model tiers and expose reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents, particularly in multi-event composite tasks.
takeaways: **Platform Architecture:** SynthCorp integrates relational databases, document stores, and data catalogs, utilizing simulation primitives to generate consistent, time-evolving corporate data.
**Benchmark Scale:** The initial release includes seven data estates containing up to 1,000 operational tables and 256 tasks spanning five business domains.
**Verification Methodology:** Gold programs are derived automatically from simulation logs using causal provenance, eliminating the need for manual annotation.
**Performance Validation:** The platform successfully identifies reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents by testing against multi-event composite tasks and cross-asset complexities.

title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
author: Xiulin Yang, Sirisha Gudavalli, Jennifer Hu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Xiulin Yang , Sirisha Gudavalli , Jennifer Hu

Abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

Notes: 30 pages, 16 figures

summary.tldr:
Researchers Xiulin Yang, Sirisha Gudavalli, and Jennifer Hu investigate how humans and AI systems utilize implicit temporal cues—specifically the duration of pauses—to achieve social coordination in the absence of explicit communication. Using the cooperative card game 'The Mind' as a testbed, the study evaluates 150 human participants against two distinct classes of AI: computer-use agents (CUAs) and standard text-prompted LLMs. The game requires players to play cards in ascending order without verbal signals, relying entirely on the passage of time to infer a partner's mental state and card values.

The study finds that human performance is best modeled by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's beliefs based on their timing. While frontier AI models demonstrate a capacity for similar probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals, they fail to exhibit the dynamic, iterative adaptation to a partner's behavior that characterizes human play. The authors conclude that while AI can perform implicit reasoning without 'experiencing' real-time, they currently lack the mechanisms to efficiently adapt to partners over the course of repeated interactions, posing a significant hurdle for multi-agent coordination.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Evaluated 150 human participants against two AI architectures (computer-use agents and text-prompted LLMs) using the cooperative game 'The Mind'.
**Human Strategy:** Human behavior is best explained by a Bayesian inference model that interprets pause duration as a signal of a partner's mental state.
**AI Performance Gap:** Unlike humans, the tested AI models failed to adapt their strategies to their partners' specific behaviors over the duration of the game.
**Cognitive Finding:** The research suggests that implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals can emerge in AI systems even without the experience of continuous real-time.

title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
author: Eve Fleisig, Joachim Baumann, Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Dirk Hovy
contentSnippet:
Authors: Eve Fleisig , Joachim Baumann , Dylan Hadfield-Menell , Dirk Hovy

Abstract: Arena-style rankings of language models are a widely used evaluation framework in online leaderboards, research papers, and model evaluation in production. These rankings aim to realistically assess model performance using pairwise comparisons of anonymous models on user prompts, aggregating votes via the Bradley-Terry model to produce the final ranking. However, we find that these leaderboards are highly vulnerable to several manipulation strategies that unscrupulous providers could use to boost a model's rank: strategic voting (individual votes that boost a model's rank, including votes on irrelevant models), strategic prompting (choosing prompts that favor a model), and strategic nomination (boosting the rank of a model by inserting irrelevant models). We demonstrate these effects on public leaderboard data, analyze the circumstances that cause these vulnerabilities, and describe approaches to safeguard against each attack. Notably, these issues hold for any preference-based evaluation using the Bradley-Terry model that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission. These manipulations boost the rank of nearly every tested model; each attack can boost a model by up to 15-20 places in a ranking and, combined, they can boost a model by up to 45 places.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Eve Fleisig, Joachim Baumann, Dylan Hadfield-Menell, and Dirk Hovy have identified critical vulnerabilities in preference-based model evaluation frameworks, such as the Chatbot Arena, which rely on the Bradley-Terry model to aggregate pairwise comparisons. The study demonstrates that these leaderboards are susceptible to manipulation through three primary vectors: strategic voting, where specific votes are cast to artificially inflate a model's standing; strategic prompting, which involves selecting prompts tailored to a model's strengths; and strategic nomination, which introduces irrelevant models to skew the competitive landscape.

These manipulation strategies are not merely theoretical; the authors validated their findings using public leaderboard data, showing that individual attacks can improve a model's ranking by 15 to 20 positions. When these methods are combined, a model can climb as many as 45 places on a leaderboard. The paper concludes that any evaluation system utilizing the Bradley-Terry model in conjunction with open prompting, voting, or model submission is inherently vulnerable to these tactics, and the authors propose specific safeguards to mitigate these risks.
takeaways: **Manipulation Magnitude:** Individual attack vectors can boost a model's rank by 15-20 places, while combined attacks can result in a 45-place improvement.
**Vulnerability Scope:** The findings apply to any preference-based evaluation framework that uses the Bradley-Terry model and permits open prompting, voting, or model submission.
**Attack Vectors:** The research identifies three distinct methods of manipulation: strategic voting, strategic prompting, and strategic nomination.
**Methodology:** The authors validated their claims by analyzing public leaderboard data and assessing the impact of these strategies on model rankings.

title: Robust Task-Aware State Estimation from Pre-trained Perception
author: Guy Azran, Sarah Keren
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents that perform state estimation using pretrained perception models, e.g., Vision-Language Models (VLMs), face the fundamental challenge that predictions are uncertain. Still, most approaches determinize these predictions into a single best-guess state and make decisions as if it were ground truth. This is brittle because when the guess is wrong, the agent's decisions may be unsafe or infeasible. At the other extreme, maintaining a full probability distribution over symbolic states is often intractable. We propose a middle path, drawing on the underlying probabilities the perception model already produces (e.g., a VLM's output-layer token distributions) to construct a $\theta$-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS$_\theta$), a minimal subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-specified belief-mass threshold. The minimality of an MBS$_\theta$ ensures that the agent considers only the most likely states, enhancing robustness in downstream decision-making while maintaining computational tractability. Using a novel three-layered belief system, we efficiently approximate individual state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints. On this belief construction, we base our MBS$_\theta$ construction, while maintaining only a lean factored representation of the belief. Our algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), takes advantage of the unique structure of this belief system to construct an MBS$_\theta$ with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case. Using a VLM as the backbone of our state estimator, we validate our method's theoretical properties, scalability with problem size, and improvement of downstream decision-making when used in a task-planning pipeline.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced a framework for robust state estimation in autonomous agents that utilize pre-trained perception models, such as Vision-Language Models (VLMs), to address the inherent uncertainty in model predictions. Rather than forcing a single 'best-guess' state—which often leads to brittle or unsafe decision-making—or attempting the computationally intractable task of maintaining a full probability distribution, the authors propose the Minimal Belief Set (MBS_θ). This approach constructs a subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-defined threshold, ensuring the agent focuses only on the most likely outcomes while maintaining computational efficiency.

The methodology relies on a three-layered belief system that approximates individual state probabilities by leveraging the output-layer token distributions already generated by the VLM, combined with task-level constraints. The core algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), exploits the structure of this belief system to build the MBS_θ with formal correctness guarantees. The authors demonstrate that PRaVaSS operates with polynomial complexity in unconstrained scenarios and maintains a lean, factored representation of the belief, making it suitable for integration into complex task-planning pipelines.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** The framework uses a 'Minimal Belief Set' (MBS_θ) to represent uncertainty, selecting the smallest subset of states that satisfies a user-specified probability mass threshold.
**Algorithm Name:** The proposed algorithm is titled Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS).
**Technical Foundation:** The system utilizes the output-layer token distributions of pre-trained VLMs to approximate state probabilities, avoiding the need for full distribution tracking.
**Complexity:** PRaVaSS provides correctness guarantees and achieves polynomial complexity in unconstrained cases.
**Research Identifier:** The paper is cataloged as arXiv:2611.14781v1.

title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
author: Abhinav Gupta, Ben Slivinski, Yashica Patodia, Michael Saldivar
contentSnippet:
Authors: Abhinav Gupta , Ben Slivinski , Yashica Patodia , Michael Saldivar

Abstract: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. We provide per-configuration results and evaluation details in the supplement.

Notes: 13 pages, 1 figure, 13 tables. Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI) at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Abhinav Gupta, Ben Slivinski, Yashica Patodia, and Michael Saldivar authored a paper accepted at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI) at NeurIPS 2026 evaluating proof-step verification pipelines on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. The pipeline rewrites solver answers into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline them.

Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 percentage points on AIME, but answers only 35% and 21% of attempts respectively. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains reach at most 5 points at the cost of losing 13 to 27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector achieves 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared to the verifier's pooled 87.6% precision (paired difference of +4.8 points with a 95% interval of [-8.2, 18.5]).

A diagnostic sample reveals that 52 out of 88 completed problems fail due to invalid proof construction without reaching a judge. External-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains ranges from 61.0% to 67.6%, lagging behind the 87.6% answer-key match rate. Furthermore, open-weight auditor pairs exhibit near-zero chance-corrected agreement, measuring consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth.
takeaways: **Precision vs Coverage Gains:** Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on GPQA and 46 on AIME, while retaining only 35% and 21% of attempts.
**MATH-500 Performance:** On near-ceiling MATH-500, accuracy gains are capped at 5 points while sacrificing 13 to 27 points of coverage.
**Self-Consistency Comparison:** An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared to the verifier's pooled 87.6% precision.
**Failure Modes:** A diagnostic sample shows 52 of 88 completed problems terminate in invalid proof construction prior to reaching an LLM judge.
**Auditor Disagreement:** External-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6% (versus 87.6% answer-key match), and open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement.

title: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering
author: Noah J. Bagazinski, Cyril Picard, Faez Ahmed
contentSnippet:
Authors: Noah J. Bagazinski , Cyril Picard , Faez Ahmed

Abstract: Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training. Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.

summary.tldr:
Noah J. Bagazinski, Cyril Picard, and Faez Ahmed introduce GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator designed to augment small engineering datasets by leveraging a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. Aimed at overcoming the data scarcity imposed by costly engineering simulations and experiments, GenPFN operates using a context of evaluated designs labeled as desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). The framework interpolates between desired designs and refines generated candidates using gated classifier gradients combined with Gaussian noise, subsequently evaluating each candidate against problem-specific constraints and objective functions before using successful results to augment regression training.

Tested across fourteen engineering problems ranging from a two-parameter benchmark to a 44-parameter hull problem, GenPFN paired with TabPFN v1 outperforms baseline generators. In paired comparisons, it achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than tested adversarial networks, variational autoencoders (VAEs), and diffusion generators, while offering lower coverage distance and greater diversity than the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), though VAEs provide greater overall coverage and diversity. Additionally, augmenting datasets with GenPFN reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% compared to context-only training, and a hull-stern case study demonstrates a 99.3% propeller-compatible candidate generation rate compared to 1.4% for randomly sampled context designs.
takeaways: **Core Architecture:** GenPFN is a training-free candidate generator utilizing a pretrained TabPFN classifier with fixed weights to guide design augmentation using labeled desired and undesired context instances.

**Comparative Benchmark Performance:** GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves superior class satisfaction and lower realism distance than tested adversarial, variational autoencoder, and diffusion generators across fourteen evaluated problems.

**Diversity and Coverage Metrics:** GenPFN delivers lower coverage distance and greater diversity than SMOTE, whereas variational-autoencoder generators exhibit greater coverage and diversity overall.
**Predictive Modeling Impact:** Data augmentation using GenPFN reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to training on context-only data.
**Case Study Results:** A 44-parameter hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates using GenPFN, compared to 1.4% achieved by randomly sampled context designs.

title: AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
author: Igor Sadalski, Minghao Guo, Benjamin Jones, Wojciech Matusik
contentSnippet:
Authors: Igor Sadalski , Minghao Guo , Benjamin Jones , Wojciech Matusik

Abstract: Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: speculative decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share.

Notes: 52 pages (9 main + references and appendix), 14 figures, 13 tables

By writing algorithms as formal proofs where assumptions are explicit, the authors formalized 89 existing algorithms across KV-cache eviction, weight pruning, and speculative decoding, verifying them using the Lean proof checker. For example, speculative decoding is framed by dropping the assumption that a model requires exactly one forward pass per token.

The 52-page paper comprises 9 main pages accompanied by extensive references and an appendix containing 14 figures and 13 tables. title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
author: Reuth Mirsky, Sarath Sreedharan, Nitay Alon, Stefan Sarkadi, Munindar P. Singh, Liz Sonenberg, Peter Stone, Silvia Tulli, Stylianos Loukas Vasileiou, Shlomo Zilberstein
contentSnippet:
Authors: Reuth Mirsky , Sarath Sreedharan , Nitay Alon , Stefan Sarkadi , Munindar P. Singh , Liz Sonenberg , Peter Stone , Silvia Tulli , Stylianos Loukas Vasileiou , Shlomo Zilberstein

Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

Notes: Part of The AAMAS Community Agentic AI Report

title: Effective Teacher Support for Reasoning Distillation
author: Lavinia Ghita, Dhruv Desai
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forward-KL language-model distillation normally computes dense teacher and student scores over the full vocabulary at every supervised position, making training and stored teacher targets expensive. We instead distill from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing the retained mass as we sweep support from 100% to 0.01%. Our main study distills Qwen3 4B -> 1.7B. We confirm the broader support-reduction finding on larger Qwen3 8B -> 4B and Nemotron Nano 12B -> 9B pairs and under answer-only supervision. We evaluate generation primarily on MMLU-Pro and secondarily on GPQA-Diamond. Across the Qwen3 settings, retaining 0.01% of the vocabulary causes no observed MMLU-Pro degradation relative to full-vocabulary distillation, although disagreement with the complete teacher distribution increases. Nemotron Nano matches full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro at 0.1%, but smaller fractions fail to emit the closing reasoning tag, showing that the reliable cutoff depends on the model family. At 0.01% support, caching the retained next-token scores from the teacher forward pass cuts training step time by 38%, while restricting student output computation to those tokens cuts peak memory by 24%; neither causes observed MMLU-Pro degradation.

By renormalizing the retained probability mass, the authors demonstrate that distillation remains effective even when support is reduced from 100% to as low as 0.01%. The study primarily evaluates Qwen3 4B-to-1.7B distillation, with additional validation on Qwen3 8B-to-4B and Nemotron Nano 12B-to-9B pairs, using MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond as primary benchmarks.

Technical results indicate that for Qwen3 models, retaining only 0.01% of the vocabulary results in no MMLU-Pro degradation compared to full-vocabulary distillation, despite increased divergence from the complete teacher distribution. The Nemotron Nano family requires a higher 0.1% threshold to maintain performance, as lower fractions lead to failures in emitting closing reasoning tags, suggesting that optimal support cutoffs are model-family dependent. Implementing this 0.01% support strategy yields a 38% reduction in training step time via cached teacher scores and a 24% reduction in peak memory usage by limiting student output computation to the restricted token set.

**Model Performance:** Qwen3 models maintain full MMLU-Pro performance at 0.01% support, while Nemotron Nano 12B-9B requires 0.1% to avoid reasoning tag generation failures.
**Methodology:** The approach replaces standard dense Forward-KL distillation with a sparse method that renormalizes the teacher's highest-probability mass.
**Evaluation Metrics:** Benchmarking focused on MMLU-Pro for primary performance validation and GPQA-Diamond for secondary assessment.

title: Can an AI Agent Be Epistemically Akratic? Higher-Order Evidence & the Limits of Self-Correction
author: Eno Agolli
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When we judge that our reasoning was defective, it seems plausible that we should abandon the conclusion it produced. This thought has special force for AI agents built to assess and correct their own work. Yet obeying such judgments can make an agent worse at distinguishing sound reasoning from defective reasoning. An AI agent may rely on information about its reasoning when deciding which conclusions to keep, while the part that judges whether those conclusions are justified cannot use that information. The agent can then exercise an epistemic competence by retaining conclusions it judges unjustified, even when its self-assessments are generally reliable. Nor is the difficulty resolved by training the agent to make its conclusions and assessments agree: agreement can be achieved by degrading either one. Crucially, I argue that a negative assessment can remain valuable by identifying conclusions requiring further scrutiny, without having authority to eliminate them. The result challenges a central assumption about AI self-correction: that bringing an agent's beliefs into agreement with its own self-assessment about their justification makes it better at correcting its mistakes.

title: MuEdit: An efficient multi-task editing method towards inter-domain knowledge conflicts
author: Songshi Liang, Ting-En Lin, Zixuan Huang, Yuchuan Wu, Yongbin Li, Zihe Wang, Rui Yan
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.

title: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs
author: Zahraa Selim, Menna Hamed, Wesam Ahmed, Sohyla Said, Sara Basheer, Rami Zewail
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.

title: Provably Optimal HBT Legalization in Seconds: Certified Optima Reveal Where the Headroom Really Lies
author: Kadhir Parani, Manjunath Bezawada, Divya M, Kesana Jathin, Kolli Sarath, Sm Zobaed
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid bonding terminal (HBT) legalization assigns every terminal of a face-to-face 3D IC to its own pitch-grid site with minimum total Manhattan displacement. Open3DBench reports that a reinforcement-learning (RL) legalizer reduces displacement by 19-22% relative to a sliding-window (SW) heuristic, but none of its legalizers is publicly released. We ask how much displacement any legalizer can still recover. We build an open benchmark of 21 design/pitch instances from Open3DBench placement data, with reconstructed greedy, SW (ViaLegal-style) and BTAssign-style baselines, and GEO-Exact, an exact solver that runs successive shortest augmenting paths over lazily generated spatial candidate edges. An independent dual certificate proves its assignment optimal on all 21 instances (relative primal-dual gap at most $8.2 \times 10^{-16}$). Against these optima, our SW reconstruction with ViaLegal's default configuration is on average 0.011% above optimal (worst 0.119%), while on the 16 contended instances BTAssign-style, a density-guided heuristic (DGHL) and greedy are 3.0%, 6.9% and 64.5% above. Headroom does appear outside this regime: with 2x2 windows SW reaches 34.1%, and above about 58% utilization, on three of six swept designs, it reaches 21.1% on bp, 27.5% on swerv and 8.9% on jpeg (217 further certified instances, and ten bp points checked against an independent exact solver). If the published 19-22% gain were measured on instances like ours, SW would have to be at least 24-28% above optimal on average, far more than any SW variant we tested at nominal pitch; the RL paper's own comparison with the Hungarian optimum puts its SW 3.05% above optimal on average. GEO-Exact is also about an order of magnitude faster than DGHL and SW in our harness (geometric means 8.1x and 40x; a compiled core against Python baselines on a shared server). Code, optimal values and certificates are released.

title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training
author: Qi Zhang, Bohan Wang, Qianru Sun, Hanwang Zhang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.

title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
author: Binghang Lu, Lang Cao, Changhong Mou, Yige Sun, Cindy Xiangrui Kong, Zheyuan Deng, Tian Yuan, Bing Hu, Runyu Zhang, Na Lu, Guang Lin
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late
author: Musa Cim, Burak Topcu, Mahmut Taylan Kandemir
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents can solve a task well before they stop working on it. We characterize \emph{termination lag}--the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run--across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution. Our analysis reveals that 38--82% of successful runs achieve a correct solution on their initial source-code edit. However, agents continue to expend substantial effort after correct patches, with post-solution steps accounting for a median of 35--37% for Qwen3-Coder and 54--60% for Laguna-XS.2 in successful runs on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Agents spend most of these additional steps verifying their work and exploring the repository. In a small fraction of cases (1--8%), this continued activity leads agents to undo their earlier correct patch, leaving the final solution incorrect.

title: Abstention Is Not Threshold Compliance: Stated Scoring Rules in Open Language Models
author: Dongsun Moon
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kalai et al. propose stating the scoring rule in the prompt with an explicit threshold t, so that a model should answer only when its probability of being correct exceeds t. We probe each requirement of compliance on shared items, in 12 checkpoints from three post-training stages of four fully open 3-8B recipes, with exploratory models up to 32B. At t = 0.75, a line limiting the reply to an answer or "I abstain" (the abstention format) raised the mean abstention rate from 20% to 91%. Yet within this format, raising t from 0.5 to 0.9 changed it by only -0.8 percentage points. Without the line, the higher threshold even lowered abstention, and up to 40% of a checkpoint's items received decisions that no compliant policy with threshold-independent beliefs could make. Given the probability that their answer was correct, the checkpoints barely responded to the threshold in a forced-choice probe. Comparisons with self-assessment signals such as P(True) depended on the grader and on answer drift between prompts. An external threshold on recalibrated P(True) made coverage non-increasing in t by construction. title: MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation
author: Kayshav Bhardwaj, Pragun Seth, Kush Bhardwaj, Vijay Nagasamy, Kurt Keutzer
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical Sanskrit poses three challenges unresolved by single-call monolithic models: morphophonemic fusion Sandhi, dense nominal compounding Sam\=asa, and discourse-level zero-anaphora forced by poetic meter. We present MITRA-Swarm, a multi-agent architecture injecting explicit linguistic structure into an otherwise monolithic pipeline: a Sandhi-splitting agent, a parallel array of generalist gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and domain-specialized gemma-2-mitra-it translators, and a discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer that consults corpus-derived register tags to avoid inventing active-voice subjects in impersonal legal and philosophical registers. Two separated judges evaluate quality: a routing judge ($J_{\text{route}}$, same model family as the generators) driving an internal critique loop, and an independent reporting judge ($J_{\text{report}}=$gpt-4o-mini, no shared vendor lineage) scoring every output exactly once. On a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses across five registers (23,990 scored verdicts, 12-condition pre-registered ablation), the full swarm reaches $85.90$ MQM against a monolithic baseline of $85.27$ ($\Delta=+0.63$, $p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018$, 95% CI $[+0.30,+0.97]$), and isolated discourse restoration alone accounts for $+0.44$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$), outperforming a call-count-matched self-refinement baseline by $+0.51$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$). Severe per-verse failures (MQM$<80$) fall from $9.0\%$ to $7.6\%$, at roughly $9\times$ the per-verse inference cost of the baseline. Additionally, $J_{\text{route}}$ scores its own family's outputs $2$-$7$ MQM higher than $J_{\text{report}}$ on every one of the 12 conditions, empirically motivating the two-judge split; and a preflight screen of a 192,151-entry retrieval index against all 12 evaluation works verifies 0 reference leaks across 269 runtime checks. These are small gains on a metric saturating near 85-86.

title: Probe What-If Worlds Before You Ship: Persona Simulation for Real-World Decision Making
author: Julie Zhu, Jianheng Hou, Zhixu Silvia Tao, Shi Bo, Yilan Fan, Yixuan He, Zhiyuan Hu, Shirley Huang, Fangyu Liu, Yijun Wang, Zibu Wei, Haimingyue Xu, Zhen Xu, Zichen Yuan, Jierui Zuo, Jintao Huang, Yifan Wang, Qianfeng Wen, Jiahan Li, Zhejian Peng, Bowen Yang, Shushu Liang, Yuexing Hao, Xiaomin Li
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: User research and system testing reveal whether products and services meet user needs, yet recruiting specialized participants, designing controlled what-if comparisons, and repeating studies as designs evolve often bottleneck design iteration and data-driven decision-making. We present a framework and execution infrastructure that translates real-world industry inquiries into controlled experiments with simulated users. Our methodology formally defines the target cohort, experimental stimuli, and decision-relevant metrics, while the pipeline supports large-scale concurrent runs over cohort-stimulus-environment combinations (survey, web, chatbot, and OS app), auditable trial-level logging, cohort-level outcome aggregation, and cross-cohort and cross-variant statistical reports. Across twelve industry partner cases spanning five domains, we show how constructing hard-to-reach or what-if persona cohorts supports exploratory studies and distills simulated responses into testable design hypotheses. Cross-model comparisons on selected cases largely preserve primary conclusions, whereas perturbing or ablating persona attributes alters service outcomes, effect sizes, and inter-group differences, indicating that grounding target cohorts in detailed personas materially shapes simulation results. Together, these studies show that persona-enabled agents can test specified cohorts at design speed, diagnose systems under test, and deliver directional evidence that focuses problem definition, steers design and strategic decisions, and guides further study.

title: Benchmarking Multilingual Document Understanding in Vision-Language Models
author: Matteo Gabburo, Daniela Baiamonte, Stefano Simonazzi, Silvia Gardini, Sean Cesare Lazzeri, Andrea Zugarini
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform strongly on multimodal tasks, Document Understanding (DU) among them, but the benchmarks that measure them mostly cover English documents and narrow problems. How well current VLMs generalize across languages, tasks, styles and layouts therefore remains unclear. We introduce MDU, a multilingual DU benchmark of 23146 examples spanning 13 tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. The tasks isolate complementary capabilities, from surface-level text and Markdown extraction through summarization, classification and named-entity recognition to layout-sensitive passage and layout extraction. We evaluate 45 state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system under the same protocol. The benchmark is far from saturated: the best average is 69.0, only eight of the 45 evaluated systems reach 65, and the two best results come from 27B models rather than from the largest systems we evaluate. Performance is uneven in ways that scale does not fix. The gap between the strongest and weakest language does not close as models grow, and it survives controlling for the domain composition of each language. Capabilities also do not improve together: once we partial out overall model quality, per-task scores are largely uncorrelated, and transcription ability in particular trades off against semantic extraction.

title: An LLM Is All You Need: Data-Efficient Adaptation to Full-Duplex, Word-Level Spoken Dialogue
author: Tairan Chen, Richard Yucheng He, Yihang Liu, Baodong Cao, Chen Xu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue, in which a system listens while it speaks and can backchannel, yield the floor, and be interrupted, is usually obtained by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. This is costly, rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and still leaves turn-taking either implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. We show that a frozen, general-purpose multimodal LLM can instead be adapted into a word-level full-duplex system with little data. Our system is a thinker-talker cascade on an 80 ms frame clock. The thinker keeps the LLM frozen and trains only lightweight adapters and a few new token embeddings (97M parameters); at every frame it emits one token of agent text, with pauses, yields, and onsets represented as tokens of the same vocabulary and kept legal by a finite-state machine. A four-stage curriculum, each stage anchored to the model's own behavior under the previous format, performs the conversion in about 30 GPU-hours. The talker reads only the thinker's discrete tokens, so the two halves are trained independently. On Full-Duplex-Bench and InteractionBench, the system is competitive with open-source full-duplex systems built through large-scale speech training: among them, it is the least likely to take the floor when the user merely pauses, backchannels most often, and leads in spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and coherence over long conversations.

title: Distributionally Robust BEST-RQ For Speech Representation Learning
author: Muhammad Khan, Xiaodong Cui, Brian Kingsbury, George Saon
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: BEST-RQ, based on random projection and quantization, has been a well-established self-supervised learning approach to learn speech representations from large-scale unlabeled audio due to its high performance and efficiency. However, in BEST-RQ representations learned by random quantization can be sensitive to the choice of quantization targets. To address this issue, we propose a distributionally robust extension of BEST-RQ that seeks representations robust across multiple quantization configurations. Specifically, we define groups by codebooks and formulate the training as a group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem. Rather than optimizing solely for the average loss across groups, our approach adaptively reweights groups to emphasize those performing poorly. Additionally, we regularize DRO with a Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent excessive distribution deviation. We evaluate our approach on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset and show that the distributionally robust BEST-RQ achieves superior performance over the conventional uniform average across multiple codebooks.

title: What Do Tokenizer Comparisons Measure? Disentangling Granularity, Root Assignment, and Word-Level Readout across Amharic and Hausa
author: Abdul Rehman Antall, Baidya Nath Saha
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Morphology-aware tokenizers are expected to help morphologically rich languages, and their reported gains over byte-pair encoding (BPE) are usually credited to their linguistic units. A comparison with BPE cannot support this attribution, since such a tokenizer also segments text more finely (granularity) and, on token-level tasks, changes how much the sub-token readout matters. We separate both factors from the effect of grouping words by their roots (root assignment) in Amharic, a Semitic language whose Ge'ez abugida hides consonantal roots inside syllabic glyphs, with Latin-script Hausa as an orthographic contrast. Our design combines a lossless root-and-pattern tokenizer with controls that change one factor at a time, in two independent implementations. In both, real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots (+4.9 and +4.7 F1), and root-frequency structure explains little of this gain. In small from-scratch models, the readout choice moves F1 by up to 13.4 points and reverses the sign of every comparison of the root-and-pattern arms with BPE, whereas in two pretrained encoders it moves F1 by less than one point. The granularity effect changes sign across languages and implementations. We recommend decomposing tokenizer effects, and reporting the readout, before a gain is attributed to linguistic structure.

title: Discharge Summary Generation Is Not Just Summarization: A Reality Check for Evaluation
author: Radhika Dua, Frederick Wolff, Kyunghyun Cho, Eric Karl Oermann
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discharge summaries combine a retrospective account of hospitalization with discharge-time decisions. Physician-written references therefore contain both facts supported by prior clinical notes and reference-only content, potentially reflecting clinical synthesis, handoffs, or discharge planning. Reference-only evaluation can conflate failure to recover available information with failure to reproduce content absent from the model input. We introduce FairSumEval, an evidence-aware, fact-level framework that assesses whether each reference and generated fact is supported by the model's evidence and captured by the other summary. The resulting outcome map separates matches, omissions, and additions. Two complementary metrics, Soft IoU-S and Soft IoU-NS, measure reference-generation agreement for facts with and without identified evidence support. On 200 MIMIC-III admissions, 18.8% of physician reference facts have identified support in the prior evidence, compared with 65.4% and 63.5% of facts generated by a general-purpose and a medically specialized model. Overlap is substantially higher for supported content (0.255 and 0.236) than for content without identified support (0.030 and 0.026). The two scores are weakly correlated across admissions (rho = 0.22 and 0.17), and conventional metrics do not consistently capture both dimensions. FairSumEval distinguishes evidence-grounded summarization from agreement on content without identified support, revealing what models omit and add in each category.

title: LLMs and the Homogenization of Teaching
author: Mei Tan, Hyunji Nam, Hari Subramonyam, Dorottya Demszky
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to lack diversity in open-ended text generation, a limitation that is especially consequential in education, where homogeneity can narrow the kinds of thinking and disciplinary work students are invited to do. We study diversity in two educational generation tasks: math items and essay feedback. We compare frontier and open-weight models with human-authored reference distributions using lexical, semantic, and domain-grounded measures. For math, we examine the mathematical activities students are asked to perform; for feedback, we examine the revision work requested and the rhetorical strategies used to communicate it. We evaluate direct prompting, two diversity prompting methods, and post-training. Across both tasks, directly prompted model outputs are markedly less diverse than human-authored content--78% higher on lexical (Self-BLEU) and 51% higher on semantic (embedding) similarity--and represent a narrower range of instructional forms. Diversity prompting and post-training increase variation largely through surface features without broadening the instructional repertoire. Models inherit and amplify the most normative routines of human instruction. Overcoming mode collapse in education will require richer instructional data and investment in teachers' creative capacity and professional judgment.

title: Is Jev a Good Multilingual Judge?
author: Wei Liu, Yi Fan, Xiyan Fu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative large language models are widely used for multilingual text evaluation, yet whether decision models that directly output judgment probabilities can serve as multilingual judges has received limited attention. We evaluate Jev against generative LLM judges on four multilingual benchmarks with human annotations, covering up to 47 language varieties and three evaluation formats: binary decisions, pairwise comparisons, and graded ratings. At approximately $1/31$ to $1/61$ of GPT-6.1's evaluation cost, Jev is competitive on most multilingual judging tasks, but falls behind GPT-6.1 on knowledge-intensive answer verification. Further analysis shows that Jev is more likely to accept incorrect answers in low-resource languages than in English and that its probability outputs help identify errors across tasks. Based on these findings, we offer recommendations on evaluation instructions, confidence-based selection, and model routing, providing empirical guidance for using Jev as a multilingual judge.

title: Hy ASR 3.0 Technical Report
author: Aoxiong Yin, Auden Li, Chao Huang, Chuanyang Hu, Eitan Wang, Ethan Zou, Fangming Feng, Guangyu Chen, Guinan Li, He Wang, Jiahong Li, Meng Yu, Mingyu Cui, Peng Wang, Rongjie Li, Steve Yves, Teddy Sun, Tian Zheng, Wei Liu, Yang Zhou, Yixuan Zhang, Zhennan Lin, Zhihang Xu, Zhuohao Li, Ziqiang Zhang, Anji Zhang, Bang Wang, Caisheng Ouyang, Chengqi Zhu, Chong Li, Conglian Xie, Dongdong Wang, Edward Wang, Evelynn Liu, Ferman Yang, Feng Lu, Gang Zhang, Jathon Zhang, Jaxl Liu, Jiachen Luo, Jian Li, Jingxi Gui, Kysun Wang, Liang Dong, Longsha Zhou, Na Hu, Qi Chen, Rilin Chen, Rui Yuan, Shanshan Sang, Siyu Yan, Steven Hong, Taihui Wang, Weiwei Li, Xiangyu Zhang, Xiaotong Yang, Xue Hu, Xue Jiang, Yameng Li, Yifu Sun, Yuhuan Zhou, Zhiang Chen, Zhibin Wang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Hy ASR 3.0, a large language model (LLM)-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) system that delivers strong recognition accuracy, supports flexible contextual conditioning, and maintains robust recognition performance across diverse speech conditions. Hy ASR 3.0 supports Mandarin Chinese, English and 13 Chinese dialect groups, including Cantonese. Among the evaluated systems, it achieves the lowest aggregate error rates on public Mandarin Chinese, English, and Cantonese benchmarks and the lowest error rates on the corresponding internal test sets, alongside first-tier dialect recognition performance. Beyond audio-only transcription, Hy ASR 3.0 supports multiple forms of external context, including hotword lists, question--answer dialogues, and summaries, enabling the use of task-relevant information during recognition. The model also leverages intra-utterance context to disambiguate homophonic and phonetically similar keywords using information from other parts of the same utterance, without requiring a separate contextual input. Evaluations demonstrate strong contextual recognition in both external-context and intra-utterance settings, as well as robust recognition of long-form speech, children's and older adults' speech, low-volume speech, and speech in noisy environments. This report describes the model architecture and training methodology and presents evaluations across recognition accuracy, context utilization, and robustness.

title: ToolTurns: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Multi-Turn Dialogue
author: Milad Gholami, Brendan King, Jeffrey Flanigan
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.14925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language models are increasingly deployed in conversational settings, yet most large-scale tool-use benchmarks focus on isolated requests. We introduce ToolTurns, a benchmark of 2,620 problems spanning 1,827 tools and 11,004 API endpoints across 47 categories. Each dialogue begins with an intentionally underspecified request and continues through two context-dependent follow-ups, testing clarification, tool use, and retention of conversational context. We also introduce an open-source user simulator that reveals withheld context through dialogue and generates follow-up requests, with a checker--fixer pipeline for improving its turns. Across nine language models, the best agent resolves 69.6% of individual requests but completes only 39.8% of full dialogues. Under this evaluation protocol, every evaluated model receives lower success scores on follow-up requests than on the initial request, and dialogue-quality rubric scores and task success can rank models very differently. Paired turn-level evaluation shows that the checker--fixer reduces detected dialogue defects, and blind human evaluation favors the revised turns. ToolTurns provides a testbed for evaluating whether agents sustain task success across multi-turn dialogue with tools.

summary.tldr:
