summary.tldr:
Nvidia has introduced 'Scale-In,' a new architectural pillar for AI networking designed to secure and manage agentic AI factories. As autonomous agents increasingly operate within enterprise infrastructure, Scale-In provides a framework for tenant isolation, secure data movement, and predictable performance. The architecture is built to address the unique security challenges of multi-agent environments, ensuring that agents remain contained within sandboxes and preventing unauthorized access to memory, storage, and compute resources.

The technical foundation of Scale-In relies on the integration of Nvidia BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs), the Nvidia DOCA software framework, and Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. BlueField-4 serves as the hardware-based security engine, performing out-of-band monitoring of system telemetry across CPUs, GPUs, and storage. This is complemented by the open-source OpenShell runtime, which governs agent execution and access. The recently announced OpenShell Reference Architecture further incorporates Nvidia Sentry, a DOCA-based enforcement layer that continuously monitors agent behavior and can automatically quarantine agents that attempt to breach defined software boundaries.
takeaways: **Hardware Foundation:** Scale-In utilizes the fourth-generation BlueField-4 DPU, which features in-silicon security engines for out-of-band monitoring.
**Software Framework:** Nvidia DOCA provides the APIs and software-defined infrastructure necessary to offload, accelerate, and isolate workloads at the DPU level.

**Agent Governance:** The OpenShell runtime manages agent execution and inference routing, while the OpenShell Reference Architecture adds Nvidia Sentry for independent, hardware-enforced quarantine capabilities.
**Network Connectivity:** The architecture is interconnected via Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet, optimized for the high-performance requirements of large-scale AI factories.

title: Liquid AI Releases LiquidCodec, a 74M-Parameter Streaming Audio Codec
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Liquid AI has released LiquidCodec , the audio codec behind its LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B models. The LiquidCodec audio codec is a ~74M-parameter streaming speech tokenizer. It turns speech into tokens a language model can predict, then converts those tokens back into audio. Liquid AI had 2 goals: easy-to-predict tokens and fast conversion back to speech. The weights are on Hugging Face . TL;DR Size: ~74M parameters (73.6M on the model card ); 24 kHz audio, 12.5 Hz frames, 12 codebooks. Runs on: a single CPU thread (tested on an Apple M4 Max laptop, FP32); CUDA GPUs via Transformers; Q4_0, Q4_K_M and Q8_0 GGUF builds for llama.cpp. Performance: best ViSQOL and lowest mel distance on all 8 test sets versus X-Codec 2, NanoCodec and Mimi. Best: ~361x real-time encoding on 1 CPU thread (encode RTF 0.0028 vs Mimi’s 0.0361). What is LiquidCodec? LiquidCodec is a Liquid AI speech codec that compresses 24 kHz audio into 12 token streams. Each 80 ms frame becomes 12 discrete tokens, per the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . It replaces Kyutai’s Mimi , which Liquid AI used in LFM2-Audio-1.5B. Mimi has 96.2M parameters. How does LiquidCodec work? The pipeline is encode, quantize, decode. Liquid AI uses blocks from its LFM3 architecture in both the encoder and decoder. The 2 halves are symmetric, and the encoder is fully causal, which suits streaming. Quantization uses grouped finite scalar quantization (GFSQ) instead of residual vector quantization (RVQ). In RVQ, each codebook encodes what the previous one missed. GFSQ groups are independent, so all 12 codebooks can be predicted in parallel by MaskGIT-style transformers. The decoder predicts spectral coefficients directly. This avoids learned transposed-convolution upsampling, a common cost in waveform decoders. How was it trained? Training ran in 2 stages. Stage 1 used 264,000 hours of speech across 107 languages. It applied waveform and spectral losses, without adversarial losses. Stage 2 fine-tuned on 55,000 hours of full-band speech (24 kHz or higher) with adversarial critics. Liquid AI says this removed metallic artifacts left after stage 1. A final decoder-only quantization-aware training (QAT) step targets edge inference. How fast is LiquidCodec? Liquid AI measured speed in FP32 on 1 CPU thread of an Apple M4 Max MacBook Pro. LiquidCodec ran at ~361x real time for encoding and ~87x for decoding. These are self-rep

summary.tldr:
Liquid AI has released LiquidCodec, a 73.6M-parameter streaming speech tokenizer designed to serve as the foundational audio codec for its LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B models. Replacing the 96.2M-parameter Mimi codec used in previous iterations, LiquidCodec is optimized for high-speed, low-latency speech-to-token conversion. The model is available on Hugging Face and supports deployment via CUDA GPUs or CPU-based inference using GGUF formats (Q4_0, Q4_K_M, and Q8_0) for llama.cpp, achieving 361x real-time encoding on a single Apple M4 Max CPU thread.

Technically, LiquidCodec utilizes a symmetric encoder-decoder architecture based on Liquid AI’s LFM3 blocks, featuring a fully causal encoder for streaming applications. Unlike traditional codecs that rely on residual vector quantization (RVQ), LiquidCodec employs grouped finite scalar quantization (GFSQ). This approach allows the 12 codebooks to be predicted in parallel by MaskGIT-style transformers, as the groups are independent rather than sequential. The decoder generates spectral coefficients directly, bypassing the computational overhead of learned transposed-convolution upsampling. Training occurred in two stages: an initial 264,000-hour speech dataset across 107 languages using waveform and spectral losses, followed by a 55,000-hour fine-tuning stage with adversarial critics to eliminate metallic artifacts, concluding with a quantization-aware training (QAT) step for edge performance.
takeaways: **Architecture Specs:** 73.6M parameters, 24 kHz audio sampling, 12.5 Hz frame rate, and 12 discrete codebooks per 80ms frame.
**Performance Benchmarks:** Outperforms X-Codec 2, NanoCodec, and Mimi across all 8 test sets in ViSQOL scores and mel distance metrics.
**Inference Speed:** Achieves ~361x real-time encoding and ~87x real-time decoding on a single Apple M4 Max CPU thread (FP32).
**Quantization Method:** Uses Grouped Finite Scalar Quantization (GFSQ) to enable parallel token prediction, replacing the sequential Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) standard.

title: Democrats launch Nvidia investigation, write scathing letter on Huang’s ‘scheme’ with Trump
author: Julie Bort
contentSnippet:
Democrats on Thursday opened an inquiry into how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China. Earlier on Thursday, the company ousted its CEO Jensen Huang . He also agreed to testify to a different set of Republican-led Congressional committees.

Huang was removed from the company he founded after he confessed to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. (He has since been accused of having more affairs , with Nvidia employees.)

The alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that U.S. officials suspect of helping route advanced Nvidia chips into China. The Democratic inquiry comes from Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. As the minority party, they can ask questions but can’t compel answers.

Their humdinger of a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asks the department to preserve records about an arrangement they find questionable and, they allege, illegal.

“The scheme worked like this,” as the letter describes it. President Trump agreed to sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China as long as the chips, manufactured by Taiwan, were first shipped to the United States. On arriving, Trump added a tariff “effectively taking a cut of Nvidia’s sales to China through what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system,” the letter said. Then the Commerce Department, under Lutnick, issued an export license.

By the way, the deal between Trump and Nvidia to share revenue was public. In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD both agreed to share 15% of their revenue from chip sales to China with the U.S. government as part of a deal to secure export licenses, the AP reported at the time.

But the letter questions why Lutnick continued to allow Megaspeed to buy chips even after he was reportedly informed by U.S. intelligence of their suspicions of Alice Huang and of Jensen Huang’s relationship with her. It questions why the department reportedly green-lit other Asian companies to buy Nvidia chips “with no physical presence at their listed addresses.” So the inquiry is aimed at the administration, not just at Nvidia and Huang.

The letter also questions how Nvidia’s donations to Trump’s projects factored in. It notes that the export deal

summary.tldr:
Democratic lawmakers, led by Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.) and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), have launched a formal inquiry into the Trump administration’s oversight of Nvidia’s chip exports to China. The investigation centers on allegations that the administration facilitated a revenue-sharing scheme involving H200 chips, where Nvidia and AMD agreed to pay 15% of China-related revenue to the U.S. government in exchange for export licenses. The inquiry specifically questions why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick continued to approve sales to Singapore-based customer Megaspeed despite intelligence reports linking the firm to an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, and the subsequent scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang.

Jensen Huang has been ousted as CEO of Nvidia following revelations of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, and reports of additional affairs with Nvidia employees. The Democratic letter to the Commerce Department alleges that the administration may have leveraged knowledge of Jensen Huang’s personal conduct and a $26 million donation from Nvidia to Trump-affiliated projects to secure the revenue-sharing arrangement. The inquiry also probes the Commerce Department's approval of export licenses for Asian entities that reportedly lacked physical presence at their registered addresses. Concurrently, a separate Republican-led Congressional investigation involving the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party has secured Huang's agreement to testify in a closed-door session.
takeaways: **Revenue Sharing Agreement:** In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD reportedly agreed to share 15% of revenue from China-bound chip sales with the U.S. government to secure export licenses.

**Alleged Quid Pro Quo:** Lawmakers are investigating whether $26 million in Nvidia donations to Trump projects were linked to the administration's approval of export deals following the disclosure of Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

**Export Licensing Concerns:** The inquiry questions the Commerce Department's decision to green-light sales to Megaspeed and other entities despite intelligence warnings regarding their legitimacy and physical operational status.
**Leadership Transition:** Jensen Huang has been removed as CEO of Nvidia following public reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an executive at a key customer firm.

**Congressional Oversight:** Two separate investigations are underway: a Democratic inquiry into the Commerce Department's regulatory conduct and a Republican-led probe requiring Huang to provide closed-door testimony.

title: Muse can now place calls to US businesses — if you pay
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
After initially testing the feature in September, Meta’s consumer AI agent Muse is now able to place calls to U.S. businesses on behalf of its users. However, only paid subscribers have access to the feature, the company says.

Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users , the company said last month, has been working to make consumer AI a mainstream product for everyday users. Placing calls is one of the ways it aims to get there, as it could handle another task on people’s to-do lists.

Notes Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and head of its Superintelligence Labs division, the feature could be used to take care of calls people don’t want to make, like those to their cable company, the DMV, or to a restaurant that doesn’t offer online reservations.

🚨MUSE FEATURE ALERT!!!🚨 lots of you have been asking for this one… muse can make phone calls for you! ☎️📞📲 let muse take care of all those calls you don’t want to make. insurance? cable? DMV? dinner res? not your problem anymore. out now to paid subs in the US 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/dsyMNmI2Ub

Previously, only a select number of Muse early adopters were able to try this feature after asking the AI for access. Now, anyone who pays for Muse can make this type of request. Currently, Muse subscription plans start at $20 per month for 500 million Muse tokens per week. Heavier AI users can opt to pay $100 per month for 3 billion tokens.

Muse is not the only AI agent able to place calls to businesses; the startup Instinct has been offering a similar option , as has Google’s Gemini . However, while the AI tools are now certainly capable of handling the task, the reception on the other end of the line can be mixed. Many businesses and receptionists hang up on calls from AI agents as soon as they identify that it’s not a human on the phone. But with AI now better able to mimic a real human voice, being able to tell the difference between a customer and an AI working on the customer’s behalf will get tougher.

Despite the challenges, this feature is one that could appeal to consumers who have grown frustrated with the state of customer service over the years. For too long, customers have been forced to navigate complex phone trees, and then sit on hold waiting for a human representative to pick up. If they’re lucky, that person can actually help them, and not transfer them to another department. Now, those c

summary.tldr:
Meta has officially rolled out the ability for its consumer AI agent, Muse, to place phone calls to U.S. businesses on behalf of users. Previously restricted to a limited group of early adopters, the feature is now available to all paid subscribers. The service is positioned as a tool to automate tedious administrative tasks, such as scheduling restaurant reservations or contacting government agencies like the DMV, which often involve long wait times or complex phone trees.

Muse currently offers two subscription tiers: a $20 per month plan providing 500 million tokens per week, and a $100 per month plan providing 3 billion tokens per week. While the AI agent market is becoming increasingly crowded with competitors like Google’s Gemini and the startup Instinct offering similar functionality, Meta faces the ongoing challenge of businesses identifying and hanging up on AI-generated calls. Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, noted that while the call feature remains behind a paywall, other features—such as the ability to generate a Muse email address—will soon be extended to free users.
takeaways: **Subscription Pricing:** Muse plans are priced at $20/month for 500 million tokens/week and $100/month for 3 billion tokens/week.
**User Base:** Meta reported that Muse reached over 10 million users as of last month.
**Feature Availability:** The automated calling feature is currently restricted to paid subscribers located in the United States.
**Competitive Landscape:** Muse competes with Google Gemini and the startup Instinct, both of which offer similar AI-driven phone calling capabilities.
**Roadmap:** Meta plans to roll out the Muse email address generation feature to free-tier users in the near future.

title: What to expect during SC26: Join theCUBE Nov. 17–19
author: Mark Albertson
contentSnippet:

High-performance computing and artificial intelligence are converging , driven by advances in exascale computing, accelerated systems, data storage and high-speed networking.

The system will use Nvidia’s Vera Rubin CPU-GPU platform and Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking inside Dell’s integrated rack systems and PowerEdge servers to support large-scale scientific computing and data-int

summary.tldr:
The SC26 conference, taking place in Chicago from November 17–19, 2026, focuses on the convergence of high-performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence, and exascale systems. Industry leaders including Dell Technologies, Google, and Nvidia are utilizing the event to showcase advancements in integrated compute, storage, and networking architectures designed to move AI from experimental phases to production-ready deployments. Key themes include the integration of quantum computing with classical HPC, the rise of agentic AI, and the shift toward system-level architectural optimization over individual chip performance.

Technical highlights include Dell’s collaboration with the U.S. Department of Energy to develop the Doudna supercomputer at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, which will feature Nvidia’s Vera Rubin CPU-GPU platform and Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking. Additionally, Google Cloud is scaling its HPC initiatives via the H4D virtual machine, which utilizes fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors to deliver over 12,000 GFLOPS of performance and memory bandwidth exceeding 950 GB/s. These systems are currently being deployed for large-scale scientific research, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System.
takeaways: **Doudna Supercomputer Specs:** The system, currently under development for Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, integrates Nvidia Vera Rubin CPU-GPU platforms with Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking inside Dell PowerEdge servers.
**Google H4D VM Performance:** Powered by 5th-gen AMD EPYC processors, the H4D VM achieves whole-node performance exceeding 12,000 GFLOPS and memory bandwidth over 950 GB/s.

**Data Collaboration:** Omni Analytics is developing a solution that enables direct data access to cloud warehouses without the need for preloading or data duplication.

title: Deploy frontier AI models on AWS Trainium with SGLang-Neuron
author: Alex Nails
contentSnippet: Today, Amazon announced that SGLang-Neuron is publicly available and can be accessed through an AWS Deep Learning Container, released by RadixArk in collaboration with Annapurna Labs. With SGLang-Neuron, you can serve models and generate reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts with SGLang on AWS Trainium using the same SGLang interface you use today. Trainium is a portfolio of AWS AI chips that delivers strong economics for AI training and inference at scale. Now, running SGLang on Trainium follows the SGLang workflow you already know: you launch models through SGLang’s server interface and invoke the endpoint using the same generation APIs. Underneath that interface, SGLang-Neuron runs on native PyTorch. With its out-of-tree plugin design, Trainium support and SGLang core develop independently and iterate faster. How SGLang runs on Trainium SGLang-Neuron is an out-of-tree plugin that connects SGLang with AWS Trainium. Installing the plugin registers the neuron platform through SGLang’s plugin entry points, and setting SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron selects it when the server starts. SGLang core continues to provide the API server, request lifecycle, RadixAttention, and prefix-cache bookkeeping. The plugin implements the Trainium-specific models, attention, mixture of experts (MoE), and the graph runner. Figure 1: SGLang-Neuron on AWS Trainium TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device. SGLang-Neuron uses standard PyTorch operations for the model execution path and incorporates kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for performance. It compiles these operations and kernels into executable programs using torch.compile , which the graph runner prepares and executes during serving. SGLang-Neuron also supports PD disaggregation . In this configuration, a prefill server computes the prompt KV cache and transfers it to a decode server using NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) . The decode server then generates the remaining tokens. Each server still uses SGLang’s scheduler and request lifecycle, while the plugin manages the Trainium execution and KV-cache transfer path. Serving models on AWS Trainium using SGLang-Neuron To follow this walkthrough, you use a Trainium3 Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance with a pytorch-inference-sglang-neuronx container. Here are the steps: Start the container. docker run --rm -it \ --privileged

summary.tldr:
Amazon has announced the public availability of SGLang-Neuron, a plugin developed by RadixArk in collaboration with Annapurna Labs that enables the SGLang framework to run on AWS Trainium AI chips. The integration allows users to serve models and generate reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts on Trainium hardware using the standard SGLang interface, APIs, and workflow. By utilizing an out-of-tree plugin architecture, the system decouples Trainium support from the SGLang core, allowing for independent development and faster iteration cycles.

Technically, SGLang-Neuron operates by registering the Neuron platform via SGLang’s plugin entry points, activated by setting the environment variable SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron. The system leverages native PyTorch, utilizing torch.compile to transform model operations and Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) kernels into executable programs. The architecture maintains SGLang’s core features, including RadixAttention, prefix-cache bookkeeping, and request lifecycle management, while offloading model execution, MoE (Mixture of Experts) handling, and graph running to the plugin. Additionally, the system supports PD (Prefill-Decode) disaggregation, where prompt KV caches are computed on a prefill server and transferred to a decode server via NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA).
takeaways: **Architecture:** SGLang-Neuron functions as an out-of-tree plugin that integrates with AWS Trainium via TorchNeuron, which registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device.
**Performance Optimization:** The plugin incorporates kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) and utilizes torch.compile for graph execution.
**Deployment:** Users can access the technology via the pytorch-inference-sglang-neuronx AWS Deep Learning Container on Trainium3 Amazon EC2 instances.
**Disaggregation:** The system supports PD disaggregation, enabling KV cache transfer between prefill and decode servers using NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA).

title: Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: Google says its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model can give more helpful answers to complex questions, including “questions with multiple parts, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests.” The new model can break down your questions and address each part in its responses. It’s available starting today in search, the Gemini app, all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, and in Google Antigravity for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Robby Stein, VP of product at Google Search, says it’s “now the new default model in AI Mode & being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google says Gemini 4 Hydrogen also gives users a wider range of links in its responses by “conducting simultaneous queries across all the relevant subtopics.” Its responses have more visuals, too, like images, comparison tables, graphs, and maps. One of Stein’s examples shows the AI generating an interactive animated driving simulation in response to a user’s question about how phones locate which lane of a highway a car is on in areas without cell service. Google says the new model also has improved language understanding “across all supported AI Mode languages.” [Media: https://twitter.com/rmstein/status/2120941443359576166?a=NQ8Q5PwHUHcmejMYRl4&s=20] Users have more thinking level options with Gemini 4 Hydrogen, as well, including low, medium, high, and a new “xhigh” mode. According to Google, the new model “delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence” compared to Gemini Flash 3.8, and it “matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class,” like Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra.

summary.tldr:
Google has released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a new model designed to improve performance on complex, multi-part queries, ambiguous inputs, and highly specific requests. The model is now the default for AI Mode and is integrated into AI Overviews, Google Search, the Gemini app, Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, and Google Antigravity for Pro and Ultra subscribers. According to VP of Product Robby Stein, the model is capable of generating complex outputs such as interactive animated simulations and provides a broader range of source links by executing simultaneous queries across relevant subtopics.

Technically, Gemini 4 Hydrogen introduces a new 'xhigh' thinking level, expanding upon existing low, medium, and high options. Google claims the model offers significant improvements in speed and intelligence over the previous Gemini Flash 3.8. In internal benchmarks, Google asserts that Gemini 4 Hydrogen matches or exceeds the performance of competing models, specifically citing Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra. The update also includes enhanced language understanding across all supported AI Mode languages and the ability to generate richer visual content, including comparison tables, graphs, and maps.
takeaways: **Model Availability:** Gemini 4 Hydrogen is available immediately across Google Search, Gemini app, AI Studio, Gemini API, and Google Antigravity for Pro/Ultra subscribers.
**Thinking Modes:** The model introduces an 'xhigh' thinking level, supplementing the existing low, medium, and high settings.
**Performance Benchmarks:** Google claims the model outperforms or matches Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra while improving upon Gemini Flash 3.8.
**Functional Capabilities:** The model supports simultaneous subtopic querying for broader link sourcing and generates interactive visual content like animated simulations.

title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Ariel Jirau
contentSnippet: At Natera , a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations. This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows. SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives. The challenge: Knowledge continuity Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale. With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop. Why Natera chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision: Autonomous processing of high-volume support tickets without human intervention. Deep integration with existing operational tools such as Jira and Confluence. Built-in security and observability (encryption, AWS Identity and A

summary.tldr:
Natera, a cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing firm, has deployed SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to automate lab equipment maintenance. Led by Ariel Jirau, the engineering team developed SWARM to address the loss of institutional knowledge caused by technician turnover and the inefficiency of manual ticket resolution. The system manages over 65 daily support tickets across three Jira queues, aiming to reduce instrument downtime that previously delayed patient reporting.

SWARM utilizes Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to integrate with existing operational infrastructure, specifically Jira and Confluence, to capture and deploy diagnostic patterns. The system has achieved a 130x improvement in first response time, reducing the wait from an average of 17.4 hours to minutes. Additionally, the platform reports 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets. The architecture focuses on autonomous processing, security, and observability, allowing the system to scale diagnostic capabilities across diverse equipment families without requiring additional headcount.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** SWARM reduced first response time by 130x and achieved 96.2% automated coverage for support tickets.
**Operational Scale:** The system processes over 65 tickets per day across three distinct Jira queues.
**Technical Foundation:** Natera utilized Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for its native integration with Jira and Confluence and its built-in security and observability features.
**Problem Context:** Prior to SWARM, Natera faced an average first response time of 17.4 hours for lab equipment maintenance tickets.

title: CopilotKit Releases OpenBot 1.0: An MIT-Licensed, Self-Hostable AI Coworker With Built-In Governance
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Most AI coworker products are vendor locked. They pick the model, host the data, and write the rules. CopilotKit is taking the opposite route. OpenBot 1.0 , was released November 9th, an MIT-licensed , self-hostable agent workspace. What sets it apart is, a company brings their own models, agents and infrastructure. Governance is fully baked in, and every Bot action is checked against a policy before it runs. What is OpenBot? OpenBot is a modular agent workspace from CopilotKit , the team behind the AG-UI protocol. You give a Bot a task and watch it work. You review findings, interact with results and approve next steps in the same conversation. Each Bot gets a computer of its own . That is a container with its own Chromium browser, logins and files. It reaches only the tools you grant. Answers can come back as charts, checklists, tables and cards. In the new v1.0, Bots now reply in Markdown by default and draw components when they help. How does the governance gateway work? Every browser click, file write, MCP tool call and component goes through one gateway. It evaluates a CEL policy, writes the audit row first , then acts. Deny rules run before allow rules, and a broken rule refuses rather than opens. On top of that, the business tier adds: Single sign-on and SCIM sync for users and groups. The README documents Google, Microsoft (Entra) and Okta, plus SAML and OIDC. On-behalf-of tokens, usually scoped to a subset of the person’s permissions. Tool grants per Bot, per role or per person, with access requests to an admin. Policies that block actions or route sensitive work to a human for approval. Spend visibility per Bot, role, team or person, plus daily, weekly or monthly token limits. A full audit trail with SIEM export, multi-tenancy and an admin plane. EU AI Act content labeling, retention controls and deletion on request. CopilotKit itself holds SOC 2 Type II. Which agents and models can you bring? Any agent that speaks AG-UI plugs in. The site lists 8 frameworks: Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain, Google ADK, Mastra, AWS Strands, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI. The repo also ships Agno, AG2, LlamaIndex and Pydantic AI examples. For models, teams can use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini or Grok through existing subscriptions or API keys. Open models such as Kimi, DeepSeek, Qwen, Nemotron and Mistral are also supported. Sandboxes, MCP hubs and bro

Most AI coworker products are vendor locked. They pick the model, host the data, and write the rules. CopilotKit is taking the opposite route.

OpenBot 1.0 , was released November 9th, an MIT-licensed , self-hostable agent workspace. What sets it apart is, a company brings their own models, agents and infrastructure. Governance is fully baked in, and every Bot action is checked against a policy before it runs.

title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
author: Sai Pavan Kasani
contentSnippet: Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt. Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data. To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching . For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance . For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock . Where inference cost comes from Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens. Prompt cache duration Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration. For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching , which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching. This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it: { "cachePoint": { "type": "default", "ttl": "1h" } } For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control . A longer duration is not automatical

title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
author: James O'Donnell
contentSnippet: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. title: Tokenomics at scale: Track and cap Amazon Bedrock spend per IAM principal with CUR 2.0 and AWS Budgets
author: Arun Chandapillai
contentSnippet: Generative AI spend is hard to attribute. Before an organization expands AI access, CFOs and CTOs usually want three answers: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there. In our previous post, Tokenomics at Scale: How Jamf Built Real-Time Spend Enforcement for Amazon Bedrock , we explained a custom enforcement loop built on AWS IAM Identity Center , Amazon Athena over Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs , and AWS Lambda . This approach gives near-real-time control, but it requires code you then own and operate. This post shows how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. The approach relies on three things: IAM principal attribution , which Amazon Bedrock records automatically; AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 or AWS Cost Explorer for reporting; and AWS Budgets with budget actions for enforcement. By the end, you will have per-identity cost reporting and an automatic guardrail that restricts Amazon Bedrock access when a threshold is crossed. Solution overview The solution has three parts: attribute, report, and enforce. Attribute. Amazon Bedrock captures the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal identity, the IAM user or role , for every inference request. This happens automatically, with no change to your Amazon Bedrock model inference calls. If several people share one role, you add per-user detail with session tags passed at role assumption time. If each person or application has its own role, principal tags on the role are enough. Report. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags, then read the data either in Cost Explorer for a console-only view, or in a CUR 2.0 data export for detailed line-item analysis and SQL queries. Enforce. Create an AWS Budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock and filtered to one identity or tag value, then attach a budget action that applies a Deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed. The following sections show each part in more detail, alongside the implementation steps. Prerequisites To deploy this solution, you need: An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock model access enabled. Permissions to tag IAM principal , activate cost allocation tags , create data exports , and create budgets and budget actions. Amazon Bedrock accessed through

summary.tldr:
AWS has released a native framework for managing and capping Amazon Bedrock expenditures per IAM principal, eliminating the need for custom-coded enforcement loops like those previously implemented by Jamf. The solution leverages three core AWS services: Amazon Bedrock’s automatic IAM principal logging, AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 for granular line-item analysis, and AWS Budgets for automated enforcement.

The architecture functions through a three-stage process: attribution, reporting, and enforcement. Amazon Bedrock automatically logs the IAM user or role for every inference request; organizations can further refine this by using session tags during role assumption or principal tags on roles. Once these tags are activated as cost allocation tags, administrators can track spend via AWS Cost Explorer or SQL queries in CUR 2.0. Enforcement is achieved by configuring an AWS Budget scoped to specific identities or tag values, which triggers an automated IAM 'Deny' policy once a predefined financial threshold is breached.
takeaways: **Attribution Mechanism:** Amazon Bedrock automatically records the IAM principal for every inference request without requiring modifications to existing model invocation code.
**Granular Identification:** Organizations can distinguish between individual users sharing a single role by utilizing session tags passed during role assumption.
**Reporting Tools:** Cost visibility is provided through AWS Cost Explorer for console-based monitoring or CUR 2.0 data exports for detailed SQL-based analysis.
**Automated Enforcement:** AWS Budgets can be configured with budget actions that automatically apply a 'Deny' IAM policy to a specific principal once a spending limit is exceeded.

title: Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.”

While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement.

The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level.

In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode.

In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question.

Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains.

The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode.

Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can

summary.tldr:
Google has introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a new model optimized for fast execution and agentic workflows, marking what the company describes as its most significant Search upgrade to date. While Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon models remain the primary choice for deep reasoning, Hydrogen is engineered to balance speed and intelligence, specifically targeting multi-step tasks and complex user queries. The model is currently rolling out globally to all Google Search users and is available across Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the Antigravity development platform for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

Technically, Hydrogen delivers performance 2.5 times faster than the previous Gemini 3.8 Flash model. Despite its focus on speed, it reportedly outperforms the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index when set to its default 'high' thinking level. The model features four distinct thinking levels—low, medium, high (default), and a new 'xhigh' tier—all designed to optimize for speed and reduced token output. In Search, Hydrogen enhances the 'fan-out' technique, which decomposes complex, multi-part prompts into subqueries to improve the relevance of search results, visual responses, and comparison tables. It also demonstrates improved robustness against typos and natural language nuances, and currently holds the No. 5 ranking on the Agent Arena benchmark for multi-step tasks like data analysis and codebase navigation.
takeaways: **Performance Metric:** Gemini 4 Hydrogen executes tasks 2.5 times faster than the Gemini 3.8 Flash model.
**Benchmark Ranking:** The model is ranked No. 5 on the Agent Arena benchmark for multi-step tasks including deep research and codebase navigation.
**Thinking Tiers:** Hydrogen introduces four configurable thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new 'xhigh' tier, all optimized for lower token counts.
**Search Integration:** The model improves Search 'fan-out' capabilities, allowing for more precise handling of multi-part queries, visual responses, and comparison tables.
**Availability:** The model is available globally in Search, Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the Antigravity development platform.

title: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
author: Lauren Forristal
contentSnippet:
Nectar , an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN . The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.

Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from the

summary.tldr:
Nectar, an AI-powered marketing operating system founded by former Meta employees Misbah and Farah Uraizee, has launched a new 'Creator Agent' designed to automate the end-to-end influencer marketing lifecycle. The tool handles creator discovery, personalized outreach, contract management, and campaign performance tracking. By leveraging a database of over 300 million creator profiles, the agent performs contextual video analysis to assess brand fit and safety, moving beyond simple keyword matching to evaluate content tone and platform-specific nuances.

The system integrates directly into brand workflows, drafting messages in a brand's specific voice and managing logistical tasks like product gifting and shipping. A notable feature includes monitoring creator milestones—such as life events—to suggest personalized engagement strategies. The agent is currently available globally for Instagram and TikTok, with plans to integrate via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling interoperability with AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot. title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview . We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

Indirect prompt injections, hidden in user data, are mostly ignored by LLMON models due to explicit instruction/data separation. For some benchmarks, attack success rates drop to nearly zero, whereas regular instruction-tuned models get hijacked with high probability. This is achieved while maintaining general capability relative to Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

Unrelated passages, old chat turns, and tool outputs don’t get pulled into the answer because each instruction is bound to the exact data it applies to.

Instructions, data, and requirements are clearly marked so that their structure and meanings at the application’s code level can be leveraged by t

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced LLMON (LLM Object Notation), an LLM-native markup language designed to replace JSON for structuring LLM context. By utilizing XML-like tags wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters, LLMON explicitly separates instructions, data, and requirements, allowing models to bind specific instructions to data payloads. This structural clarity aims to solve the brittleness of smaller models and mitigate indirect prompt injection attacks by ensuring the model treats data and instructions as distinct, addressable entities rather than a flattened string of text.

To support this, two experimental preview models—granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview—have been released, derived from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints. These models were trained on a re-serialized instruction-tuning corpus where every component is an addressable block. Benchmarks on the OPI, ASB, and StruQ datasets indicate that LLMON models achieve near-zero attack success rates against static indirect prompt injections, outperforming the best frontier models by 47% and the best open-source models by 95% in robustness, all while maintaining general capabilities comparable to standard Granite 4.1 Instruct models.
takeaways: **Architecture:** LLMON uses six reserved special tokens as delimiters to define tags, ensuring structural markers are distinct from content tokens, unlike JSON where structural characters (brackets, quotes) are ambiguous.

**Security Performance:** On the OPI benchmark, LLMON models demonstrated 47% higher robustness against indirect prompt injection than the best-tested frontier model and 95% higher than the best open-source model.

**Model Availability:** Two preview models, granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview, are available, alongside a GitHub repository containing conversion tools for existing JSON pipelines.

**Implementation:** The models integrate with standard chat templates via an 'exec' block, which explicitly defines which instructions to run, which data to use, and where to output the result, without requiring manual changes to existing message lists.

**Training Methodology:** Models were trained from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints using a re-serialized instruction-tuning corpus, ensuring LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than applied as a wrapper.

title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
author: Jie Wang
contentSnippet: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

title: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock
author: Majd Arbash
contentSnippet: Part 1 of this series built the operating model that controls Amazon Bedrock spend: attribution with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal tags and Cost and Usage Report 2.0, observability with model invocation logging, enforcement at three tiers, and a review cadence. That layer answers who spent it, and you can stop them. It can’t tell you whether the spend was well spent. This post answers two questions that Part 1 deliberately left open. First: Why is this workflow expensive? The answer requires thinking in cost per task, not cost per token. Second: Is the agent better than the humans were? The answer requires baselines, controlled experiments, and a scorecard tied to decisions. In this post, you learn a framework for calculating true model cost (including four hidden cost drivers that the pricing page doesn’t show), techniques for reducing cost per task through caching, routing, and output constraints, and a discipline for measuring agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard. This post is written for two audiences: the application and platform engineers who own the optimization levers, and the product owners and FinOps partners who need to justify agent spend to leadership. Cost per task, not cost per token Price per token invites quick comparison, but it doesn’t reflect what you actually pay. The published rate reflects the cost of a single token. Your bill reflects the cost of completing a task. A task is one complete unit of work your application asks a model to do: resolve one support email, extract fields from one invoice, or answer one user question. A task runs from the request through to a usable result, however many model calls it takes. The lower-priced model might not be the cheaper one to run. A cheaper model might fragment your text into more tokens, pad responses with filler, misread your tool schema and loop through corrections, or burn thousands of reasoning tokens before answering. None of these costs appear on the Bedrock pricing page . The four hidden cost drivers Four model characteristics determine what that published rate actually costs you on your workload. Tokenizer efficiency A token isn’t a word, and it is not equal across models. Every model family uses a different tokenizer and vocabulary. The same text, code, or JSON payload splits into different token counts. If Model A’

summary.tldr:
This article outlines a framework for evaluating Amazon Bedrock expenditure by shifting focus from per-token pricing to 'cost per task.' The author argues that published model rates are insufficient for ROI analysis because they ignore the operational reality of completing a full unit of work, such as resolving a support ticket or extracting invoice data. The methodology emphasizes that lower-priced models can become more expensive due to inefficient tokenization, verbose output, tool-use failures, or excessive reasoning cycles.

To optimize costs, the author proposes a strategy involving caching, intelligent model routing, and strict output constraints. The framework for measuring agent ROI requires establishing human-performance baselines, conducting controlled holdout experiments, and utilizing a five-dimension scorecard. The piece identifies four 'hidden' cost drivers—tokenizer efficiency, output verbosity, tool-use reliability, and reasoning overhead—that significantly impact the final bill but are not visible on standard AWS pricing pages.
takeaways: **Cost Metric:** Shift from per-token pricing to 'cost per task' to account for the total model calls required to complete a single unit of work.
**Hidden Cost Drivers:** Four primary factors influence actual spend: tokenizer efficiency, output verbosity, tool-use schema adherence, and reasoning token consumption.
**Optimization Levers:** Cost reduction strategies include implementing caching, model routing, and enforcing output constraints to minimize unnecessary token usage.
**ROI Methodology:** Agent performance must be validated against human baselines using controlled holdout experiments and a structured five-dimension scorecard.

title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
author: Sitaraman Vijay Krishna
contentSnippet: Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants. In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. This post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models for example purposes. For a list of models and availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . This LLM gateway pattern follows a straightforward request flow from the developer, through the LiteLLM layer, to Amazon Bedrock and the underlying FM. The following diagram illustrates the production topology behind that flow. For simplicity, we don’t cover the addition of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, such as content filtering and grounding, but you would normally include appropriate responsible AI controls before deploying to production. A developer’s OpenAI-compatible client reaches the LLM gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB). It authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request draws on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) (PostgreSQL) for virtual-key and spend state. It also interacts with Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM then ultimately invokes Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task role. Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) metrics and the

summary.tldr:
This technical guide details the implementation of a self-service LLM gateway using LiteLLM and Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles to provide an OpenAI-compatible API for foundation models. By deploying LiteLLM on AWS Fargate, platform teams can centralize model access, enforce per-user API keys, and implement cost attribution and observability for AI coding assistants. The architecture is designed to abstract underlying model complexity while allowing teams to monitor latency, error rates, and token usage.

The production-ready topology utilizes a request flow starting from an OpenAI-compatible client, passing through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to reach the LiteLLM container. State management for virtual keys and spend tracking is handled by Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL), while Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey serves as a caching layer. Secrets are managed via AWS Secrets Manager, and the system uses scoped AWS IAM task roles to invoke Bedrock models, specifically citing Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku as primary examples. Metrics including requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) are captured via Amazon CloudWatch.
takeaways: **Core Architecture:** Combines LiteLLM on AWS Fargate with Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles to create an OpenAI-compatible API gateway.
**State & Caching:** Utilizes Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL) for tracking virtual keys and spend, and Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey for request caching.
**Observability:** Integrates Amazon CloudWatch to monitor key performance indicators including requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM).
**Security & Access:** Employs per-user API keys for authentication and scoped AWS IAM task roles for secure interaction with Bedrock foundation models.
**Deployment Pattern:** Leverages AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs to automate the infrastructure deployment.

title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
author: Rebecca Bellan
contentSnippet:
The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.

Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models.

Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.

Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US.

Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next.

Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.

Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.

The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to W

summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following allegations of an affair with an executive linked to an alleged Chinese espionage operation. The departure creates significant uncertainty regarding Nvidia’s strategic commitment to the open-source AI ecosystem, a cause Huang championed as a counterweight to the closed-model dominance of firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia has appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, leaving the future of several high-profile initiatives—including a pending $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face and a $6 billion non-exclusive licensing deal with coding startup Poolside—in question.

Huang’s tenure was defined by his aggressive push for open-weight models, most notably the Nemotron family, which Nvidia developed for agentic and reasoning-heavy workloads. He also served as a primary political advocate for the open-source community, leading a coalition of 25 companies—including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir—in an open letter to the U.S. government opposing strict regulations on open-weight AI. These efforts were designed to diversify Nvidia’s customer base beyond the major hyperscalers, who are increasingly developing proprietary silicon, by fostering a broader ecosystem of developers and nation-states reliant on Nvidia’s hardware.
takeaways: **Leadership Transition:** Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO following Jensen Huang's resignation.
**Pending Acquisitions:** The status of Nvidia’s $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face and a $6 billion licensing deal with Poolside is currently unclear.
**Strategic Advocacy:** Huang led a 25-company coalition, including Microsoft and Meta, to lobby against U.S. government restrictions on open-weight AI models.
**Product Focus:** Under Huang, Nvidia prioritized the Nemotron model family, specifically designed for long-running agentic AI and complex reasoning tasks.
**Market Rationale:** Nvidia’s support for open source was a strategic hedge against the vertical integration of major customers like Google and OpenAI, who are building custom AI chips.

Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity . Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token

summary.tldr:
Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a new model optimized for rapid execution, agentic workflows, and everyday coding tasks. Positioned alongside the frontier models Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon, Hydrogen is designed to serve as a high-efficiency engine for multi-model systems. It features a 1 million-token context window and is priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. The model is available across Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Google Search, and the Gemini app, as well as for subscribers of Google Antigravity.

Technically, Hydrogen introduces four distinct 'thinking levels'—low, medium, high (default), and xhigh—allowing users to balance reasoning depth, latency, and cost. In benchmarks, it achieves a score of 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default setting, rising to 54 at the xhigh level. When integrated into the new 'Orchestrator' feature in Google Antigravity, Hydrogen enables dynamic model switching; in Terminal-Bench 4.0 testing, this orchestration achieved near-Carbon performance while reducing quota consumption by 24% and improving completion speed by 19%. Compared to its predecessor, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Hydrogen is 2.5 times faster, triples Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), and reduces fabricated claims by over 5x.

Hydrogen demonstrates significant improvements in agentic capabilities, ranking #5 on Agent Arena and leading its class on benchmarks including HLE-Diamond (58.8%), Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), and the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%). It is specifically engineered for parallel file-read and search operations, which has resulted in 2x to 2.8x speed improvements in enterprise repository workflows. The model also supports advanced multimodal synthesis, capable of processing dense PDFs, spreadsheets, and video to generate structured, cited outputs.

**Agentic Benchmarks:** Ranks #1 on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%) and ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%).
**Enterprise Optimization:** Parallelizes file-read and search calls, resulting in 12% to 23% lower token usage in complex repository navigation compared to 3.8 Flash.

title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
author: Madhu Parthasarathy
contentSnippet: AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months ( METR ), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago ( McKinsey ). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments. Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable. The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents ( Deloitte ). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one. The next generation AgentCore runtime We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly comp

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced the AgentCore runtime, a managed compute layer within Amazon Bedrock AgentCore designed to address the infrastructure challenges of scaling autonomous AI agents. As enterprise adoption grows—with McKinsey reporting that 40% of large enterprises are now scaling AI agents compared to 27% a year ago—the industry faces a bottleneck in balancing secure, isolated execution with performance and cost efficiency. AgentCore aims to eliminate the need for developers to build and maintain custom sandboxes, providing a managed environment that supports the long-running, multi-step workloads characteristic of modern frontier agents.

The runtime addresses the trade-off between pre-provisioned environments, which incur costs during idle time, and on-demand environments, which suffer from cold-start latency. By providing a managed compute layer, AgentCore enables elastic scaling and usage-based economics, allowing organizations to move beyond the current industry trend where only 15% of organizations have successfully scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems. The platform is positioned as a foundational infrastructure component to ensure that secure execution does not impede the deployment of agents that require code execution, browser navigation, and access to sensitive user data.
takeaways: **Market Adoption:** 40% of large enterprises are currently scaling AI agents, up from 27% in the previous year according to McKinsey data.
**Industry Bottleneck:** Only 15% of organizations have successfully scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, with 70% citing a lack of trust and governance as primary barriers.
**Performance Metric:** According to METR, the length of tasks that frontier agents can complete autonomously doubles approximately every four months.

**Core Value Proposition:** Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a managed compute layer to eliminate the infrastructure overhead of custom sandboxes while balancing security, cold-start latency, and resource costs.

title: The Jensen Huang scandal is hardly over
