summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following a series of reports alleging personal misconduct and systemic failures in the company's export compliance. The departure follows allegations of affairs with subordinates, including Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s VP of Healthcare, and Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed—a firm accused of acting as a front for illegal GPU diversion to China. These personal scandals are reportedly being used as a pretext for an ouster driven by the board, as the company faces mounting scrutiny over its adherence to U.S. export controls on high-end AI chips.

Technical and regulatory concerns center on the diversion of Nvidia hardware to blacklisted Chinese entities. Despite Huang’s public claims that Nvidia has zero percent market share in China and no evidence of chip diversion, reports from Culper Research and The New York Times suggest that over 20% of Nvidia’s FY 2026 compute revenues may be tied to China via intermediaries. Specific entities like Megaspeed and Super Micro have been linked to the movement of billions in hardware to Chinese firms, including Alibaba. takeaways: **Export Compliance Allegations:** Culper Research estimates over 20% of Nvidia’s FY 2026 compute revenue is linked to China, contradicting Huang’s claims of zero market share.

**Megaspeed Scandal:** The firm, identified as a major Southeast Asian buyer, was found to have no active operations at its listed addresses and is linked to Alice Huang, who allegedly promised Nvidia Blackwell chips to the Chinese AI firm DeepSeek.
**Super Micro Involvement:** Co-founders of Super Micro allegedly facilitated the purchase of $2.5 billion in Nvidia chips for Alibaba through a Thailand-based front company, OBON.

**Regulatory Scrutiny:** Nvidia reportedly intervened to stop a 2025 Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, leading to political fallout for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and potential Senate investigations.

**Corporate Governance:** Jensen Huang, Nvidia's only CEO to date, resigned amid board pressure following reports of multiple affairs and allegations of potential criminal involvement in chip smuggling.

title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.

“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.

This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!

The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance.

As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space.

After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October . While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.

title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
author: Josh DeMuth
contentSnippet: With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock , you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base . Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it. Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS . The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both. In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover. AWS runs the store With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types. title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
author: Amit Chaudhary
contentSnippet: Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use. While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running. In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test. The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project , and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks. In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A , we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
author: Renya Kujirada
contentSnippet: More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see? Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base. Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee. In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
author: Yuan Wei
contentSnippet: Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “ Is this agent ready for production? ” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements. To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it. In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change. A note on terminology:  Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions. 1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. Table 1 summarizes the engineering practices needed to address each property. Table 1. What each property invalidates, and what it requires instead. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. The second report focused on Huang and Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, claiming that a bystander who recorded the two being “affectionate” at the hotel hosting Nvidia’s GTC developer conference in May was met by Huang’s security workers and asked to sign a non-disclosure agreement. title: Agents that build their own databases are forcing a data foundation rethink
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 06:02 EST / NOVEMBER 12 2026

Agents that build their own databases are forcing a data foundation rethink

AI agents are changing how enterprises create, move and govern information, and data observability is turning into a prerequisite rather than a nice-to-have. Models get most of the attention, but the data beneath them decides whether they hold up in production.

That pressure is now reaching the cloud-native community, where KubeCon organizers added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track this year. The industry has raced from chatbots to retrieval, fine-tuning and agents, yet every wave rests on the same groundwork, according to Sanjeev Mohan (pictured), principal at SanjMo, a data and AI advisory firm, and author of “Designing the AI-Driven Data Foundations.”

“AI can only be successful if it’s built on a solid foundation,” Mohan said. “You have no observability or transparency into it. No matter what you do on top of it, it will not be successful.”

Mohan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed theCUBE’s second day of coverage at the event. (* Disclosure below.)

Why AI agents demand data observability at runtime

For decades, data was created once in an operational system and then pushed through brittle pipelines for extraction, transformation, cataloging and preparation. That model works when humans consume batch reports, Mohan explained. Thousands of agents change the math.

“They’re not going to wait for this pipeline to finish. They want access to the database directly,” Mohan said.

Agents are also doing something no earlier software did. They spin up short-lived databases, copy data and test different chains of thought before picking one action, according to Mohan. An agent reviewing a loan application might query census records and social media before rejecting it, which raises the question of how that decision gets audited.

“Governance becomes really important, and this is not like governance in the past where you would govern your data and then have a deterministic CFO report dashboard run on it,” Mohan said.

That makes data observability part of the architecture itself, not an afterthought bolted onto a warehouse. Mohan’s book, published in June 2026 by John Wiley & Sons Inc

summary.tldr:
Sanjeev Mohan, principal at SanjMo and author of "Designing the AI-Driven Data Foundations" (published June 2026 by John Wiley & Sons), argues that the rise of autonomous AI agents necessitates a fundamental shift in enterprise data architecture. Traditional data models, which rely on batch processing and brittle extraction-transformation-loading (ETL) pipelines, are insufficient for agents that require direct, real-time database access to perform tasks. Mohan emphasizes that data observability must transition from a post-hoc monitoring tool to a core architectural requirement to ensure transparency and auditability in agentic decision-making.

Agents are increasingly creating short-lived, ephemeral databases to test various "chains of thought" and build context at runtime. This behavior creates a challenge for governance, as agents may query diverse sources—such as census records and social media—to inform a single decision, such as a loan rejection. Mohan posits that future data platforms must evolve into converged systems capable of handling both structured and unstructured data, as the context required for agentic tasks is highly dynamic and unique to each specific execution instance.
takeaways: **Architectural Shift:** AI agents are moving away from batch-processed data pipelines toward direct, runtime database access.
**Ephemeral Databases:** Agents are increasingly spinning up short-lived, temporary databases to test decision paths and store context during execution.
**Governance Challenge:** Traditional deterministic reporting dashboards are inadequate for auditing agentic decisions that rely on dynamic, runtime-generated context.
**Converged Systems:** Future data foundations must integrate structured and unstructured data into a single, observable architecture to support agentic workflows.

title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
author: Yubo Ruan
contentSnippet: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. Current agents shrink this history by having a model summarize it, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history it replaces, and cache-aware triggers decide when to compact while taking the size of the result as given. We present Folio, a context manager that records, folds, and recovers history through one set of handles. While the agent runs, Folio records three linked levels: a short turn note the model writes as part of its ordinary reply (L1), an event manifest of every call written by the runtime (L2), and the captured source records (L3). Because these views already exist, the runtime folds the context programmatically, selecting coarser views for older turns. The fold prints the handles that index L2 and L3, so recovery tools that read bounded pages, compute over full text in files, and keep findings in a persistent dossier reach the evidence the agent needs with little added input. The fold trigger prices an explicit landing point that includes the retained budget. On 75 LOCA-bench tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Pro behind every system, Folio solves 66 tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction and 49-59 for Claude Code, Codex, and SoL-Pi, in about half their working time, at 2.4 times lower cost than that runtime; each fold takes a median of 0.6 seconds.

title: Nebuly wants to help enterprises understand exactly what their AI investments are worth after raising $21M
author: Mike Wheatley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 05:00 EST / NOVEMBER 12 2026

Nebuly wants to help enterprises understand exactly what their AI investments are worth after raising $21M

An Italian startup called Nebuly S.r.l. says it’s going to help organizations better understand the impact their investments in artificial intelligence have on their bottom lines after raising $21 million in funding today.

The round was led by Planven and saw participation from backers including Exor Ventures, Tenacity Capital, TGVG Capital, Fastweb, Vodafone and CDP Venture Capital’s Digital Transition Fund.

The world’s biggest companies have been spending millions of dollars on artificial intelligence, but very few can actually say how much value those investments have returned. Though some leaders might be able to point to a few vanity metrics, they’ll likely stumble if pressed to come up with concrete numbers.

This is a problem because enterprise leaders are increasingly feeling the pressure to justify their investments in AI. A recent Gartner Inc. survey of business leaders found that 85% of respondents plan to step up their AI spending in the next year, but at the same time, only 22% say they have managed to scale the technology across multiple business units.

Meanwhile, spending is spiraling out of control at many companies. Famously, Uber Technologies Inc. revealed earlier this year that it had eaten up the entire budget it set aside for AI in 2026 in just four months.

Nebuly co-founder and Chief Executive Franceso Signorato told SiliconANGLE that one of the main challenges when it comes to understanding AI’s return on investment is that many companies have deployed a jumbled patchwork of AI models and applications. They’re using tools from OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic PBC, Microsoft Corp., Google LLC and others, as well as developing in-house tools under their own steam.

That makes it harder to see which projects are actually paying off and generating real business revenue. Although companies can track superficial metrics like token consumption and prompt tallies, genuine productivity gains remain obscured.

“Every enterprise is about to face the same question from its board, if it hasn’t already: What is AI actually worth to us? Nebuly exists to answer that question,” Signorato said. “Until now companies have measured AI by counting users, prompts and responses, which has fueled the rise of tokenmaxx

summary.tldr:
Italian startup Nebuly S.r.l. has raised $21 million in a funding round led by Planven, with participation from Exor Ventures, Tenacity Capital, TGVG Capital, Fastweb, Vodafone, and CDP Venture Capital’s Digital Transition Fund. The company provides an AI measurement platform designed to quantify the business value and return on investment (ROI) of enterprise AI deployments, moving beyond superficial metrics like token consumption to track actual productivity gains and revenue impact.

The platform functions as a unified control plane that connects directly to AI agents within a company’s IT environment. For internal, employee-facing agents, it measures operational efficiency, such as hours saved and capacity freed, while also tracking net-new work enabled by AI. For customer-facing agents, it monitors revenue generation, churn impact, and upsell opportunities. To ensure auditability, the platform allows financial teams to inspect the underlying math and assumptions, and it can be deployed on-premises or in private clouds to maintain data security.

Nebuly currently serves large-scale organizations, with nearly all customers generating over $100 million in annual revenue and approximately half exceeding $1 billion. Notable clients include Carl Zeiss AG, Iveco Group N.V., and Oura Health Oy. The new funding will be used to expand the company's go-to-market operations, specifically targeting growth in the U.S. market.
takeaways: **Funding Details:** Nebuly raised $21 million in a round led by Planven, with backing from major telecommunications and venture firms including Vodafone and Fastweb.
**Core Value Proposition:** The platform aims to replace 'tokenmaxxing' metrics with evidence-based ROI, tracking specific business outcomes like employee time saved and customer revenue impact.
**Deployment Architecture:** The software acts as a unified control plane for AI agents and supports on-premises or private cloud deployment to ensure data security and auditability.
**Target Market:** The company focuses on large enterprises, with a client base where 50% of companies report annual revenues exceeding $1 billion.
**Expansion Plans:** CEO Francesco Signorato intends to use the new capital to scale go-to-market hiring and operations within the United States.

title: Active Learning of Approximate LLM Ranking for Energy-Efficient Retrieval of Long Queries
author: Ohad Porat
contentSnippet: Search engines and Large Language Models (LLMs) offer complementary strengths for document retrieval: lexical retrievers which rely on keyword matching are fast and energy-efficient, whereas LLMs capture semantic meaning and excel at interpreting long, context-rich queries. However, this comes at a cost that is computationally and energetically prohibitive. We propose the LLM Active Approximation Model (LAAM), a hybrid retrieval framework that introduces a lightweight learned predictor which serves as an intermediary between semantic retrieval and LLM retrieval. LAAM is refined through an active learning loop where an LLM labels a small number of documents. By concentrating LLM evaluations on the most informative documents, the framework substantially reduces inference cost while preserving retrieval effectiveness. We evaluate the proposed framework on TREC Robust 2004 using Lucene with BM25 retrieval and DeepSeek v3 as the LLM, under three levels of query verbosity. For verbose queries, LAAM achieves 87% of average P@10 achieved by DeepSeek's reranking (0.459 vs. 0.526), while requiring only 3.3% of the per-query energy consumption. LAAM is statistically significantly better than BM25 and is indistinguishable from DeepSeek on average precision, though not on MAP (Friedman test, P<0.05 with post-hoc testing). Overall, our results demonstrate that selectively approximating LLM relevance judgments through active learning enables retrieval accuracy to be controlled directly through the evaluation (and consequently energy) budget. Rather than committing to either inexpensive (and less accurate) lexical retrieval or exhaustive (and expensive) LLM reranking, our framework exposes a continuous spectrum of operating points along the energy--accuracy curve, allowing practitioners to select how to trade retrieval quality with computational budget.

title: IBM Announces IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3: A New Processor to Support 10k Quantum Operations on 520 Programmable Qubits
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: IBM has announced IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3 , its next superconducting quantum processor. It is designed to run 10,000 quantum operations accurately across 520 programmable qubits. In 2027, IBM plans to link 2 r3 chips into a single 1,040-qubit system. For developers, the announcement is speed. The current Nighthawk r2 already runs workloads up to 19x faster than IBM’s earlier processors. TL;DR Size: Nighthawk r3: 520 programmable qubits, 2,034 physical qubits, 10 l-couplers. Nighthawk r2 (live today): 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers. Runs on: IBM Quantum Platform cloud (r2 as ibm_phoenix ). Superconducting chips in dilution refrigerators, paired with laptop-to-supercomputer classical compute. Performance: r2 executes 100,000+ circuits per second, about 25x Heron, with Heron-class gate fidelity. Best: Up to 19x speedup over earlier IBM processors on partner workloads; E.ON reports 15x. Worst: r3 is a design, not shipping hardware. Chip-to-chip links average 99% state transfer fidelity, short of the 99.9% target. Bottom line: Best: real throughput gains on a cloud chip you can use now. Worst: the 1,040-qubit system is a 2027 plan, not a result. What is IBM Quantum Nighthawk? Nighthawk is IBM’s square-lattice processor family built for quantum advantage workloads. Most qubits connect to 4 nearest neighbors, versus 2 or 3 on earlier designs. That connectivity lets circuits express more entangling structure with fewer swap operations. The current production chip is Nighthawk r2 . It has 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers and 120 reset elements. That is 458 physical quantum elements in total. How does Nighthawk r2 get 25x more throughput? The bottleneck was qubit reset. Heron uses conditional reset: measure, then flip any qubit found in the excited state. That method cannot fix leaked qubits, so the chip idles for hundreds of microseconds between shots. Nighthawk r2 replaces this with a dissipative reset gadget per qubit. A tunable coupler links each qubit to a cold environment on demand. This drops effective T1 from about 200 microseconds to roughly 25 nanoseconds. Idle time between runs falls to as little as 1 microsecond. The result is 100,000+ circuits per second. Heron manages roughly 4,000. IBM also reports about 25x lower initialization error, while neighbors stay undisturbed. What speedups are partners reporting? According to IBM, clients have run

summary.tldr:
IBM has announced IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3, a next-generation superconducting quantum processor designed to execute 10,000 accurate quantum operations across 520 programmable qubits. The company plans to link two r3 chips into a single 1,040-qubit system by 2027. Meanwhile, the current production chip, Nighthawk r2 (available on the IBM Quantum Platform cloud as ibm_phoenix), features 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers, 120 reset elements, and a total of 2,034 physical qubits across the architecture. Nighthawk is a square-lattice processor family where most qubits connect to four nearest neighbors, reducing swap operations compared to earlier designs.

Nighthawk r2 achieves high throughput by replacing Heron's conditional reset method with a dissipative reset gadget per qubit, using a tunable coupler to link each qubit to a cold environment on demand. This drops effective T1 relaxation time from approximately 200 microseconds to roughly 25 nanoseconds, reducing idle time between runs to as little as 1 microsecond. Consequently, r2 executes over 100,000 circuits per second (about 25 times the throughput of Heron, which manages roughly 4,000), alongside 25x lower initialization error. Partner workloads show up to a 19x speedup over earlier IBM processors, with E.ON reporting a 15x speedup.

Despite the performance gains of the live r2 hardware, limitations remain. Nighthawk r3 is currently a design rather than shipping hardware, and the planned 1,040-qubit system is a 2027 roadmap target. Furthermore, chip-to-chip links currently average 99% state transfer fidelity, falling short of the required 99.9% target.
takeaways: **Nighthawk r3 Specifications:** Features 520 programmable qubits, 2,034 physical qubits, and 10 l-couplers, designed for 10,000 accurate quantum operations with a 1,040-qubit linked system targeted for 2027.
**Nighthawk r2 Specifications:** Features 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers, 120 reset elements, and executes over 100,000 circuits per second with Heron-class gate fidelity.
**Dissipative Reset Innovation:** Drops effective T1 time from ~200 microseconds to ~25 nanoseconds and idle time between runs to 1 microsecond, yielding 25x higher throughput than Heron.
**Partner Performance:** Delivers up to 19x speedups over earlier IBM processors on partner workloads, including a 15x speedup reported by E.ON.
**Architectural Limitations:** Chip-to-chip links currently achieve 99% state transfer fidelity, which is below the 99.9% target, and r3 remains a design specification rather than shipping hardware.

title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors
author: Connie Loizos
contentSnippet:
It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30% . Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear whom he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour.

Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates:

title: Google’s GKE Labs turns reinforcement learning into a Kubernetes workload
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 20:51 EST / NOVEMBER 11 2026

Google’s GKE Labs turns reinforcement learning into a Kubernetes workload

Model fine-tuning through reinforcement learning is fast becoming one of the most demanding jobs in AI infrastructure. It mixes training, inference and sandboxed agent work in a single loop, often with research code tangled into the systems beneath it.

Google LLC has been tackling that problem from inside its Kubernetes engineering group, and recently donated the result, OpenRL, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation . The GKE Labs team got there by building an AI agent for Kubernetes tasks, then a benchmark to grade models on that work, according to Sunil Arora (pictured, left), senior software engineer at Google Cloud.

“If you look at reinforcement learning, I think of it as a kind of a super app of AI because it involves training. It involves sampling. It involves agents actually doing things in a sandbox and sometimes kind of evaluating the work,” Arora said. “It’s kind of a very diverse workload and it is, I think, pushing the boundaries of our infrastructure.”

Arora and Justin Santa Barbara (right), developer at Google, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed model fine-tuning and their work in GKE Labs, which puts experimental projects in users’ hands early. (* Disclosure below.)

Model fine-tuning without the infrastructure tangle

OpenRL debuted as a research preview in June 2026 , offering a self-hosted training API for a company’s own Kubernetes cluster. It splits the reinforcement learning loop from the compute plumbing, so infrastructure engineers handle scaling while researchers keep control of experiments, Arora explained.

“With OpenRL, one of the things that we are trying to do is kind of abstracting away the infrastructure as kind of core primitives so that researchers and AI engineers can just focus on their RL loop,” Arora said.

Sandboxes are where that loop meets agent infrastructure, since calculating rewards can mean running millions of isolated commands. Google’s Agent Substrate packs more of those sandboxes onto limited compute, according to Arora. For Santa Barbara, the need surfaced one step at a time.

“We built kubectl-ai, and in theory, kubectl-ai could have f

summary.tldr:
Google’s GKE Labs has introduced OpenRL, a framework designed to treat reinforcement learning (RL) model fine-tuning as a native Kubernetes workload. Donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), OpenRL aims to decouple the complex RL training loop—which involves simultaneous training, sampling, and agent evaluation—from the underlying compute infrastructure. By abstracting infrastructure into core primitives, the project allows researchers to focus on RL loops while infrastructure engineers manage scaling and resource allocation.

The architecture relies on Google’s 'Agent Substrate' to manage high-density sandboxing, which is critical for executing the millions of isolated commands required for reward calculation in RL. The project originated from internal GKE Labs experiments, including the development of 'kubectl-ai,' an AI agent for Kubernetes management. To mitigate security risks associated with autonomous agents—such as accidental disk formatting—the team implemented sandboxing to isolate agent actions from host systems. OpenRL was released as a research preview in June 2026 and provides a self-hosted training API for Kubernetes clusters.
takeaways: **Project Origin:** OpenRL was developed by Google’s GKE Labs and subsequently donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF).
**Core Functionality:** The framework provides a self-hosted training API that separates the RL training loop from compute plumbing to simplify infrastructure management.
**Security Architecture:** The system utilizes 'Agent Substrate' to pack isolated sandboxes onto limited compute, preventing autonomous agents (like kubectl-ai) from damaging host environments.
**Release Timeline:** OpenRL was first made available as a research preview in June 2026.

title: Google enters decision model market with Gemini Decisions API
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 20:22 EST / NOVEMBER 11 2026

Google enters decision model market with Gemini Decisions API

Google LLC today launched Gemini Decisions API, an artificial intelligence service designed to answer user questions in a cost-efficient manner.

It’s powered by a new AI model called Gemini Decision 1.

Traditional large language models are designed to answer a broad range of prompts. Gemini Decision 1 has a much narrower focus: It can process just three types of questions. The upside is that it answers those questions at a significantly lower cost. According to Google, the model is nearly five times cheaper than its entry-level Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite LLM.

The model can answer yes-no questions, multiple choice questions and prompts that ask it to rate an item on a user-specified scale. A cybersecurity team, for example, could ask the model to rate the severity of an antivirus alert on a scale of 1 to 10.

Gemini Decision 1 prompts include two items: the user’s questions and the dataset to which those questions pertain. The dataset can include up to 256,000 tokens worth of text, audio, images, video or some combination thereof.

LLMs usually generate verbose free-flowing text in response to user questions. Gemini Decision 1, in contrast, outputs terse answers such as “yes” or “no.” It also displays a score that indicates how confident it is in the accuracy of a given response. That score helps applications decide whether they should make use of the output.

Neural networks designed to generate brief answers to simple questions are known as decision models. The first such model, Jev, was launched in mid-September by a startup called TypeSafe AI Inc. It gained a million users within a few days. Three weeks after the launch, TypeSafe raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation.

Decision models can answer the narrow set of questions for which they’re optimized faster than LLMs. Additionally, they’re easier to integrate into applications. An application that powers some of its features using an AI model must check the model’s output for errors and filter redundant details before ingesting it. Decision models’ concise, structured responses make both tasks simpler.

summary.tldr:
Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API, powered by a specialized model called Gemini Decision 1. Unlike traditional large language models (LLMs) designed for open-ended text generation, this model is purpose-built for three specific tasks: yes-no questions, multiple-choice queries, and rating items on a user-defined scale. By narrowing the scope, Google claims the model is approximately five times cheaper than its Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite LLM, with pricing set at $0.10 per 1 million input tokens and no charge for output tokens.

Technically, Gemini Decision 1 processes multimodal datasets—including text, audio, images, and video—up to 256,000 tokens. The model avoids token-by-token decoding, achieving a median model compute latency of 50-100 ms (150-250 ms end-to-end) for contexts up to 16K tokens. It outputs concise, structured responses alongside a confidence score to assist in automated decision-making. Google reports that the model outperformed competitors, including TypeSafe AI’s 'Jev' and OpenAI’s 'Decisions API,' in seven out of nine internal benchmarks, though Jev remains slightly more cost-efficient.
takeaways: **Pricing Model:** Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1 million input tokens with zero cost for output tokens.
**Performance Metrics:** The model maintains a median end-to-end latency of 150-250 ms for contexts up to 16K tokens, with performance remaining stable for up to 100 questions per request.
**Input Capacity:** The API supports multimodal datasets (text, audio, images, video) up to a 256,000-token limit.
**Competitive Landscape:** Google claims Gemini Decision 1 outperformed OpenAI’s Decisions API and TypeSafe AI’s Jev in seven of nine internal benchmarks.
**Availability:** The service is currently accessible via the Gemini Decisions API and a limited free tier within Google AI Studio.

title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
author: Viquar Khan
contentSnippet: Java teams have established JVM tooling, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and operational patterns, yet taking AI agents from prototype to production is hard: agent frameworks do not solve scalability, governance, security, and operational concerns by default. Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks. Java remains one of the widely used programming languages in enterprise software. Teams have existing CI/CD pipelines, operational expertise, and established patterns built around the JVM. Spring AI brings AI capabilities to the JVM through familiar Spring patterns: auto-configuration, dependency injection, and composable advisors. Developers can build AI agents using the same idioms they use for REST APIs, security, and data access. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. With AgentCore, you can build, deploy, and operate AI agents at scale. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management. In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore . We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. The first is a single-agent travel assistant that demonstrates tool calling and memory. The second is a multi-agent intelligent document processing (IDP) system that shows how specialist agents, a rules engine, and alerting work together. Amazon and the Spring AI team have introduced a framework integration designed to bridge the gap between Java enterprise infrastructure and autonomous AI agent development. By utilizing Spring AI 2.0 and the newly introduced spring-ai-agentcore 2.0, Java developers can now leverage familiar idioms—such as dependency injection, auto-configuration, and composable advisors—to build agents capable of tool calling, multi-turn context management, and complex task execution. The integration aims to address common production hurdles like scalability, governance, and security that often plague prototype-to-production transitions in AI.

At the core of this architecture is Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a framework-agnostic and model-agnostic platform that provides managed runtime environments for AI agents. AgentCore supplies the necessary infrastructure for production-grade deployments, including identity management, memory, browser automation, and code execution. title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
author: Hao Li, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Hui En Pang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Hao Li , Fangzhou Hong , Zhaoxi Chen , Hui En Pang , Kairui Hu , Mingze Sun , Runmao Yao , Xinhao Ji , Xiyuan Zheng , Xuanli Chen , Yalun Dai , Yap Kim Hui , Dingwen Zhang , Yuanyuan Gao , Ziang Cao , Cheng Huang Yean , Jackson Peng , Rui Duan , Yaobo Liu , Zetong Wang , Ziwei Liu

Abstract: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

Notes: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Ropedia Xperience 2, developed by a team led by Hao Li and Ziwei Liu, is a dataset and framework designed to address the limitations of foundation models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 in executing long-horizon, contact-rich robotic tasks. The project aims to establish scaling laws for physical AI by providing a standardized, high-quality collection of environment and behavior data. The researchers argue that current models struggle with real-world physical interaction due to a lack of supervised human demonstrations and closed-loop interactive simulation environments.

The dataset consists of 1,589 metric-scale 3D scans and 4,230 egocentric recordings covering 74 distinct tasks, totaling 131 hours of data. The Ropedia Xperience 2 framework enables the conversion of these static scans into physically interactive simulation environments. Furthermore, the system supports the retargeting of human motion into whole-body robot trajectories and facilitates the generation of additional robot behaviors through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory synthesis. This methodology is presented as a gold standard for scaling physical AI, providing the necessary infrastructure to evaluate and improve robotic policies in continuous, closed-loop settings.
takeaways: **Dataset Composition:** Includes 1,589 metric-scale 3D scans and 4,230 egocentric recordings spanning 74 tasks and 131 hours of human behavior.
**Simulation Conversion:** Provides a pipeline to transform static 3D scans into physically interactive simulation environments for policy rollout and evaluation.
**Motion Retargeting:** Features a mechanism to map human motion data directly onto whole-body robot trajectories.
**Behavior Generation:** Supports automated long-horizon trajectory generation and virtual teleoperation to expand the available robotic behavior set.
**Research Objective:** Aims to establish scaling laws for physical AI by identifying how model capabilities correlate with the scale of environment and behavior data.

title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
author: Haochen Liu, Qianhao Zhu, Zixuan Wang, Dingming Li
contentSnippet: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
author: Jaemyung Yu, Byeongho Heo, Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han
contentSnippet: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam

title: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?
author: Zhiyu Hou, Wen-Jie Shu, Harold Haodong Chen, Weilin Ruan
contentSnippet: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of 432 strictly paired test cases across 48 executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a 3 times 3 factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across 12 representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to 64%), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

title: UniSpark: Exploring Hybrid Attention for Multimodal Understanding and Generation
author: Jiancheng Pan, Yuzheng Liu, Hengyuan Cao, Qiyuan Zhang
contentSnippet: We present UniSpark-9B, a unified multimodal model that investigates hybrid attention for visual understanding and generation. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts backbone with approximately 9B parameters in each branch, UniSpark combines full attention for explicit token interactions with GatedDeltaNet linear attention for compact context propagation. Autoregressive text prediction and visual flow matching jointly support visual question answering, text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and interleaved text-image prediction. In interleaved generation, noisy visual targets are isolated from subsequent predictions, while clean visual representations provide context for later outputs. A blockwise protocol enforces this distinction through attention masks in full-attention layers and recurrent-state retention rules in linear-attention layers. The selected training sources contain 159.7M generation samples, 213.4M understanding samples, and 624.8K interleaved sequences. A four-stage curriculum jointly trains multimodal understanding and visual generation, refining answer accuracy and instruction following while extending image synthesis to 2K. UniSpark scores 2470.3 on MME-S and 0.83 on GenEval. Qualitative examples further illustrate its capabilities in interleaved image generation, video synthesis, and video editing. Together, these results demonstrate that hybrid attention provides an effective backbone for unified multimodal understanding and generation.

title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
author: Yuxuan Chen, Xiaojie Li, Hao Chen, Juncheng Ma
contentSnippet: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair.

We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair.
We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

title: From Large Language Models to Efficient System One Models via Adaptive Computation
author: Minh-Anh Nguyen
contentSnippet: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose , which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.

title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement
author: Doyoung Kim, Byeongguk Jeon, Kailin Zhang, Sherry Yang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Doyoung Kim , Byeongguk Jeon , Kailin Zhang , Sherry Yang

Abstract: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering (\ace{}) harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, \acerl{}, evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, \acerl{} achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Doyoung Kim, Byeongguk Jeon, Kailin Zhang, and Sherry Yang have introduced Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning (ACERL), a method designed for recursive self-improvement in LLM agents. Traditional reinforcement learning trains agentic tasks using scalar rewards while discarding fine-grained environment feedback like error logs. While existing harness methods preserve past experiences through reflections or playbooks, the creation of those handed-off artifacts is typically unlearned. ACERL bridges this gap by combining gradient updates from scalar rewards with the utilization of environment information for experience handoffs.

Using the Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) harness as a concrete testbed, ACERL trains a single model to simultaneously act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. The framework evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts based on their direct downstream impact on future actor rollouts, co-optimizing role-specific behaviors including the action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator under a fixed scaffold. Across standard agentic benchmarks, ACERL demonstrates higher held-out performance compared to baseline training methods.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** ACERL co-optimizes role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) within a fixed Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) scaffold.

**Experience Evaluation:** Candidate experience-handoff artifacts are evaluated and optimized by measuring their downstream effect on future actor rollouts rather than relying solely on immediate scalar rewards.
**Benchmark Performance:** ACERL achieves higher held-out performance across agentic benchmarks compared to traditional baseline methods that discard fine-grained environment feedback.

title: DeepStress: Stress-Testing Deep Search Agents
author: Ismael Rousseau, Geraldine Damnati, Frederic Bechet
contentSnippet: While search agents demonstrate impressive capabilities in multi-step question answering, their robustness to poor-quality evidence remains under-explored. Such evidence is rare in benchmark corpora, and resulting failures are hard to reproduce. We propose DeepStress, a dynamic stress-testing framework that subjects agents to degraded evidence at controlled rates. It replaces the retrieval module with a synthetic environment where documents are generated dynamically for each query, under independent control of their trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. To characterize behavior under stress, we go beyond binary accuracy with a five-way classification of final-answer outcomes and two new reliability-aware metrics, RAS and CoPRAS, which credit cautious behavior and account for computational cost. Evaluating 12 systems on questions from HotpotQA and BrowseComp-Plus, we find that several open-weight agents answer confidently when sources contain obvious credibility red flags, and that many HotpotQA questions are answered from parametric knowledge even when all returned documents are factually wrong.

title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
author: Chin-Yang Lin, Ryo Hachiuma, Jaesung Choe, Min-Hung Chen
contentSnippet: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io

title: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes
author: Robert Fonod, Nikolas Geroliminis
contentSnippet:
Authors: Robert Fonod , Nikolas Geroliminis

Abstract: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.

Notes: 50 pages, 17 figures, 24 tables. Code at this https URL and data at this https URL and this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Robert Fonod and Nikolas Geroliminis have introduced a benchmark to address 'consensus capture' in reference-based UAV video stabilization, a phenomenon where moving objects in a scene—such as vehicles at an intersection—bias homography estimates during frame registration. While traditional benchmarks assume only camera motion, this study highlights how mutually consistent correspondences from moving foreground objects can mislead stabilization pipelines, even when inlier statistics appear normal. The authors provide a two-part benchmark: a static protocol using 4K aerial frames with known homographies, and a dynamic protocol that evaluates pipelines based on the coherence of moving foreground objects against manually audited ground control points.

Testing ten common pipelines, the study found that while AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT, and BRISK perform best on static scenes, they remain susceptible to consensus capture in dynamic environments. Specifically, unmasked ORB was captured in 28 out of 304 real-time dynamic pairs, resulting in a median corner error of 18.8 pixels despite maintaining typical inlier counts. The research demonstrates that object masking effectively eliminates consensus capture across all tested pipelines without degrading performance on static scenes. The authors have released the full dataset, code, and results, which are detailed across 50 pages, 17 figures, and 24 tables.
takeaways: **Consensus Capture Impact:** Unmasked ORB pipelines exhibited a median corner error of 18.8 pixels in dynamic scenarios where moving objects biased the homography estimate.
**Pipeline Performance:** AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT, and BRISK were identified as the leading pipelines for static aerial scene stabilization.
**Masking Efficacy:** Implementing object masking successfully removed consensus capture for all ten tested pipelines without negatively impacting performance on static scenes.
**Benchmark Scope:** The study evaluated pipelines under both offline and real-time computational budgets using 4K aerial footage and manually annotated ground control points.

title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
author: Zhengxu Yu, Ke Xu, Meng Fang, Haitham Ammar
contentSnippet:
Authors: Zhengxu Yu , Ke Xu , Meng Fang , Haitham Ammar , Weilin Luo , Jun Wang

Abstract: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $\lambda$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.

Notes: 20 pages, 3 figures

summary.tldr:
Researchers Zhengxu Yu, Ke Xu, Meng Fang, Haitham Ammar, Weilin Luo, and Jun Wang have introduced the Hybrid Decision Model (HDM), a framework that replaces traditional adaptive-reasoning methods—which typically truncate or skip token generation—with a 'zero-or-T' thinking paradigm. In this architecture, a single frozen backbone model operates in one of two modes: a fast mode that relies on implicit internal processing without generating tokens, or a slow, autoregressive mode that incurs a cost of T tokens. A lightweight self-routing block determines which mode to employ by estimating the 'value of thinking'—the expected utility gain of the slow mode over the fast mode—based on the implicit processing already performed. The slow mode is triggered only when this estimated value exceeds a user-defined cost threshold, λ.

To train the routing block in environments lacking per-decision labels, such as episodic agentic tasks, the authors developed Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes routing based on episode-level returns. Empirical evaluations demonstrate significant efficiency gains: on the JevBench benchmark, the HDM-4B model achieved a score of 0.857 compared to the baseline's 0.851, while reducing median latency by 72.5% (from 0.652s to 0.179s). Furthermore, in agentic tasks on MiniWoB, the HDM-27B model reduced total token consumption by 80.1%. The research is detailed in a 20-page paper featuring three figures.
takeaways: **Core Paradigm:** The 'zero-or-T' thinking model forces a binary choice between implicit, zero-token processing and full autoregressive reasoning.
**Routing Mechanism:** A lightweight self-routing block estimates the utility of slow-mode reasoning and triggers it only when the value exceeds a configurable cost parameter, λ.
**Training Methodology:** Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO) enables training the routing block using only episode-level returns, bypassing the need for per-decision labels.
**Performance Metrics:** HDM-4B on JevBench improved accuracy to 0.857 (vs 0.851) while cutting median latency by 72.5%.
**Agentic Efficiency:** HDM-27B demonstrated an 80.1% reduction in token costs when applied to the MiniWoB agentic benchmark.

title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
author: Ellis Brown, Chris Hoang, Shengyi Qian, Shang-Wen Li
contentSnippet: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage.

title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
author: Vahid Haratian
contentSnippet: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.
