title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
author: Amanda Silberling
contentSnippet:
Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security.

United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported.

The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang , and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang

After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wa

summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing a mounting corporate and national security crisis following reports of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based Megaspeed executive whom U.S. officials allege is a Chinese intelligence operative. The situation has escalated into a federal investigation by the Department of Justice, with House committee chairs threatening subpoenas if the CEO does not participate in a closed-door briefing regarding potential breaches of U.S. chip export restrictions. The controversy has triggered an internal board-led investigation and reports that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang, causing the company's stock to decline 11% over a five-day period.

Technical and commercial scrutiny centers on Megaspeed, an AI infrastructure firm that purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia hardware over two years. Investigations by U.S. and Singaporean authorities suggest Megaspeed acted as a conduit for bypassing export controls, with reports indicating the firm facilitated $7.5 billion in chip acquisitions, including restricted models, for Chinese entities like Alibaba. Further complicating the leadership crisis, the New York Times reported a second extramarital relationship between Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s Vice President of Healthcare, who reports directly to him. Huang has admitted to infidelity in a public letter but has not confirmed specific details regarding the allegations involving Alice Huang.
takeaways: **Corporate Governance:** Nvidia’s board has initiated an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, with reports suggesting active preparations for his removal following the dual-affair allegations.

**Export Control Violations:** Megaspeed International is under federal investigation for allegedly smuggling restricted Nvidia chips into China, with reports citing $7.5 billion in total chip acquisitions facilitated by the firm.

**Congressional Oversight:** Three House committee chairs—John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford—have requested a closed-door briefing, threatening a subpoena if Huang fails to address national security concerns.
**Market Impact:** Nvidia shares fell 8% in after-hours trading on November 11, 2026, contributing to an 11% decline over the preceding five-day period.

**Intelligence Allegations:** A secret memo supervised by Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly identified Alice Huang as an operative for China’s Ministry of State Security, a finding briefed to President Trump.

title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
author: Shivi Bhatia
contentSnippet: Developers increasingly use Codex with Amazon Bedrock to explore unfamiliar code, make changes, and handle repetitive engineering work. For platform teams, the challenge is to make those tools available without creating a second model-access, identity, and operations stack. Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. In this post, we show how to fit that path into the AWS identity, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Regional, and observability practices your organization already uses. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls. We begin with a small, least-privilege pilot and work through the checks that matter before access expands. The examples use GPT-5.6 Sol. Before starting the pilot, review Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock to confirm that Sol, Terra, or Luna is available in the AWS Region and inference path you plan to use. Recommended default: Start with Native AWS Access for a small, least-privilege pilot. Choose AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. A custom integration is the advanced version of the LLM Gateway pattern, not a quick start. The examples come from the open source Guidance for Codex on AWS repository. It includes quick starts for Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and the Amazon CloudWatch setup used later in the post. Choose the quick start that matches your architecture, use it for the pilot, and adapt it to your environment. Choose your rollout path Authentication is only one part of an enterprise rollout. Decide who can use the service and which models and Regions are approved. Also define where configuration lives, what telemetry to collect, how usage is allocated, and which skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are allowed. The following table maps those needs to an access path and an owning team. Choose the access path that provides the controls you need now. The most straightforward path that meets the requirement usually has the lowest operational overhead. De

summary.tldr:
AWS has published guidance for integrating OpenAI Codex with Amazon Bedrock, enabling developers to utilize OpenAI models while maintaining existing AWS identity, access management (IAM), and observability infrastructure. The integration allows Codex to run on local developer workstations while routing model requests through Amazon Bedrock, effectively centralizing operational controls and security policies within the AWS ecosystem. The documentation specifically references the use of 'GPT-5.6 Sol' as a model example, alongside mentions of 'Terra' and 'Luna' model variants, emphasizing the need to verify regional availability via the Amazon Bedrock supported models list.

To facilitate deployment, the guidance outlines three primary architectural patterns: Native AWS Access for least-privilege pilots, the AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore) for managed routing and Guardrails, and custom LLM Gateway implementations for advanced policy enforcement. AWS provides an open-source 'Guidance for Codex on AWS' repository containing quick-start templates for these patterns, including configurations for LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and Amazon CloudWatch integration. Platform teams are advised to evaluate requirements for telemetry, usage allocation, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server permissions when selecting an access path to minimize operational overhead.
takeaways: **Model Support:** The documentation cites GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna as models available for inference via Amazon Bedrock.
**Deployment Patterns:** Recommended architectures include Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway for managed routing/Guardrails, and custom LLM Gateway integrations.
**Tooling Integration:** The 'Guidance for Codex on AWS' repository includes pre-built quick starts for LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, ADOT, and Amazon CloudWatch.
**Operational Scope:** The architecture supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and requires centralized management of telemetry, usage allocation, and regional model availability.

title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
author: Ferhat Erata
contentSnippet: When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and , can get lost in that noise. A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification , which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found. One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB , the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first. Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy c

summary.tldr:
The article introduces a semantic diffing engine for formal policies that utilizes anti-unification—a technique derived from Plotkin’s 1970 research—to identify meaningful behavioral changes rather than superficial syntactic ones. By operating over an e-graph that tracks expressions known to be equivalent through supplied algebraic laws and domain rules, the engine isolates shared logic while highlighting specific points of divergence. This approach addresses the noise inherent in textual diffs, where minor reorderings or predicate swaps often obscure actual policy shifts.

Beyond policy auditing, the engine serves as a critical tool for autoformalization workflows, where LLMs translate natural language requirements into formal languages like SMT-LIB, Cedar, Dogwood, OpenShell, or Common Expression Language (CEL). Because LLMs can generate multiple, non-identical formalizations for the same prompt, the semantic diffing engine allows developers to compare candidates, identify consensus, and focus human review on the specific segments where the model outputs disagree. The engine effectively treats the absence of remaining differences as proof of equivalence under the provided rule set.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Uses anti-unification to find the most specific common pattern between two expressions, implemented over an e-graph to account for known algebraic and domain-specific equalities.
**Target Languages:** Supports formal policy formats including SMT-LIB (for Z3/cvc5 solvers), Cedar, Dogwood, OpenShell (YAML-based), and Common Expression Language (CEL).

**Autoformalization Utility:** Enables comparison of multiple LLM-generated formal artifacts to isolate discrepancies and verify consistency across different prompts, models, or sampling temperatures.
**Limitations:** The engine's ability to prove equivalence is bounded by the completeness of the provided algebraic laws and the underlying search mechanism.

title: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
author: Siddharth Senger
contentSnippet: Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself. In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land: A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces. A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint. A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update. We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository . How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circ

summary.tldr:
Amazon Web Services has introduced a detection and recovery framework for silent data corruption (SDC) within Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, specifically targeting distributed training environments where hardware errors occur without triggering standard system alerts. SDC, often caused by marginal transistors or silicon aging in GPU tensor cores, can propagate incorrect values through gradients and weights, leading to model divergence that remains undetected for hours. Meta reported that during the 54-day pre-training of Llama 3 405B on 16,000 H100 GPUs, 6 of 419 job interruptions were explicitly attributed to SDC, highlighting the scale of the issue in large-cluster training.

The proposed solution integrates three specific checks into the PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop: a non-finite gradient check for NaNs and Infs, a ring replay audit that recomputes micro-batches across nodes to compare loss and gradient fingerprints, and a weight fingerprint comparison to verify optimizer updates. When a check identifies a corruption, the system maps the fault to the specific rank and node, allowing SageMaker HyperPod to automatically replace the compromised hardware. AWS validated this methodology using software-injected faults on a cluster of 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances, totaling 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
takeaways: **SDC Prevalence:** Meta identified 6 SDC-related job interruptions out of 419 total during the 54-day Llama 3 405B pre-training run on 16K H100 GPUs.

**Detection Methodology:** The framework utilizes three distinct checks: non-finite gradient detection, ring replay audits for bit-for-bit loss comparison, and weight fingerprinting post-optimizer update.
**Hardware Validation:** AWS tested the recovery workflow on a cluster of 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs) using software-injected faults.
**Recovery Mechanism:** Upon detection, the system isolates the suspect rank and triggers the SageMaker HyperPod automatic node recovery process to swap out the faulty hardware.

title: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang
author: Amanda Silberling
contentSnippet: Posted: 3:28 PM PST · November 11, 2026 Image Credits: Tomohiro Ohsumi / Getty Images Amanda Silberling Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang Nvidia is reportedly planning to oust its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who has led the company for the last 33 years, the Wall Street Journal reports . Sources told the newspaper that the Nvidia board is meeting as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang’s future at the company. On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman purported by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. On Wednesday evening, the New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with an executive who reports to him. Nvidia has become one of the most valuable companies in the world as it designs the chips that power the AI boom, but in the midst of Huang’s ongoing scandal , Nvidia stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday. The stock is down about 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company also has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. Nvidia’s board of directors is reportedly preparing to remove co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang following a series of personal scandals. The board is scheduled to meet as early as Wednesday to deliberate on Huang's future at the company, which he has led for 33 years. The potential leadership change follows public admissions by Huang regarding an extramarital affair with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy, as well as a separate report from the New York Times alleging an affair with an executive who reported directly to him.

Nvidia’s stock price reacted sharply to the news, declining approximately 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and marking an 11% drop over the preceding five-day period. title: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Shubham Divekar
contentSnippet: AI agents and applications that answer questions about recent events, product releases, prices, or regulations need information newer than their model’s training data. Until now, Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore delivered that information to agents through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. That means creating a gateway and a web search target and calling the tool from an MCP client. The setup fits platform teams that share one search policy across many agents, but it’s more than you need when your own code only requires search results. Today, we’re announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With it, your own code can search the web with a single API call. It returns ranked results from a web index that Amazon operates, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), signed with the same AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials you use for your other AWS services. There are no resources to create first. Authenticate, call, and get results. Use it in an application, an agent loop you write yourself, or a data pipeline. Why a standalone API? The AgentCore Gateway is the recommended path for most agentic workloads. It gives agents one secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with your other tools. It also handles inbound and outbound authentication, semantic tool selection, and optional MCP sessions . But developers told us they also need a lower-level integration point for scenarios where the gateway is not the right fit: Custom orchestration frameworks –  Developers building their own agent loops, or using frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, want to call web search directly as a tool within their orchestration logic rather than routing through a gateway. Non-agent use cases –  Not every application that needs web grounding is an agent. Search-powered dashboards, fact-checking pipelines, content enrichment workflows, and monitoring systems all benefit from real-time web results without requiring agent infrastructure. Tighter control over the request lifecycle –  Some developers want to manage retries, caching, and error handling themselves rather than delegating to the gateway. Simpler integration for existing applications –  Applications that already h

summary.tldr:
Amazon has launched the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, providing a direct, programmatic method for developers to retrieve real-time web information without the overhead of the previously required AgentCore Gateway. The API returns ranked search results from an Amazon-operated index, including text extracts, page titles, URLs, and publication timestamps. It is accessible via standard AWS SDKs and the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), utilizing existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials for authentication.

This standalone API is designed for developers who require granular control over the request lifecycle, such as custom retry logic, caching, or error handling. It specifically targets use cases outside of the AgentCore Gateway ecosystem, including custom orchestration frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, non-agentic applications such as content enrichment pipelines, fact-checking dashboards, and monitoring systems. While the AgentCore Gateway remains the recommended solution for managing complex agentic workloads and Model Context Protocol (MCP) sessions, the new API provides a lower-level integration point for developers building their own agent loops or integrating search grounding into existing software architectures.
takeaways: **Access Method:** Developers can invoke the Web Search API directly through AWS SDKs or the AWS CLI using standard IAM credentials.
**Data Output:** Each API call returns ranked search results containing text extracts, page titles, URLs, and publication times.
**Target Use Cases:** The API is intended for custom agent loops (LangChain, LlamaIndex), non-agentic data pipelines, and applications requiring direct control over retries and caching.
**Architectural Shift:** Unlike the AgentCore Gateway, the Web Search API requires no pre-provisioned resources or MCP client configuration, allowing for immediate, stateless integration.

title: Google tests Tabletop, letting groups build planning tools with an AI agent
author: Duncan Riley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 17:37 EST / NOVEMBER 11 2026

Google tests Tabletop, letting groups build planning tools with an AI agent

Google LLC today began testing Tabletop, a Google Labs experiment in which groups share an online space and ask an artificial intelligence agent to build the planning tools they need.

In a blog post , Roman Nurik, design and engineering lead at Google Labs, wrote that coordinating a family trip or a potluck goes more smoothly when the whole group can pitch in from one place. Whoever sets up a space adds the links, files and ideas the group has collected, and from there a request to @tabletop produces the tool.

Tools Google lists include itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets, and there is a set of starter templates that Tabletop users can access as well. Once the space is shared through an invite link posted in the group’s existing chat, everyone can work on those tools at the same time, “like in a Google Doc,” Nurik wrote.

When a guest at an office party in one of Google’s demos ends up seated next to the boss, a request to @tabletop turns the seating chart into one where name badges can be dragged between tables. Any tool can be reworked the same way, according to the Tabletop site .

Google did not say which of its models run Tabletop. When Labs released its Disco browser experiment last December , Gemini 3 was the model it used to turn a person’s open tabs into small web apps. Tabletop also follows Google’s move in September to let up to six members of a household share the division’s CC agent. Rival OpenAI Group PBC added group chats to ChatGPT a year ago , and up to 20 people can now talk to the chatbot in one thread.

In ChatGPT the chatbot sits inside the conversation as one more member, and OpenAI said at launch that it had taught the model to judge when to join in. Replies in those chats initially came from GPT-5.1 Auto, which chooses a model based on the prompt and on the subscription of whoever ChatGPT is answering. OpenAI also kept personal memory out of group chats entirely.

Tabletop is limited for now to U.S. users 18 and older who sign up through the waitlist at tabletop.google , with Google saying it will let more people in each week. Google’s announcement does not mention pricing or a release outside the U.S.

Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community.

summary.tldr:
Google Labs has launched Tabletop, an experimental platform designed for collaborative group planning via an AI agent. Users create a shared online space where they can aggregate files, links, and ideas, then prompt the @tabletop agent to generate specific planning tools. These tools, which include itineraries, expense splitters, dinner polls, and interactive seating charts, allow for real-time, multi-user editing similar to a Google Doc. The platform is currently in a testing phase, accessible via a waitlist for U.S. users aged 18 and older.

While Google has not disclosed the specific underlying model powering Tabletop, the experiment follows the company's recent integration of AI into collaborative environments, such as the household-sharing features for its CC agent introduced in September. Tabletop functions as a direct competitor to OpenAI’s group chat functionality for ChatGPT, which allows up to 20 participants per thread and utilizes the GPT-5.1 Auto model. Unlike OpenAI’s approach, which treats the AI as a conversational participant, Tabletop focuses on the generative creation and manipulation of functional, interactive planning interfaces.
takeaways: **Platform Functionality:** Tabletop allows groups to generate custom planning tools like tournament brackets and draggable seating charts by prompting an AI agent with collected project data.
**Collaborative Model:** The platform supports real-time, multi-user interaction within shared spaces, functioning similarly to collaborative document editing.
**Access Restrictions:** Participation is currently limited to U.S. users aged 18+ via a waitlist at tabletop.google, with Google planning to expand access on a weekly basis.
**Competitive Context:** The tool competes with OpenAI’s group chat feature, which supports up to 20 users and uses the GPT-5.1 Auto model to manage responses.

title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
author: Tymofii Kryvtsun
contentSnippet: At AWS, we believe AI builders should be able to choose the right model for every task, trust their agents in production, and see clearly what their AI workloads cost. That belief guides how we invest across our portfolio. Amazon Bedrock gives you access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely. We extend this foundation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , which provides the platform to build, connect, and optimize agents using any model and any framework. That includes Strands , our open source agent development toolkit. Together, they take you from first prototype to production. As agents move into core business workflows, the bar rises. You need the flexibility to use different models as tasks, budgets, and latency targets change. When a primary model is throttled or unreachable, your agents must keep working. They also must act within limits you set and return output other software can use as is. Their answers must stay grounded in sources you allow, and their cost must hold up at high volume. What we shipped in October addresses each of these needs. New models help you match each task to the right price and speed, from high-volume subagents to real-time voice. Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore updates keep agents available, hold them to the processes you define, and help you trust what they return. New pricing and cost reporting make spend more predictable. Strands adds new ways to build, contain, and test agents. Match the model to the task on Amazon Bedrock Run fast, low-cost subagents. Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it is the most capable Haiku yet and costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It is also the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence for each task. In a multi-agent setup, a model such as Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku. This keeps running many agents in parallel affordable. Get near-flagship results at a lower price. OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it performed on par with GPT-6 Astra and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Its input and output token prices are at least 50 percent lowe

summary.tldr:
In October 2026, AWS expanded its AI infrastructure portfolio with updates to Amazon Bedrock and the introduction of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform designed for building, connecting, and optimizing agents across diverse models and frameworks. The release includes the open-source agent development toolkit, Strands, aimed at facilitating the transition from prototyping to production-grade agentic workflows. These updates focus on improving agent reliability, cost predictability, and operational flexibility, allowing developers to switch models dynamically based on latency, budget, and availability requirements.

Model updates include the general availability of Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra on Amazon Bedrock. Claude Haiku 5.5 features new effort controls to balance cost against intelligence and is priced approximately 75% lower than Claude Haiku 4.5. OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra is positioned as a high-performance alternative, matching the performance of GPT-6 Astra on the 'Agents’ Last Exam' benchmark while executing tasks over three times faster than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, with input and output token costs reduced by at least 50%.
takeaways: **Claude Haiku 5.5 Pricing:** Costs approximately 75% less than Claude Haiku 4.5 and introduces effort controls for task-specific intelligence tuning.
**GPT-6.1 Terra Performance:** Achieves parity with GPT-6 Astra on the 'Agents’ Last Exam' benchmark while delivering 3x faster task completion than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
**Agent Infrastructure:** Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides a unified platform for agent orchestration, supporting multi-agent setups where models like Claude Opus 5.5 delegate tasks to Haiku 5.5.
**Open Source Toolkit:** Strands is now available as an open-source agent development toolkit integrated with the Bedrock AgentCore ecosystem.

title: Gemini Decisions API
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models

summary.tldr:
Google has entered the decision model market with the release of the Gemini Decision 1 API, positioning it as a direct competitor to Jev and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna. The model supports three primary question types: yes/no (referred to as 'Noul'), choice, and rubric-scoring. Unlike its competitors, Gemini Decision 1 is natively multi-modal, capable of processing text, images, audio, video, and PDF inputs. Pricing is set at $0.10 per million input tokens, with output tokens provided free of charge, matching the pricing structure of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna but remaining more expensive than Jev, which costs $0.042 per million input tokens.

Technically, Gemini Decision 1 distinguishes itself through its output format. While Jev and OpenAI typically return binary 1.0 or 0.0 values for yes/no queries, Gemini Decision 1 provides granular probability scores. In testing against video content, the model returned specific floating-point confidence intervals (e.g., 0.923 for robot detection) rather than absolute binary classifications. While Jev is restricted to text and JSON inputs and OpenAI supports text and images, Gemini’s broader modality support allows for direct analysis of complex media files like video.
takeaways: **Pricing Structure:** Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens with free output, matching GPT-6 Luna but exceeding Jev's $0.042 per million rate.
**Modality Support:** Gemini Decision 1 supports text, images, audio, video, and PDFs, whereas Jev is limited to text/JSON and OpenAI supports text and images.
**Output Methodology:** Unlike Jev and OpenAI which return binary 1.0 or 0.0 values, Gemini Decision 1 returns specific probability scores for yes/no queries.
**Question Types:** The API supports the same three standard decision model categories: yes/no (Noul), choice, and rubric-scoring.

title: United won’t let your AI agent book your flight
author: Lauren Feiner
contentSnippet: United says it won’t let personal AI assistants book tickets on the airline, citing both privacy and regulatory concerns. The company says it hasn’t yet seen many people try to use AI agents to book their flights, The Wall Street Journal reports, in line with observations from other businesses like Doordash. But United is concerned that agents could expose customers’ information or make purchases they didn’t intend, and potentially skirt federal rules about the kind of information airlines need to share with customers — like having them attest that their bags don’t have explosives. While agents can still show users United flights, they won’t be able to actually complete the transaction on their behalf. The decision, and others like it, could limit the potential usefulness of newer personal AI assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” United CEO Scott Kirby said at an event on Tuesday, according to the Journal. Across sectors, businesses are grappling with whether to let AI agents transact on their sites, and United is not alone in blocking access for unauthorized agents. eBay appeared to block agents from browsing the site, and several major banks have also placed restrictions on them. United suggests it could reconsider its decision based on future advancements. “As third-party AI agents advance, we see the opportunities they present. However, at the same time, allowing them to interact directly with a United account or booking could involve sensitive actions, and we want to make sure we have established protections for travelers first.”

summary.tldr:
United Airlines has officially prohibited personal AI agents from completing flight bookings on its platform, citing significant concerns regarding data privacy, regulatory compliance, and the potential for unauthorized transactions. While these agents are still permitted to display flight availability and pricing, the airline is blocking the final transaction step to prevent AI-driven errors or the circumvention of mandatory federal safety disclosures, such as hazardous materials attestations. CEO Scott Kirby stated that the company aims to avoid introducing unnecessary middlemen into the booking process, reflecting a broader industry trend where firms like eBay and various major financial institutions are similarly restricting automated agent access to their transactional systems.

This policy directly impacts the utility of emerging personal AI assistants, including Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, which are designed to perform autonomous tasks on behalf of users. United maintains that while it recognizes the potential utility of these technologies, it will not allow direct interaction with customer accounts or booking flows until robust security and protection frameworks are established. The airline has indicated that it may reconsider its stance as AI agent technology matures and security standards evolve, but for now, it remains committed to maintaining direct control over the passenger booking experience.
takeaways: **Booking Restriction:** United Airlines allows AI agents to display flight information but explicitly blocks them from completing the final ticket purchase transaction.

**Regulatory Compliance:** The airline cites federal requirements, such as mandatory passenger attestations regarding explosives in luggage, as a primary barrier to allowing autonomous AI agents to manage bookings.

**Industry Precedent:** United joins other major entities, including eBay and various financial institutions, in implementing technical blocks against unauthorized AI agents browsing or transacting on their platforms.
**Executive Stance:** CEO Scott Kirby expressed a strategic desire to avoid creating new intermediaries in the airline's direct-to-consumer booking model.

title: Google Launches Gemini Decisions API With Gemini Decision 1 at $0.10/M Tokens
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API , powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1 ( gemini-decision-1 ). The Gemini Decisions API does not generate text. It scores up to 1,000 typed questions against one shared input and returns calibrated probabilities. For developers, this targets the small branching calls inside agents: routing, policy checks, tool selection and grading. Google prices it at $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with zero output tokens billed. TL;DR Size: Context is 262,144 tokens (256K) across shared input and all questions. Runs on: Google-hosted API only (Gemini Developer API, v1beta). No open weights or self-hosting. Performance: Leads 7 of 9 accuracy benchmarks in Google’s table, with the lowest calibration error. Best: 92.2% on JevBench (public split). Worst: 58.7% Macro-F1 on Amazon ESCI, its lowest score. It also trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call (79.9% vs 82.0%). Bottom line: Best: multimodal, calibrated decisions in 150-250 ms. Worst: not the cheapest; Jev 1.14 costs $0.68 vs $0.88 on the shared suite. What is the Gemini Decisions API? Gemini Decision 1 is a specialized multimodal model from Google built for closed-set decisions. It reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in one prefill pass. Output token usage is always 0. Your code branches directly on the returned numbers. Each request has 3 parts: a model ID, a shared input , and a map of questions. The docs define 3 question types: noul (yes/no): returns the probability of yes, bounded between 0.01 and 0.99. choice : picks 1 of 2 to 255 options and returns normalized probabilities for every option. score : rates input on 2 to 255 ordered rubric levels and returns a probability-weighted score. Every answer carries a confidence value from 0 to 1. Google suggests routing low-confidence cases to a fallback or a human reviewer. Questions are scored in parallel and cannot see each other. How does Gemini Decision 1 work? Standard models decode an answer token by token, then your code parses it. Gemini Decision 1 instead scores your candidate options in one forward pass. Google reports median model compute of 50-100 ms and 150-250 ms end to end. That holds for inputs up to 16K tokens and stays nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions. Billing follows the same design. The shared input is billed once per request, however many questions you ask. Each question adds only its own instruction and crit

summary.tldr:
Google has introduced the Gemini Decisions API, powered by the specialized Gemini Decision 1 (gemini-decision-1) model. Unlike standard generative models, this API does not produce text; instead, it processes a shared input—supporting text, images, video, audio, and PDFs—and scores up to 1,000 concurrent questions against that input to return calibrated probabilities. Designed for agentic workflows such as routing, policy enforcement, tool selection, and grading, the model is available exclusively via the Google-hosted Gemini Developer API (v1beta) with no open weights or self-hosting options.

The architecture optimizes performance by performing a single forward pass to score candidate options, bypassing the token-by-token decoding process. This results in end-to-end latency of 150-250 ms, with model compute times between 50-100 ms for inputs up to 16K tokens. The API supports three question types: 'bool' (yes/no probabilities), 'choice' (normalized probabilities across 2-255 options), and 'score' (probability-weighted ratings across 2-255 rubric levels). Each response includes a confidence value (0 to 1) to facilitate fallback logic for low-confidence decisions.
takeaways: **Pricing Structure:** The API is priced at $0.10 per 1 million input tokens, with zero output tokens billed, as the model returns numerical probabilities rather than generated text.
**Context Window:** The model supports a 262,144-token (256K) context window shared across the input and all concurrent questions.
**Benchmark Performance:** Gemini Decision 1 achieved a 92.2% accuracy on the JevBench public split, though it trails Jev 1.14 on the When2Call benchmark (79.9% vs 82.0%).
**Operational Efficiency:** The system processes up to 1,000 questions in parallel per request, with latency remaining nearly flat regardless of the number of questions asked.

aws-emulator . Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so.

summary.tldr:
AWS has released an official emulator designed to allow developers to run tests against local clones of various AWS services, eliminating the need to provision paid API keys for testing environments. The project, highlighted by AWS VP Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog, was developed using a high-velocity approach, recording 29,684 commits within its first three weeks of existence.

title: Automating AWS Agent Registry updates with push-based architecture
author: Prachi Kulkarni
contentSnippet: Every time a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record must be updated too. Without automated push-based sync, consumers discover stale metadata. For organizations managing multiple MCP servers across accounts, such a sync keeps catalog records current within an existing governance workflow. In most enterprise deployments, a catalog’s value depends on its freshness. If a developer deploys a new tool on Monday, but the registry record still reflects last week’s schema, consumers lose trust in the catalog. Stale metadata directly reduces registry reliability, leading teams to inadvertently build dependencies on inaccurate information. When an engineer adds a tool to an MCP server but forgets to update the catalog: Consumers miss out on the new capability entirely. Applications might call the tool using an outdated schema, causing unexpected runtime behavior or silent workflow deviations. Multiplied across teams, this lack of automation erodes trust in the registry. Organizations ultimately fall back on ad hoc discovery mechanisms like hardcoded endpoints, informal knowledge sharing, and stale documentation. In this post, we outline an event-driven architecture that automates these updates using AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda. Architecture overview The following solution brings these services together into an event-driven pipeline that detects runtime changes and synchronizes them to the registry automatically. The architecture supports both multi-account and single-account environments: Single-account setup: For straightforward deployments, all components reside within Account A. Cross-account forwarding setup isn’t needed as events flow directly within Account A. Multi-account setup: This involves two accounts where runtime events from Account B are securely forwarded to Account A. Account A (registry account) owns the AWS Agent Registry, the Amazon EventBridge rule, the push-sync Lambda function, and CloudTrail logs. Account B (MCP server account) hosts the MCP server runtime and the Amazon Cognito OAuth provider used for authentication. The sample uses two accounts, but you can scale the architecture for multiple accounts, with Account A as the registry account and multiple AWS accounts similar to Account B

summary.tldr:
Amazon has detailed an event-driven, push-based architecture designed to automate metadata synchronization for the AWS Agent Registry, a capability within Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The solution addresses the issue of stale metadata, which occurs when Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers update their tools or schemas without corresponding updates to the central registry. By automating this process, the architecture prevents runtime errors, silent workflow deviations, and the erosion of developer trust that occurs when applications rely on outdated tool definitions.

The proposed architecture utilizes a pipeline composed of AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda to detect runtime changes and propagate them to the registry. The system supports both single-account and multi-account deployments. In a multi-account configuration, the 'Registry Account' (Account A) hosts the registry, EventBridge rules, and the synchronization Lambda function, while the 'MCP Server Account' (Account B) hosts the MCP server runtime and Amazon Cognito OAuth provider. Events from Account B are securely forwarded to Account A, allowing the registry to maintain a current catalog across distributed organizational environments.
takeaways: **Core Components:** The architecture integrates AWS CloudTrail for event detection, Amazon EventBridge for event routing, and AWS Lambda for executing the registry synchronization.

**Deployment Models:** The system supports single-account setups for localized deployments and multi-account setups where runtime events are forwarded from an MCP server account to a centralized registry account.

**Problem Addressed:** The automation mitigates risks associated with stale metadata, including runtime failures, inaccurate tool schema usage, and the reliance on ad hoc discovery methods like hardcoded endpoints.
**Authentication:** The multi-account reference architecture utilizes Amazon Cognito as the OAuth provider for securing the MCP server runtime.

title: Google DeepMind Releases AlphaGenome 2 for Cell-Type-Specific Variant Effects
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2 , a DNA model that predicts variant effects in specific cell types. AlphaGenome 2 is a conditional sequence-to-function model. It reads 1 Mb of DNA plus a target cell state. Its predecessor averaged across bulk tissues. The new model resolves closely related cell types and adapts to unseen single-cell datasets without fine-tuning. It is available through the AlphaGenome API for non-commercial research. TL;DR Size: Input is a 1 Mb (1,048,576 bp) DNA window, human or mouse. Runs on: Hosted API only for now. Training used 2048 TPU v4 chips; weights come “upon final publication”. Performance: Beats fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1, Borzoi and Scooby on single-cell eQTL and enhancer-gene benchmarks. Best: 43% recall at 90% sign accuracy on TenK10K sc-eQTLs, versus 23% for AlphaGenome 1 fine-tuned. Worst: Outside accessible chromatin, sign prediction AUROC reaches only 0.63. Bottom line: Best: cell-state conditioning from raw scRNA-seq. Worst: no local weights, non-commercial only. What is AlphaGenome 2? AlphaGenome 2 is a U-Net style model with a convolutional encoder, an 11-block transformer and a decoder. AlphaGenome 1 predicted a fixed catalog of thousands of tracks in parallel. AlphaGenome 2 instead predicts outputs for 1 condition per call. The condition is a 256-dimensional embedding. It modulates activations through FiLM layers in the encoder, transformer and decoder. Conditioning only the decoder or output layers gave minimal gains. Conditioning the encoder and transformer drove most of the improvement. Outputs cover RNA coverage, CAGE, splicing, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, TF binding and contact maps. CpG methylation is new. How was AlphaGenome 2 trained? Training runs in 4 stages: Pre-training across bulk data plus 3,977 single-cell RNA and ATAC pseudobulk tracks from 36 studies. Condition refinement , which tunes only the embeddings and FiLM layers. Distillation of 8 teacher models into 1 student, using mutated input sequences. Post-training that maps a single-cell expression encoder into the frozen model’s condition space. That encoder was trained on over 100 million human scRNA-seq profiles, largely from CELLxGENE. Researchers can pass raw counts and get a condition embedding. The docs allow up to 256 cells per call. How does AlphaGenome 2 perform on benchmarks? On GTEx tissues, median Pearson r for cros

summary.tldr:
Google DeepMind has unveiled AlphaGenome 2, a conditional sequence-to-function model designed to predict DNA variant effects within specific cell types. Unlike its predecessor, which relied on bulk tissue averaging, AlphaGenome 2 processes a 1 Mb (1,048,576 bp) DNA window alongside a target cell state, enabling it to resolve closely related cell types and adapt to unseen single-cell datasets without requiring fine-tuning. The model is currently accessible exclusively via the AlphaGenome API for non-commercial research purposes, with model weights slated for release upon final publication.

Architecturally, AlphaGenome 2 utilizes a U-Net style design featuring a convolutional encoder, an 11-block transformer, and a decoder. It incorporates FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) layers across the encoder, transformer, and decoder to integrate a 256-dimensional condition embedding, which provides superior performance compared to conditioning only the output layers. The model was trained in four stages: pre-training on bulk data and 3,977 single-cell RNA/ATAC pseudobulk tracks, condition refinement, distillation of eight teacher models into one student, and post-training to map a single-cell expression encoder into the model's condition space. This expression encoder was trained on over 100 million human scRNA-seq profiles, primarily from CELLxGENE.

In benchmark testing, AlphaGenome 2 outperformed fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1, Borzoi, and Scooby models on single-cell eQTL and enhancer-gene tasks. It achieved 43% recall at 90% sign accuracy on TenK10K sc-eQTLs, significantly higher than the 23% recall achieved by the fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1. While the model excels at cell-state conditioning from raw scRNA-seq, it faces limitations in regions outside accessible chromatin, where sign prediction AUROC drops to 0.63. Training required 2,048 TPU v4 chips.
takeaways: **Architecture:** U-Net style model with a convolutional encoder, 11-block transformer, and FiLM-modulated decoder.
**Input Capacity:** Processes a 1 Mb (1,048,576 bp) DNA window for human or mouse sequences.
**Performance Metric:** Achieved 43% recall at 90% sign accuracy on TenK10K sc-eQTLs, doubling the 23% recall of the fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1.
**Training Infrastructure:** Utilized 2,048 TPU v4 chips across four distinct training stages.
**Conditioning:** Uses a 256-dimensional embedding derived from raw scRNA-seq counts to modulate model activations.

title: How DXC Technology built a multi-model AI substrate on Amazon Bedrock
author: Asif Fouzi
contentSnippet: This post is co-written with Nick Tamburro of DXC Technology. When an AI agent can act on a production server at a bank or a hospital, access to a capable foundation model is only the starting point. Recent public incidents, in which autonomous agents took destructive actions their operators never intended, show that the real risk is rarely the model alone. It’s an agent holding more authority than its task requires, with nothing in the architecture to stop it. Avoiding that starts with a substrate that governs model access at the infrastructure level. Amazon Bedrock provides that substrate. Through a single managed interface, it gives DXC OASIS access to multiple foundation models: Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova , Meta Llama, and open-weight families. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforce content filtering, personally identifiable information (PII) redaction, and denied-topic policies uniformly across every model. AWS PrivateLink keeps inference traffic within the customer’s virtual private cloud (VPC), and serverless scaling avoids self-managed GPU infrastructure as a failure point. Because these are system-level controls rather than bolt-ons, they gave DXC Technology a governed foundation for what no model layer can deliver on its own: a trusted harness that orchestrates, governs, and audits AI agents across enterprise IT operations at scale. Model availability varies by AWS Region. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . DXC Technology runs managed IT services for some of the world’s most regulated organizations: banks, hospitals, and government agencies. With more than 115,000 employees across 70 countries, DXC operates mission-critical systems where resilience and governance are non-negotiable. When DXC set out to build DXC OASIS, the harness for mission-critical IT operations, the team separated the problem into two layers. The first is a governed model substrate built on Amazon Bedrock. The second is the trusted harness built on top: DXC’s own orchestration, governance, and assurance layer. In this post, we explore how DXC built the resilient, flexible model substrate beneath DXC OASIS on Amazon Bedrock. We also show where DXC drew the line between what the substrate provides and what the harness must provide. Since general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS has reduced resolution time by 95% on average across 56 measured use cases. Acro

summary.tldr:
DXC Technology has developed DXC OASIS, an orchestration and governance platform for mission-critical IT operations, utilizing Amazon Bedrock as its underlying model substrate. The architecture is designed to mitigate risks associated with autonomous agents in regulated sectors like banking and healthcare by enforcing infrastructure-level controls. By leveraging Amazon Bedrock, DXC gains access to a multi-model environment including Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova, and Meta Llama, while offloading security and compliance tasks to AWS-managed services.

The platform architecture separates concerns into two distinct layers: a governed model substrate and a proprietary orchestration harness. The substrate utilizes Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for uniform content filtering, PII redaction, and denied-topic policies, while AWS PrivateLink ensures inference traffic remains within the customer's virtual private cloud (VPC). This serverless approach eliminates the need for self-managed GPU infrastructure. Since its general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS has been deployed across 56 use cases, reportedly reducing incident resolution time by an average of 95%.
takeaways: **Platform Performance:** DXC OASIS has achieved a 95% reduction in average resolution time across 56 measured use cases since its March 2026 general availability.
**Model Support:** The substrate provides access to Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, and various open-weight model families via a single managed interface.
**Security Architecture:** Infrastructure-level governance is enforced through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for PII redaction and topic denial, with network isolation provided by AWS PrivateLink.
**Operational Scale:** DXC Technology manages IT services for clients in 70 countries, utilizing the platform to govern AI agents across highly regulated environments including hospitals and banks.

title: Why the data center you dread might never even be built

title: Meta is losing its longtime head of  infrastructure
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet: Posted: 12:12 PM PST · November 11, 2026 Image Credits: Marcin Golba/NurPhoto / Getty Images Lucas Ropek Meta is losing its longtime head of infrastructure A key figure in Meta’s growth into a social media and tech industry powerhouse is leaving the company. Santosh Janardhan, the company’s longtime head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, will be stepping down, Meta told TechCrunch. He will be replaced by Dave Brown, who joined the company as vice president of infrastructure earlier this year, the company added. It sounds like Janardhan will remain at Meta for a little bit, although he is expected to leave next year. “Santosh will stay on for transition and he is moving into an advisory role on Meta Compute,” said a Meta representative. Janardhan, who originally joined the company in 2009, helped the firm grow into the massive internet presence that it is today. Bloomberg originally reported Janardhan’s departure, citing an internal memo that had recently been circulated. It’s unclear why Janardhan is stepping down from the role. The memo did not specify the reasons for his departure and Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for clarity on the issue. However, Janardhan’s memo apparently cited the need to “pass the baton.” In recent years, the company’s investment in infrastructure has exploded , as it seeks to keep up with its competitors in the AI race. Earlier this year, Janardhan was tasked with leading Meta Compute , the company initiative to scale its data center investments and strategy. title: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets
author: Sabine Khan
contentSnippet: If you’re building generative AI solutions, reusable assets can help you stop rebuilding components that already exist: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, document processors, agent scaffolding, and so on. This has a compounding cost: time not spent solving the customer’s actual problem. This post shows you how to access a curated catalog of 23 production-ready assets from the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, now part of AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services. These assets can reduce your development time from months to weeks, with evidence from companies like DoorDash , Lyft , and Ricoh . Since 2023, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center has published open source reusable assets. These production-grade building blocks give you a validated foundation to start from instead of a blank file. These assets have powered customer solutions delivering measurable results: 50x increases in testing capacity, 90 percent reductions in engineering hours, and deployment timelines compressed from months to weeks. In this post, you will learn why teams keep rebuilding generative AI components, what makes an asset truly reusable, how companies like DoorDash and Ricoh achieved measurable results by using these assets, and how to access and deploy 23 open source assets from the catalog. For a complete list of all available assets, see the asset catalog at the end of this post. The problem: Why teams keep rebuilding Three root causes drive redundant development across generative AI teams: No single source of truth – Assets scatter across repositories, wikis, and drives. Builders can’t find what exists, so they rebuild from scratch. No quality signal – Without verification of production readiness, security reviews, or maintenance status, builders have no way to trust existing solutions and default to writing their own code. No reuse culture – Sharing remains informal and ungoverned. What one team builds stays with that team, and problems get solved repeatedly. The cost of rebuilding compounds. Each redundant build consumes engineering hours, delays customer delivery, and creates maintenance burden. Even AI-generated code requires production hardening, security reviews, testing at scale, and ongoing maintenance.
