title: MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. TL;DR Size: 29B-parameter diffusion transformer (MMDiT), dense. Inputs: text plus an optional first frame. Output: 704×1248 video at 24 fps, up to 20 s. Runs on: Data-center GPUs. Each worker holds the full 29B model in BF16, with block offloading as fallback. Performance: Leads 6 tested models on full plans. Trails MiniMax-H3 on single actions and human preference. Best: 34.0% full-plan completion on 100 multi-step tasks, the highest of all models tested (self-reported). Worst: About 2 in 3 plans miss a step. Physics-IQ system default: 37.48 vs 42.91 for MiniMax-H3. Bottom line: Best: a fully open world model that leads on multi-step plans. Worst: long plans still fail often, and hardware needs are high. What is PAN 2? PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. How does PAN 2 work? PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : Conceptual reasoning : An LLM reads the observation and the requested actions. It writes the next world state as structured JSON: events, timed actions bound to actors, and camera motion. Any instruction-following LLM can fill this role. IFM’s report uses Kimi K3 by default. Perceptual reasoning : A 29B MMDiT predicts the video latents. IFM trained it from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos. A frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder conditions it. The Wan 2.2 VAE decoder renders the final frames. IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footag

summary.tldr:
The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI has released PAN 2, a 29B-parameter dense diffusion transformer (MMDiT) designed for physical intelligence and simulative reasoning. Released under an Apache 2.0 license, the model is intended for robotics and agent developers to validate plans in simulation before physical execution. It accepts text prompts and an optional first frame, outputting 704×1248 video at 24 fps for durations up to 20 seconds. The model requires data-center GPUs, with the full 29B parameters stored in BF16 format, utilizing block offloading as a fallback mechanism.

PAN 2 utilizes a two-stage reasoning architecture: conceptual reasoning, where an LLM (defaulting to Kimi K3) generates structured JSON defining events and camera motion, and perceptual reasoning, where the 29B MMDiT predicts video latents conditioned by a frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder and rendered via a Wan 2.2 VAE decoder. In internal benchmarks, PAN 2 achieved a 34.0% success rate on 100 multi-step tasks, outperforming five other tested models in full-plan completion. However, it trails the MiniMax-H3 model in single-action accuracy and overall Physics-IQ scores (37.48 vs 42.91). Ablation studies highlight the critical nature of the conceptual reasoning stage; removing it causes full-plan completion to collapse from 34.0% to 0.0%.
takeaways: **Architecture:** 29B-parameter dense MMDiT trained from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos.
**Performance:** Achieved 34.0% full-plan completion on multi-step tasks, leading six tested models in that specific metric.
**Dependencies:** Requires a conceptual reasoning LLM (e.g., Kimi K3) to generate structured JSON; without this, full-plan completion drops to 0%.
**Hardware Requirements:** Full 29B model in BF16 requires data-center grade GPUs with block offloading support.
**Output Specifications:** Generates 704×1248 resolution video at 24 fps for up to 20 seconds.

title: Nvidia’s crisis has corporate governance experts reaching for the popcorn
author: Connie Loizos
contentSnippet:
Nvidia’s stock sank 5.47% on Tuesday, following a 4% drop on Monday, a loss of about 9.5% in two days, even though there wasn’t much news out of the company. CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly been trying to conduct business as usual after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The biggest development: the board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an internal investigation.

What comes next is mostly a guessing game, even for the people who study how boards are supposed to handle crises. Two corporate governance professors, Ann Lipton of the University of Colorado and Todd Henderson of the University of Chicago, say there is no real precedent for a CEO caught up in a suspected honeypot. And while they have views on what the investigation should ask, like everyone else, they’re watching to see how it plays out.

“There have actually been affair cases and sexual harassment cases,” Lipton said, but was quick to add that she doesn’t know of previous cases that also involve potential national security compromises. Henderson, whose research interests include corporations, securities regulation, and law and economics, said much depends on facts few people have yet, including, most importantly, what, if anything, Alice Huang got out of Jensen Huang. (Secrets about Nvidia’s fabs or chip designs would matter to the Justice Department. Ordinary corporate information probably would not.)

Lipton described the investigation led by Nvidia’s independent board members, with their own outside counsel, as perhaps the most “standard” aspect of the whole affair so far. She also observed that an investigation will be “exactly as thorough” as the directors running it want it to be, which is also standard. Henderson made a related point about incentives, saying that Washington law firms that conduct internal investigations “know who pays their bills.” He didn’t suggest that’s happening here.

Lipton said she sees three lines of inquiry, including whether the law was broken, whether Huang violated Nvidia’s internal policies, and whether the board was misled, including how forthcoming he was and when he was on notice. It’s notable, as Wired reported Monday , that Huang hired a PR crisis firm known for handling sex scandals a full year ago. Of course, the driver could have been about th

summary.tldr: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is currently the subject of an internal investigation by the company's board following reports of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an individual identified by U.S. intelligence agencies as a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia’s stock price declined approximately 9.5% over a two-day period following the news. The board has retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent inquiry into the matter, specifically examining whether the CEO violated internal policies, misled the board, or compromised national security and proprietary technology.
takeaways: **Legal Investigation:** Nvidia’s board has engaged Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to determine if Huang violated corporate policy or misled directors regarding the nature of his relationship.
**Market Impact:** Nvidia shares dropped 5.47% on Tuesday following a 4% decline on Monday, totaling a 9.5% loss in market value over 48 hours.

**Governance Concerns:** Experts highlight risks regarding Nvidia’s lack of a formal succession plan, a flat organizational structure with over 60 direct reports to the CEO, and the employment of three family members in senior roles.

**Shareholder Litigation:** Nvidia is currently facing a proposed class-action lawsuit alleging that the company and Huang misled investors by concealing the relationship while characterizing dealings with the woman's former employer as routine.

**Ownership Structure:** Unlike many tech peers, Nvidia does not utilize dual-class shares; Jensen Huang owns approximately 3.6% of the company, theoretically providing the board more leverage to remove him than if he held super-voting control.

title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

Copyright Complaints

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

Key Highlights

Benchmark results

Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.

summary.tldr:
Tether AI Research has released BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter agentic language model optimized for on-device personal assistant tasks. Built upon the Qwen3.5-0.8B architecture, BotPsy is designed for function calling and multi-turn agentic workflows, including web research, commerce, and device control. The model is released under the Apache 2.0 license and is available in bf16, Q8, and Q4 precisions via Hugging Face safetensors and GGUF formats for use with the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp.

BotPsy utilizes a four-stage training pipeline: full-parameter supervised fine-tuning (SFT), multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of reinforcement learning (RL). This methodology leverages imitation of reference trajectories, token distributions from larger 4B-parameter teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards. The model demonstrates significant efficiency gains, requiring 3x fewer reasoning tokens on GPQA Diamond and 2.7x fewer on MMLU-Pro compared to its base model, while reducing repetitive reasoning loops from 22.9% to 1.4%.
takeaways: **Benchmark Performance:** BotPsy outperforms models up to 1.2B parameters across six benchmarks, including BFCL v4, ACEBench, and τ-bench, and surpasses the 2B-parameter Qwen3.5-2B-Think on five of those six metrics.

**Agentic Reliability:** The model achieves an 86.1% score on BFCL v4 hallucination tests (declining invalid tool calls) and an 82.5 score on τ²-bench telecom tasks, significantly outperforming larger 2B-parameter counterparts.
**Safety Improvements:** Automated red-teaming shows an unsafe response rate of 21%, down from 36% in the base model, with prompt-injection vulnerability dropping from 46% to 31%.
**Instruction Following:** BotPsy achieves an IFBench score of 55.9 and an IFEval score of 90.8, marking the highest performance in its weight class for instruction following.
**Training Methodology:** The model is post-trained using a sequential four-stage process involving SFT, MOPD, and two rounds of RL, utilizing three specialized Qwen3.5-4B teacher models.

title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
author: Haoran Zhang, Huizhen Sun, Hanbin Wen, Jie Leng, Jiaxin Zhu, Zhaohua Sun
contentSnippet:
Authors: Haoran Zhang , Huizhen Sun , Hanbin Wen , Jie Leng , Jiaxin Zhu , Zhaohua Sun

Abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

Notes: 23 pages, 9 figures, 18 tables. Project page: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Haoran Zhang et al. have introduced EarthRecord, a benchmark designed to evaluate the capability of multimodal agents to perform land-change analysis using raw, multi-sensor satellite archives. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on curated or preprocessed datasets, EarthRecord requires agents to process raw data from Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 spanning four decades. The benchmark includes 238 land-change questions across ten distinct analysis tasks, with performance measured against global product references, method agreement, and visual interpretation.

Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that while current models can execute end-to-end analysis workflows, they struggle significantly with mapping specific pixel data to accurate land-change conclusions. The study utilizes two control mechanisms: a 'closed book' test that removes the satellite record to isolate prior knowledge, and an 'instrument pair' test that alters satellite data to check for grounding. Results indicate that agents often rely on prior knowledge rather than pixel-level evidence; when satellite data is artificially altered, 50% of the agents' previously 'correct' answers shift to match the altered data, suggesting a lack of true grounding in physical Earth observation.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** EarthRecord covers 56 sites with four decades of raw data from Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2.
**Task Complexity:** The benchmark consists of 238 land-change questions categorized into ten specific analysis tasks.
**Agent Performance:** Testing of twelve multimodal agents shows they can complete workflows but fail to accurately map imagery to real-world ground changes.
**Grounding Failure:** In instrument pair tests, 50% of correct answers followed artificial data alterations, indicating reliance on prior knowledge over raw pixel data.

title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
author: Sachith Abeywickrama, Emadeldeen Eldele, Min Wu, Xiaoli Li, Chau Yuen
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced ConceptTime, a self-supervised framework designed to address the trilemma of accuracy, interpretability, and abstention in time-series classification for risk-sensitive domains. Unlike traditional methods that rely on fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, ConceptTime utilizes a frozen probabilistic forecaster to generate a 'predictive surprise' signal—the divergence between predicted and realized observations. This signal simultaneously identifies segment boundaries and characterizes segments based on their dynamical behavior relative to expectations, rather than raw visual features.

The architecture processes these segments into a learned vocabulary of dynamical regimes, or 'concepts,' which are then fed into a lightweight classification head. By measuring the distance to the nearest concept, the model provides an inherent reliability metric for abstention. ConceptTime achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art black-box models while outperforming existing interpretable baselines. Notably, the model requires no domain expert annotations, language model integration, or external labels to function, as demonstrated by its performance across 17 public benchmarks.
takeaways: **Performance Metric:** ConceptTime retains near-98% accuracy on the Epilepsy dataset while utilizing only 1% of available labels.
**Methodology:** The model replaces manual annotation with a self-supervised 'predictive surprise' signal derived from a frozen probabilistic forecaster.

**Benchmarking:** The framework was evaluated against 17 public benchmarks, demonstrating competitive performance with black-box models and superiority over interpretable baselines like SHAP, TimeX, and TimeX++.
**Reliability:** The system enables abstention by design, calculating reliability based on the distance between input segments and the learned concept vocabulary.
**Availability:** The implementation is open-source and available at https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.

title: Auditable Human-Agent Teams for Autonomous X-ray Experimentation
author: Gunik Luthra, Ronald J. Pandolfi, Benjamin T. Diroll, Ricky Ronquillo, Ruipeng Li, Christopher B. Murray, Marcus M. Noack, Kevin G. Yager, Esther H. R. Tsai
contentSnippet:
Authors: Gunik Luthra , Ronald J. Pandolfi , Benjamin T. Diroll , Ricky Ronquillo , Ruipeng Li , Christopher B. Murray , Marcus M. Noack , Kevin G. Yager , Esther H. R. Tsai

Abstract: Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic systems may lower this barrier, although sustained operation on physical instruments remains largely unexplored. Here, using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, we demonstrate autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under evolving, human-defined objectives. Complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts enable an audit that reconstructs decision provenance and characterizes the division of cognitive labor. Across three experiments, 61-67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, while the share of methodological and scientific contributions increased from 46% in the setup-focused first experiment to 56-61% in later experiments. Provenance showed that 59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants and that about half of all decisions incorporated the input of another participant. These results may guide design principles for multi-agent scientific systems and inform future agent harnesses, model training, and accessible autonomous experimentation.

summary.tldr:
Researchers led by Gunik Luthra and Marcus M. Noack have demonstrated a framework for autonomous synchrotron X-ray experimentation using agentic systems to study nanoparticle superlattices. By deploying coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, the team enabled closed-loop experimentation where agents operated under evolving, human-defined objectives. The study focuses on the auditability of these systems, capturing complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts to reconstruct decision provenance and analyze the division of cognitive labor during physical instrument operation.

Quantitative analysis of three distinct experiments revealed that 61-67% of all communication involved interpretation or judgment tasks. The researchers observed a shift in the nature of agent contributions: methodological and scientific inputs rose from 46% during the initial setup phase to 56-61% in subsequent experimental runs. The provenance data indicated that 59-68% of error corrections required multi-participant collaboration, and approximately 50% of all decisions were derived from the input of at least one other participant, highlighting the collaborative nature of these human-agent teams.
takeaways: **Experimental Focus:** Autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments conducted on nanoparticle superlattices.
**Communication Metrics:** 61-67% of agent-human/agent-agent messages were categorized as interpretation or judgment.
**Methodological Shift:** Scientific and methodological contributions increased from 46% in the first experiment to 56-61% in later stages.
**Collaborative Decision-Making:** 59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants, with roughly 50% of all decisions incorporating input from another participant.

title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
author: Rishikesh Mallagundla, Pranav Patel
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors that run at generation time have so far been trained to detect harmful content and are limited to two or three classes. We introduce TopicScope, a framework for training causal topic classifiers on SAE features that assign a topic to every token, so that the label can change partway through a response. We train three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics. Across Gemma-3 1B and 4B, monitors trained on features extracted from prefill hidden states were able to generalise to decoding. We also found that the classifiers are robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points when off-topic asides are inserted, topics are removed or sections are reordered. Ablations conducted to understand the contribution of the SAE revealed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without it were several times larger. Our findings show that compact topic monitors can be trained inexpensively in prefill and deployed during generation. More broadly, our work shows where SAEs are useful beyond safety classification. Our code, dataset and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mercity-AI/SAE-Guardrails and https://huggingface.co/collections/Mercity/online-guardrails-using-sparse-autoencoders-6ac602940468c62fefb2b9e8

summary.tldr:
Researchers at Mercity AI have introduced TopicScope, a framework for real-time, token-level topic monitoring in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Unlike traditional activation-based monitors typically restricted to binary or ternary safety classification, TopicScope enables dynamic topic labeling that can shift mid-response. The framework was validated on Gemma-3 1B and 4B models, demonstrating that classifiers trained on SAE features extracted from prefill hidden states successfully generalize to the decoding phase.

The methodology involves training three distinct detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic datasets spanning seven categories. The researchers found that these monitors maintain high robustness, with a maximum drop of 5 macro-F1 points when subjected to perturbations such as reordered sections, removed topics, or the insertion of off-topic asides. Ablation studies confirmed that SAE-based classifiers are significantly more compact than baseline models; classifiers achieving equivalent performance without SAE features were several times larger in parameter count. The project code, datasets, and model checkpoints are publicly available via GitHub and Hugging Face.
takeaways: **Model Compatibility:** Validated on Gemma-3 1B and 4B architectures using SAE features for token-level classification.
**Performance Robustness:** Classifiers retain performance under perturbations, losing no more than 5 macro-F1 points during topic reordering or aside insertion.
**Efficiency Gains:** SAE-based monitors are significantly smaller than non-SAE baselines, allowing for inexpensive training in prefill and deployment during generation.
**Scope:** Supports seven distinct topics with the ability to update labels dynamically as the model generates tokens.
**Resource Availability:** Code, datasets, and checkpoints are hosted on GitHub (Mercity-AI/SAE-Guardrails) and Hugging Face.

title: LandslideFM: A Foundation Model Towards Unified Landslide Perception and Understanding
author: Shanwen Wang, Sirui Wang, Xin Sun, Jungong Han
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model designed to integrate visual perception with contextual scene understanding for landslide detection. The model addresses the scarcity of labeled disaster data by employing a 'Source-Agreement Graduated Trust' semi-supervised learning framework, which utilizes both limited labeled datasets and large volumes of unlabeled imagery. By connecting visual landslide detection with a parameter-efficient fine-tuned Vision-Language Model (VLM), LandslideFM enables automated reasoning and interpretation of landslide events beyond simple pixel-level classification.

To facilitate standardized evaluation, the authors also released LandslideVL, a new benchmark dataset that pairs visual imagery with specialized textual prompts for landslide analysis. Experimental results indicate that LandslideFM outperforms general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning tasks. The project's source code and implementation details are publicly available at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** LandslideFM utilizes a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework to bridge visual perception and contextual interpretation.
**Benchmark Dataset:** The authors introduced LandslideVL, a new benchmark combining visual imagery and textual prompts specifically for landslide analysis.
**Technical Approach:** The system uses parameter-efficient fine-tuning to adapt a Vision-Language Model for landslide reasoning, guided by spatial predictions from the visual perception module.
**Performance:** LandslideFM demonstrates superior quantitative and qualitative performance compared to general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide scene analysis.
**Availability:** The project code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.

title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models
author: Chih-Hao Hsu, Feng-Chun B. Chou, Pin-Hao A. Chen
contentSnippet:
Authors: Chih-Hao Hsu , Feng-Chun B. Chou , Pin-Hao A. Chen

Abstract: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric structure? We address this question using a cross-persona paradigm across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B-14B, base and instruct). Given responses on one psychological scale from real individuals (N = 272 Taiwanese university students), models predict responses on six other scales. At the behavioral level, larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations; amplification persists after correcting the seven-scale human correlations for measurement attenuation. We then examine whether this structure is reflected internally. Contrastive direction analysis finds geometry aligned with the human matrix in larger instruct variants, but little alignment in base variants under this assay. Across models, geometry strength is associated with behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008; partial r = 0.69 controlling for log size). To relate internal structure to output behavior, a matched activation-probing paradigm shows that probe slopes vary less than behavioral slopes (1.38-1.77 vs 0.52-1.53). A synthetic control shows that ridge probing can inflate these slopes; after subtracting a baseline based on a reliability proxy from another analysis, adjusted slopes remain associated with behavior (r = 0.88). We term the measured probe-behavior gap readout attenuation. These results establish decodability and geometric alignment under the tested assays, without showing that the measured directions mediate the cross-persona answers.

Notes: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

summary.tldr:
In a study accepted at NeurIPS 2026, researchers Chih-Hao Hsu, Feng-Chun B. Chou, and Pin-Hao A. Chen investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) internally represent psychological constructs or merely mimic psychometric structures in their outputs. Using a cross-persona paradigm, the authors tested 14 model variants from the Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5 families (ranging from 0.5B to 14B parameters, including both base and instruct versions). By training models on responses from 272 Taiwanese university students across one psychological scale, the researchers evaluated the models' ability to predict responses on six additional scales. The study found that larger model variants not only reproduce but amplify human cross-scale correlations, even after correcting for measurement attenuation.

Technically, the authors utilized contrastive direction analysis to assess internal geometric alignment with human psychometric matrices. They discovered that larger instruct-tuned variants exhibit significant geometric alignment, whereas base models show minimal alignment under the same assay. A strong correlation (r = 0.68) exists between internal geometry strength and behavioral amplification. Using a matched activation-probing paradigm, the researchers identified a 'readout attenuation' gap, where probe slopes (1.38–1.77) differ from behavioral slopes (0.52–1.53). Even after adjusting for ridge probing inflation using a synthetic control, the internal structure remains significantly associated with behavioral output (r = 0.88), though the authors note that this does not definitively prove the measured directions mediate the models' cross-persona answers.
takeaways: **Model Scope:** Evaluated 14 variants across Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5 families, spanning 0.5B to 14B parameters.
**Behavioral Finding:** Larger model variants consistently amplify human cross-scale correlations observed in a cohort of 272 Taiwanese university students.

**Geometric Alignment:** Contrastive direction analysis revealed that internal geometric alignment with human psychometric matrices is present in larger instruct variants but largely absent in base models.

**Readout Attenuation:** Identified a discrepancy between internal probe slopes (1.38–1.77) and behavioral output slopes (0.52–1.53), suggesting a gap between internal representation and external expression.
**Statistical Correlation:** Found a strong partial correlation (r = 0.69, controlling for log size) between internal geometry strength and the amplification of human-like psychometric behavior.

title: Graph Visualizations in Prompts for Knowledge Graph Question Answering
author: Luiz do Valle Miranda, Andreas L. Opdahl, Grzegorz J. Nalepa
contentSnippet:
Authors: Luiz do Valle Miranda , Andreas L. Opdahl , Grzegorz J. Nalepa

Abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.

Notes: Accepted at AACL-IJCNLP conference

summary.tldr:
Researchers Luiz do Valle Miranda, Andreas L. Opdahl, and Grzegorz J. Nalepa evaluated the efficacy of multimodal prompting for Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) using six Vision-Language Models (VLMs). The study, accepted at the AACL-IJCNLP conference, utilized a dataset of 1,500 questions from the WebQSP and CWQ benchmarks to compare standard text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization. The findings indicate that incorporating graph images yields an average improvement of 1.85 F1 points, with the most significant gains observed in precision for low-complexity questions, where performance increased by 4.65 F1 points.

The research highlights that performance gains are not strictly correlated with model parameter scale but are highly sensitive to the visual encoding of the graph. Hierarchical layouts generated via Graphviz consistently outperformed less structured renderings. Furthermore, the study found that decomposing large subgraphs into distinct, separated paths significantly enhances model performance, whereas image-only prompting without textual context leads to sharp performance degradation. The authors advocate for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively apply structured diagrams to visually sparse subgraphs to balance accuracy with inference efficiency and token overhead.

**Complexity Impact:** Low-complexity questions saw the highest benefit, with a 4.65 F1 point increase in precision.
**Layout Sensitivity:** Hierarchical Graphviz layouts and path-decomposed subgraphs were identified as the most effective visual representations for VLM reasoning.
**Scaling Observations:** Multimodal performance gains were found to be largely independent of model size, suggesting visual design is a more critical factor than parameter count for this task.
**Optimization Strategy:** The authors recommend avoiding visual clutter on complex queries to minimize token overhead and maintain inference efficiency.

title: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments
author: Jayakody Kankanamalage Chamani Shiranthika
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning has achieved tremendous success in recent years. Extending its scope from the traditional complex games such as Atari, Go, Pokeman, and Chess, reinforcement learning has caught researchers' attention on modelling real-life scenarios. Personalized medicine and the dynamic treatment regimen are two such preliminary research fields; researchers are focusing their mindsets currently. Estimating the optimal dynamic treatment regimens from the observational real clinical data is being popularized among the researchers, widening its scope towards more advanced versions of reinforcement learning algorithms. This research is about a research study that focused on reinforcement learning techniques that have been approached in the context of cancer chemotherapy treatments. Primarily this thesis addresses the result of the study by means of the state-of-the-art on reinforcement learning techniques used in generating the optimal policy for sequential treatments, including the existing online reinforcement learning approaches. Thereby a simulation for cancer chemotherapy via traditional Q-learning would be presented. Secondly, the study will extend towards using offline reinforcement learning in the optimal policy generation. Thus, the proposed solution follows a data-driven approach, which works on the real human colon cancer clinical data. The novelty of the proposed solution resides in the implementation of an offline reinforcement learning approach by means of a model-based architecture using the conservative Q-learning and the model-based offline policy optimization algorithm. As per the experimental results and the evaluations, it was revealed that the proposed Chemo RL model caters well the problem of cancer chemotherapy treatment scheduling and serves as a supportive model for the junior oncologists in deciding their treatment decisions.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced 'Chemo RL,' a reinforcement learning framework designed to optimize sequential cancer chemotherapy treatment regimens. The study, documented in arXiv:2611.12940v1, transitions from traditional online Q-learning simulations to a more robust offline reinforcement learning approach. By leveraging real-world human colon cancer clinical data, the model aims to provide data-driven decision support for oncologists, specifically targeting the complex challenge of dynamic treatment scheduling.

The technical architecture of the Chemo RL model utilizes a model-based approach, incorporating Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) and Model-Based Offline Policy Optimization (MOPO). This methodology allows the system to derive optimal treatment policies from static, observational clinical datasets without requiring real-time interaction with patients. The study positions this framework as a supportive tool for junior oncologists, demonstrating that offline reinforcement learning can effectively navigate the constraints of clinical data to generate actionable treatment schedules.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** The Chemo RL framework utilizes a model-based architecture integrating Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) and Model-Based Offline Policy Optimization (MOPO).
**Data Source:** The model is trained and evaluated using real-world human colon cancer clinical data.
**Core Objective:** The system is designed to generate optimal sequential treatment policies for chemotherapy, serving as a decision-support tool for junior oncologists.
**Methodological Shift:** The research moves beyond traditional online Q-learning, which is often impractical for clinical settings, to an offline reinforcement learning paradigm.

title: AI Governance Should Prioritize Control and Knowledge Boundaries Over Limiting Intelligence
author: Hendrik Luuk
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomously acting AI agents makes the governance of agentic systems urgent. We propose the competence circuit, summarized as IKC + KC + C, that decomposes an agent's real-world impact into three pathways: intelligence-mediated discovery, procedural know-how, and direct control. Using the canonical fast-takeoff debate as a stress test, we formalize the conditions for intelligence-mediated fast takeoff as a conjunction jointly sufficient for fast catastrophic supremacy, showing that most rely on rapid knowledge acquisition or control attainment rather than intelligence alone. We operationalize epistemic intelligence as hypothesis-selection efficiency and validate this framework via stochastic simulation on NK fitness landscapes across six scenarios spanning the conjunctive chain. An analytic bound supported by the simulations shows that intelligence-driven speedup is capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels regardless of task difficulty. The simulations also expose a fast-takeoff dilemma: a large intelligence-driven speedup multiplier materializes only when the hypothesis space is noisy, but the absolute timescale remains constrained by the time required for capability-critical tests, so a large multiplier need not imply rapid progress. Simulations also indicate that institutional chokepoints disproportionately slow down superintelligent agents when mandatory authorization delays are large relative to the negligible time these agents spend on unproductive search. We argue that the dominant safety levers are restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries rather than limiting intelligence alone, and this applies to agentic systems at any capability level. Purely digital domains weaken these bottlenecks, strengthening the case for architectures that intentionally "put physics in the loop."

The authors utilize this framework to stress-test the 'fast-takeoff' hypothesis, arguing that catastrophic supremacy is primarily driven by rapid knowledge acquisition or control attainment rather than intelligence scaling alone. By operationalizing epistemic intelligence as hypothesis-selection efficiency and running stochastic simulations on NK fitness landscapes, the study demonstrates that intelligence-driven speedup is mathematically capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels, independent of task difficulty.

The simulations reveal a 'fast-takeoff dilemma' where large intelligence-driven speedup multipliers only emerge in noisy hypothesis spaces, yet absolute progress remains constrained by the time required for capability-critical testing. The findings suggest that institutional chokepoints, such as mandatory authorization delays, are disproportionately effective at slowing superintelligent agents because these agents spend negligible time on unproductive search. Consequently, the authors conclude that safety governance should prioritize restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries over limiting raw intelligence, particularly in digital domains where physical bottlenecks are absent, advocating for architectures that integrate 'physics in the loop' to maintain safety.

**Intelligence Bound:** An analytic bound derived from simulations shows intelligence-driven speedup is capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels, regardless of task complexity.
**Fast-Takeoff Dilemma:** Large speedup multipliers only occur in noisy hypothesis spaces, but absolute progress is limited by the time required for capability-critical testing.
**Governance Strategy:** Institutional authorization delays are highly effective against superintelligent agents because they target the small fraction of time agents spend on unproductive search.

title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation
author: Ismail Hossain Polas
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict from a labelled context in a single forward pass. A recent benchmark reported that they decisively outperform tree ensembles for customer churn, but it compared them with untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and scored only ranking metrics, while a retention campaign is judged in money. We re-evaluate TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast and TabICL v2 against Optuna-tuned GBDTs on five public telecom churn datasets over 10 seeded splits. We separate three questions: whether a model ranks churners well, whether that ranking earns more expected maximum profit (EMP), and whether its probabilities can drive a threshold policy. With a split-aware test and Holm correction over 20 pre-declared comparisons, TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more EMP than the best tuned GBDT on Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%), and these two gains also hold against each of the three tuned GBDTs separately. On Orange it is ahead in all 10 splits (14.3%), but the gain is not significant after correction (Holm p = 0.155). The splits resample the same datasets, so these results do not stand for independent operators. TabICL v2, the earlier benchmark's leader, beats the best tuned GBDT only on Iranian, not all three of them, and underpredicts Orange churn by 2.1 points on a 7.3% base rate. On the datasets and splits where we tested them, a substantially larger tuning budget and a duplicate-aware split leave the main conclusions unchanged. Retuning the baseline cuts the earlier headline gap from 6.1 to 4.0 PR-AUC points without closing it. The licence of the TabPFN-3.5 weights we used (License v1.0), not scoring cost, is what stands between its gains and production use.

title: SetPrint: Black-Box LLM Fingerprinting via Setwise Correspondence of Response Changes
author: Jinmo Han, Ju Yeon Kang, Jimin Hong, Sunghwan Ahn, Yonghyeon Jun, Nam Soo Kim
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Black-box LLM fingerprinting aims to determine whether a target model was derived from a source model when only the output responses to input queries are observable. One way to reveal this relationship is to perturb each query and observe the resulting responses of both models, yielding two corresponding sets of response variations. These sets provide two complementary sources of information: the relations among response changes within each set, and the correspondence of response changes between the two sets. Existing approaches, however, have not fully exploited both. We introduce \textbf{SetPrint}, a training-free method that jointly captures both within-set relations and between-set correspondence. SetPrint expresses each response change relative to the mean change of its own set, and then compares changes from the two models that were induced by the same perturbation. On LeaFBench, SetPrint consistently outperforms existing training-free black-box fingerprinting methods. Further analyses attribute these gains to both within-set relations and between-set correspondence.

title: Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs
author: Subhrangshu Nandi, Hitesh Arora, Yunfei Bai, Udita Patel, Chirag Shah, Hannah Kwon, Wei Zhang, Weian Chen, Chloe Ruoqi Li, Alberto Sconfienza, Ayush Goyal, Yasmine Lee, Ming Xiong, Prathap Ramachandra
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprises increasingly use large language model agents to execute standard operating procedures (SOPs): long, branching, tool-intensive workflows. Yet there is little controlled evidence for choosing among competing agentic architectures. Holding the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varying only the architecture, we compare four designs (a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm; eight arms) across 13 enterprise SOPs, and introduce a skill-definition quality rubric to build matched high and low-quality skill corpora. Three takeaways emerge. (1)~\textbf{There is no universal best architecture; the right choice is SOP-dependent.} On a given SOP, task success ranges from under $10\%$ on the hardest to near $100\%$ on the easiest; no architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and added structure only plausibly pays off on complex, branching SOPs (a directional, not yet significant, trend). (2)~\textbf{Added architecture cost must be justified by a task-success gain.} Every coordinated arm (multi-agent or skill-augmented) spends $1.4$--$4.7\times$ the tokens and $2.6$--$5.8\times$ the latency of the single agent for gains that are usually small and rarely significant, making the single agent the efficient default; high-quality skills do lift success (to $73.1\%$ from $67.4\%$) while degraded skills fall below it. (3)~\textbf{Implementation quality outweighs the single- versus multi-agent choice.} A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline ($75.6\%$ vs.\ $67.4\%$).

title: Physics2Weight: Direct Neural Network Architecture and Weight Generation from Physical Laws Using Large Language Models
author: Shogo Sato, Tomoyasu Shimada, Kazuhiko Murasaki, Takashi Sano
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled weight-space programming (WSP), which directly generates neural network weights without gradient-based optimization. However, extending WSP to physical problems remains challenging, particularly in achieving both solution accuracy and physical consistency. In this paper, we propose Physics2Weight (PtW), a framework that extends WSP to solving partial differential equations by directly generating neural network weights and editing architectures based on governing equations and initial and boundary conditions. PtW introduces physics-constrained prompting and physics-guided architecture editing, combined with iterative weight refinement from WSP, to improve solution accuracy and physical consistency without gradient-based optimization. Experiments on four PDEs, namely the heat, advection, Burgers', and Allen--Cahn equations, demonstrate lower solution errors than conventional physics-informed neural networks, while revealing limitations in satisfying the governing equations for nonlinear PDEs.

title: Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable
author: Yihang Che, Zhongwei Yu, Yang Li, Xingyu Lu, Hongxia Yu, Jun Wang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.

title: Monitoring One Channel Is Not Communication Control: Causal Evidence for Adaptive Reallocation of Joint Message--Route Codes
author: Liu Hung Ming (PARRAWA AI, cyril.liu@gmail.com, equal contribution), Tian Xia (PAII, TianXia0209@gmail.com, equal contribution)
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monitoring a visible channel can change how learned agents communicate without removing why communication is useful. We test this distinction in an end-to-end game where a sender and receiver learn a discrete protocol and route policy without communication supervision. In two independent 20-seed batches, 20/20 and 19/20 protocols form. Online partial coverage increases shadow-route share over no monitoring by .701 [.574,.826] and .575 [.412,.737], while task accuracy remains .905/.913 and signed frozen message contribution remains .592/.563. Complete coverage removes most selective migration without removing communication. Frozen interventions, including a fresh pre-outcome confirmation, show that route is semantic: joint message--route shuffling changes .668 of receiver predictions and route alone retains .388 accuracy versus .25 chance. A corrected explicit-silence cost makes 18/20 policies fully silent and lowers mean sending to .050, but its strict complete-suppression gate fails because two seeds retain communication. Failed semantic-evasion and operational gates further bound the result. The evidence supports adaptive reallocation of a joint message--route code under partial monitoring, not open-world route discovery, emergent encryption, or a universal defense.

title: IIT Patna at "ICPR 2026 TVRID Competition on Privacy-Preserving Person Re-Identification from Top-View RGB-Depth Camera"
author: Abhinav Kumar, Swagatam Pati, Advait Deshmukh, Aditya Mehrotra, Bibek Das, Kumari Priya, Utsav Kumar Nareti, Saba Akram, Chandranath Adak
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy-aware person re-identification (Re-ID) from top-view cameras replaces frontal appearance with anthropometric shape, while depth sensing further reduces color-based identity cues. The ICPR 2026 TVRID competition evaluates this setting using 86 identities captured by four synchronized Intel RealSense D455 cameras with RGB and Depth streams across flat, ascent, descent, and oblique viewpoints. Performance is measured using mAP and CMC@1 across within-camera in/out, ascent-descent, and flat-oblique scenarios. The competition had 147 registered participants and 33 final submissions. Three teams from IIT Patna participated: 'abhinavkumar03' and 'sjkdgfhl_' ranked 5th and 7th among 31 ranked participants, and 'vivek katuri' reached 77.67% CMC@1 / 85.20% mAP on the RGB track. This paper presents the methods of the two top-10 teams. Methodology 1 (abhinavkumar03) achieves 93.51% mAP and 90.42% CMC@1 on Depth, ranking 4th of 28, while Methodology 2 (sjkdgfhl_) reaches 99.63%/99.35% on RGB and 86.26%/80.34% on Depth. Both substantially outperform the 57.19% track-average Depth mAP, with Methodology 1 yielding a 7.3-point gain over Methodology 2. These results demonstrate the importance of depth representation and supervision for privacy-preserving Re-ID.

title: RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients
author: Shuaijun Chen, Omid Tavallaie, Xin Chen, Wentao Gao, Nguyen Tran, Albert Y. Zomaya
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.

title: BuySideFlow: A Point-in-Time Benchmark for LLM Agents in Investment Research
author: Dong Bo, Fanjin Zhang, Ke Cheng, Xinxin Zhao, Xiaowei Su, Yang Wang, Jinghang Xu, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, Jing Zhang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate SQL and SQL--Python workflows for investment research, but ensuring point-in-time (PIT) validity remains challenging. Agents must enforce disclosure cutoffs and select the appropriate historical states and record versions throughout data retrieval and financial analysis. We introduce \textsc{BuySideFlow}, a benchmark of 408 practitioner-derived Chinese-language tasks spanning equities, funds, fixed income, and macroeconomics over a fixed snapshot from a licensed production financial database. We provide executable references and a taxonomy of temporal errors, pairing result checks with expert audits of executed workflows. We evaluate nine agent configurations on all tasks, with result accuracy ranging from 16.2\% to 36.8\%. An audit of 900 runs on 100 shared tasks confirms PIT violations in 193 of the 380 runs that pass result checks (50.8\%), showing that output agreement alone does not establish temporal validity.

An audit of 900 runs on 100 shared tasks confirms PIT violations in 193 of the 380 runs that pass result checks (50.8\%), showing that output agreement alone does not establish temporal validity.

title: TrustMod-SM: A Multi-Axis Benchmark for Evaluating Trustworthiness of LLMs in Social Media Content Moderation
author: Aizan Zafar, Sreekantam Sai Venkata, Gathik Jindal, Ritu Raj Sharma, Zishan Ahmad, Tulika Saha, Srinath Srinivasa
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential for social media content moderation, but their trustworthiness beyond overall accuracy remains underexplored. We introduce TrustMod-SM, a benchmark of roughly 29,000 instances across eight datasets, to evaluate LLM moderators on five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity. Evaluating 16 open-weight models (0.5B-284B parameters, spanning text-only and vision-language architectures) and one closed frontier model, we find persistent trustworthiness gaps. Higher detection accuracy often coincides with greater demographic disparity, and models frequently comply with concealment or exaggeration prompts, assign high confidence to wrong predictions, rarely escalate ambiguous cases, and struggle to separate hate speech from counter-speech or reclaimed language (especially below 8B parameters). Scaling does not uniformly resolve these issues, and no single model excels across all five dimensions.

title: ZeroPoint: Lightweight Energy-Based Decision Model
author: Javier Mar\'in
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) assign a scalar energy to every joint value of the observed and predicted variables. In decision models, the prediction is chosen from a finite list of options provided with each input. Inference then reduces to comparing the energies of the options, and training lowers the energy of the correct option relative to the others. A complete decision must also account for the possibility that no option is acceptable. However, the energies learned by a standard EBM define only relative compatibility: adding the same input-dependent quantity to all energies leaves the predictions, the Gibbs distribution, and the usual training losses unchanged. The model therefore has no learned reference level against which to decide whether any option fits. We propose ZeroPoint, an EBM that makes the empty answer a state of the model with energy zero for every input. This fixed state provides an explicit reference for the energies of all listed options, whose non-negative depths measure their compatibility with the input relative to the empty answer. The options and the empty answer share one distribution, in which an option at zero depth receives no probability. The decision to select an option or to abstain is thus part of ordinary inference, trained with the negative log-likelihood loss, rather than a separate rejection rule. The energy function is a small multilingual encoder that reads the input together with all the options and is invariant to their order. Ablations show that most of the benefit comes from training with examples in which no option fits. With the same encoder and data, the fixed zero separates inputs with and without an acceptable option slightly better than a learned rejection class and clearly better than a thresholded softmax, while leaving the choice among options unchanged.

title: Seeing Is Not Believing: Counterfactual Lesion Erasure Teaches a Small Medical Vision-Language Agent to Report Only What the Image Shows
author: Bhaskar Gurram
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) often report a finding because the question names it; standard benchmarks miss this. From public segmentation datasets we build counterfactual views without manual annotation: the lesion erased by inpainting, a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and unedited lesion-free images. The evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) is the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit; it is zero for a model that ignores the image or reacts to both edits alike. MedScope-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, LoRA, image tools) was trained on label-derived trajectories, selected by a pre-registered rule and tested once against nine frontier and six open VLMs; four pre-registered checks then probed the mechanism. On 507 internal cases across five imaging types, MedScope-4B reached ESG 0.758 and claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases, against 0.27-0.47 and 41-62% for the frontier models (all p<0.001), without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. Without counterfactual views ESG fell to 0.279+-0.107 (three seeds); the effect replicated on MedGemma 1.5 4B and two unseen inpainting tools. At four external centres the advantage held but frontier models detected more real lesions; on a fresh external test MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films, with net utility below gemini-4-argon's (-0.36 [-0.50, -0.23]). Matching the control edit was not shown to matter; over three seeds no fresh-external ESG advantage over removal-based DPO was established; a paired-view consistency objective did not beat a matched-compute control, while that continuation alone cut erased-lesion claims on unseen tools at every seed, at a cost in sensitivity at one. Training on erased and edited images gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models; it does not improve perception, and rare critical findings need coverage.

title: From Relevant Posts to Attributable Spans: Explicit Symptom Evidence for Depression Questionnaire Inference
author: Sumanth Manduru, Carlotta Domeniconi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Longitudinal social-media histories offer an opportunity to assess depression, potentially supporting the inference of standardized depression questionnaire responses. However, this task requires evidence that is semantically relevant to a symptom and attributable to the user, while being sufficiently specific to support an individual questionnaire item. Existing approaches rely on semantic similarity to retrieve posts, which can introduce misleading or non-attributable evidence, particularly in multi-symptom posts and discussions of others' experiences. We propose SREE (Symptom Retrieval and Evidence-Grounded InfErence), an evidence-grounded pipeline that extracts first-person and symptom-specific text spans, selects a representative subset using a Facility Location-inspired objective, and performs Evidence-Gated Inference over the selected evidence. We evaluate evidence retrieval on BDI-Sen and evidence-conditioned questionnaire inference on eRisk 2019-2021. Compared with state-of-the-art retrieval approaches, SREE achieves relative improvements of 70% in post-level precision and 59% in F1, while retaining at least 30% fewer posts. On multi-symptom sentences, it also outperforms dense retrieval in precision and F1 even with twice the retrieval budget. Across all three eRisk collections, SREE achieves the highest exact item-level agreement while remaining competitive on ordinal and aggregate metrics. These results highlight the importance of localizing attributable evidence and controlling its composition before inferring depression questionnaire responses.

title: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding
author: Zhongxing Xu, Zhonghua Wang, Zhe Qian, Shiyan Su, Ming Hu, Xiaocheng Zou, Wei Feng, Mingquan Lin, Yuyin Zhou, Yifan Peng, Hamid Rezatofighi, Zongyuan Ge
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

title: TimeOmni-o1: Bidirectionally Coupling Time Series Foundation Models and LLMs for Multimodal Reasoning and Forecasting
author: Ziyang Zhang, Shenyi Li, Wen Wu, Chao Zhang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time series from real-world systems are often accompanied by text, such as a report on an event that affects them. Two common tasks on these series are understanding, e.g., answering questions about a series, and forecasting its future values. Both tasks require reasoning over the series and the text together. Moreover, understanding outputs text while forecasting outputs a time series, so serving both requires a model that reads and generates both modalities. Large language models (LLMs) read time series as digit tokens and handle long series poorly. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast well from large-scale pretraining but typically neither read nor generate text. Time series language models add a time series modality to the LLM but forecast on the LLM side, leaving the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability unused. We present TimeOmni-o1, which couples a pretrained TSFM and an LLM bidirectionally. In one direction, the TSFM encodes the series in compressed form for the LLM, which reasons over it together with the text. In the other, the LLM's reasoning is fed back into the TSFM, which produces the forecast conditioned on it. One model architecture thus reads and generates both series and text, reasons in text, and draws on the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability. To train it, we build MMTR, a multimodal time series reasoning dataset with annotated reasoning traces, covering both tasks across 12 domains with 500k+ samples. On MMTR, TimeOmni-o1 outperforms existing models on both understanding and forecasting across most domains, as well as the LLM and the TSFM inside it when used individually. The gains carry over to three open benchmarks, where it outperforms the dedicated time series models.

title: SELD: Detecting Silent Evidence Loss in Context Compression beyond the Answer
author: Wentao Lei, Li Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer. Existing checks compare the reader model's answer or its most likely words, and thus miss a frequent failure, silent evidence loss: key evidence is removed while the answer stays the same, leaving the answer unsupported and risky for other models that reuse the context. To address this challenge, we propose SELD (Silent Evidence Loss Detector), which needs no training and no labels. Its principle is that when evidence is lost, a reader model's preferences among the answers it leaves unsaid shift even if its answer does not, so comparing these preferences before and after compression reveals losses that answer checks cannot see. We also build SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of length-matched evidence and control deletions from three question-answering datasets. Quantitative and qualitative experiments with five reader models on it show that SELD consistently outperforms strong and recent baselines across compressors, compression rates and models, identifying the evidence-removing edit in 83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline. These results show that evidence loss in compressed contexts can be detected even when the answer is unchanged.

title: Actionable Feedback: Improving Model Capabilities from User Edit Data on Clinical Documentation
author: Daniel P. Jeong, Yewon Byun, John Giorgi, Peng Xu, Zachary C. Lipton, Michael Oberst
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in clinical documentation workflows, where clinicians review and edit their outputs before use. In principle, these clinician edits represent a scalable source of supervision for model training. In practice, not all edits represent actionable feedback: for instance, on data drawn from real-world deployment of an AI clinical documentation product, our review suggests that over 45% of edited outputs contain user-added information that is not directly supported by the inputs to the model. Naively fine-tuning on such edits risks teaching the model to hallucinate. In this paper, we develop a method to address this challenge. Given that real clinician edits on deployed documentation tools are not publicly available, we first develop a taxonomy of clinician-editing behaviors, informed by data from a deployed AI clinical documentation product. Then, we develop a method for generating semi-synthetic clinician-edit data, informed by our taxonomy, on a discharge-summary generation task based on MIMIC-III, a public dataset. Finally, we introduce simple filtering methods for identifying actionable edits, with accuracy evaluated by expert review. We show empirically, on our semi-synthetic dataset, that naive fine-tuning on raw edited output increases ungrounded content, while our approach of progressively filtering toward grounded edits enables improvement on clinician-alignment metrics while retaining faithfulness to the input context.

title: Brasilidade: Measuring Brazilian Identity for Large Language Models
author: Jos\'e Roberto Homeli da Silva, Felipe Jorge do Nascimento, Lucas Coutinho Freitas, William Alberto Cruz Casta\~neda, Marcellus Amadeus
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a new benchmark that aims to address the limitations of current methods for evaluating LLMs in Brazilian Portuguese. We introduced Brasilidade, an assessment methodology comprised of standardized tasks distributed across four different domains, and we are making available the tasks from its first domain, which address nuances of the language, grammar, and variations of Brazilian Portuguese. The results show that model size, by itself, does not determine performance; several medium-sized models outperformed larger models in the protocols evaluated. Specific models for Portuguese, in general, did not perform above average, despite their targeted training. Different task levels revealed significant nuances: while some tasks proved easy for most models, others posed extreme challenges, and some yielded mixed results, with wide variations in performance. This clearly illustrates the need for benchmarks that address the limitations of the models in Brazilian Portuguese, allowing future training cycles to seek to overcome them. Project repository https://github.com/soberania-oficial/brasilidade
